div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISMICT CRICKET LEAGUE. The Champions. As we announced last week, the championship of the above League has been won by the Sankey Club. Formed several years ago by a number of enthusiastic juniors, the form of the members has steadily improved and the team may now be regarded as one of the strongest in the district. For two successive years the Junior Championship was won, but the abilities of the players were still to be shown in a snore marked degree. Making a successful application for membership of the Warrington and District League, the club, although practically a junior organisation, gave the Warrington Conservatives a rare fright in the race for honours. This year, however, they have gone one better by wresting the championship from last year's winners, having defeated them on two occasions during the past season. Only two games were lost, and the team have thus every reason to be proud of their record. Financially, the club is very strong, but a more successful season is anticipated nest year. and intend- ing members should make an early application for particulars regarding rules, &c., to the secretary, Mr. Daintith, Hood-lane, Sankey.

div.head: TO-DAY'S COUNTY MATCH.
div.p: TO-DAY'S COUNTY MATCH.

Last season Cumberland proved much the strongest of the county sides and deservedly won the champion- ship, and it will be interesting to see what sort of a show the County Palatine thirteen, composed of Lancashire born men, makes, for this is the first occasion on which none but purely native players have been selected. The teams are as follows : Cumberland.—G Davidson (Aspatria) ;W F Kitchen lom), J Morgan (Millom), G Hall (Egremont and 'Bradford), Treloar (MIllom) ; Price (MIllom) and J Lomas (Oldham); J Ferguson (Oldham and Brooklands) (captain), W Ward (Leeds and Egremont), W Winskill (Broughton Rangers and Penrith), J Clampitt and It Clampitt (Broughton Rangers and .Millom), and Clark (Huddersfield and Brooklands). Lancashire.—J Sharrocks (Wigan) ; T Johnson (Leigh), W Harris (Broughton), II Taylor (Widnes), J Flannagan (St Helens) • F Gleave (Wigan), H Gautey (Leeds); A Lee (Leigh), R Ramsdale and T Winstanley (Wigan),J Prescott (St Helens),W Longworth (Oldham), and R Parr (Barrow).

There was a margin of twenty-one points between the sides last season, when Cumberland won at War- rington by 28 points to seven, and whilst the home county seem to have the stronger side for to-morrow's encounter, the campaign is so young that there is no telling what may happen. As the match is in Cumberland, however, everything seems against Lancashire winning, but they should make a very good fight of it.

div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.

LATCHFORD. The First Eleven opened with a win of 7-0 versus Sale" A "at Sale last Saturday. The first half as evenly fought. Banks with a stinging shot scored for the visitors after 20 minutes and then Sale made great efforts to equalise, but the defence against them was sound. Pearson increased the lead with a clever little shot near half-time. The pace of the first half and the warm weather were apparently too much for the home team, who were kept defending a good portion of the second half, and Latchford got through five times. The Sale forwards could not get going at all. Knight and Fletcher were in great form among the Latchford backs, and Banks, Pearson and Dale were the best for- wards. The goals were scored by Pearson (4), Sanas (2), Travis (1). The Second Eleven met with a big defeat at the hands of Ashley First by 10-1. This is somewhat of a " startler" to commence with, but there is no cause for alarm, because whereas the Ashley Club had been rein- forced by some of the disbanded Altrincham Club players, Latchford were only able to put a weak side out owing to several of the regular players being away on holiday, &c. All credit is due to Ashley, however, for playing so well and Saturday's victory will atone for several thrashings they have in the past received from Latchford and which they have taken as real good sportsmen without grumbling. Every dog has his day. The First Eleven v Winnington to•ciay is :—E Wright, goal; W Fletcher. H Lees, backs ; W Isherwood, J B Wilkinson, A Knight, halves ; ft A Dale, J Pearson, D Travis, E Banks, A Starkey, forwards. Bully-off

div.head: NOTES BY " MUST."
div.p: NOTES BY " MUST."

After Salford the deluge! The Wirepullers never anticipated being thrashed at home, 15 points to 2, by the same team that they beat last April by 31 points to none. The Reds had never Vilal at Wilderspooi since 1905, when James Lomas was a power in their ranks, but they had their chance on Saturday and took it with both hands. Warrington were well beaten by a better team.

And yet they had their chance of winning. At threequarter time Salford were only leading by 5 points to 2, when the Warrington backs got away with the ball. Brookes had broken through the Salford defence and passed to Rushton ; the latter had Mclntyre and Clare on his left, with not a Salford man between him and the goal-line. A try behind the posts seemed a certainty when Brookes called for a re-pass on the inside, which was given with fatal results. Had Rushton passed out to the wing as he should have done, War- rington would certainly have got the lead, and I believe they were capable of keeping it. When this chance was missed, all the fire seemed to go out of the forwards, who had played a splendid game, and Salford forged ahead. As Warrington deteriorated, the Reds improved, and when the final came they were in possession of the handsome lead of 15 points to 2. -- Warrington had so few chances of scoring that to miss the one referred to was calamitous. There was practically no combination among the backs, and the fault again lay with the half backs. Rushton played a better game than in any previous match, but Brookes was a failure as the connecting link with the threequarters. He worked tremendously hard, but he was dead out of form, and that is the long and short of it. Renwick got a bad knock early in the game and never recovered his full vigour, while Mclntyre was obviously slow and out of condition. He will need to do some hard training if he means to retain his place.

Jolley was hard Dressed on Saturdv, but he played a fine game, with the one exception of an error of judgment which he has been guilty of before. On Saturday it cost his side five poihts. I refer to the young full-back's fondness for following up a long kick and leaving his half of the field unguarded. It is all right trying to get under a short or high kick, but nothing else should tempt the full back out of his place unless he has possession of the ball.

-- Salford were strong whet e Warrington were weak. May and John played a fine game at half back. in fact the little Welshman seemed to be playing the whole Warrington team in the last :.1() minutes. He made innumerable openings and enhanced the value of a moderate threequarter line by fifty per cent. His play was an object lesson on the value of half-backs to a team. The best back in the third line was Meeley, who ran speedily and well deserved the two tries which he got on the left wing. Though bigger forwards, the Reds were never ahead of the Warring- ton front rank until the closing stages of the game, when Warrington seemed to give up the ghost.

The defeat of Oldham at Leeds, of St. Helens at home by Hunslet, and of Hull at home by Batley should be an encouragement to Warrington. Several of the teams of " local " players are coming to the front, and it is not always the expensive sides gathered from all quarters of the globe which secure the points. Hunslet and Batley and Dewsbury are teams almost wholly composed of players from their own immediate districts.

It is to be hoped that Warrington touched rock- bottom on Saturday. They are nearly at the, bottom of the league and they have got the worst points record in the whole competition. Still only one try to the credit of the team in four league games ! When is the next one coming? Well, I am a bit hopeful about to-day if not exactly confident.

The Committee have taken the bull by the horns and made drastic changes in the team to visit Runcorn. Experiments were absolutely essential, and though there seems to be a prejudice in Warrington against changing players from one position to another, the Committee seem to have realised that necessity knows no law. As a result we are to see Brookes on the wing, Renwick at outside half, and Tranter in the centre. Now these are drastic changes but they are justified, and they may come off. I have long thought that Tranter was worthy of a trial among the backs. He has strength, pace and ideas, and if he will make a point of preferring running and passing to punting he may develop surprisingly as a centre. Wing was the inly place for Brookes, if he had to be retained:at all and I am averse to seeing him dropped without a trial in a position where he was once a big success.

The selected team is: Jolley,lifil back ; Maclntyre, Dickenson, Tranter and Brookes, threequarters ; Rushton and Renwick, half-backs ; Thomas, Cheaters, Skelhorn, rearnley, Bevan, and Critchley, forwards.

Twist would have kept his place, but it was not thought advisable to play him alongside Tranter, and thus have two inexperienced threequarters together. The Widnes lad has done well so far and only needs to persevere.

The" A" team will be : Brown,full back; Davies, Hudson (Elindley), Moore, and Twist, threequarters ; Douglas and Warren, half-backs : Naylor, Gibbs, Cooper, Bramwood, Valentine and Fletcher, forwards. Young Warren dodged so cleverly at Salford that he is to have a trial at half back, where there will be more scope for his trickiness.

I am sorry to say that Buckley, of Normanton, has been transferred to Wakefield Trinity. Warrington made an error of judgment when they did not sign this promising youngster when he was down here on trial before the commencement of the season.

div.head: FATAL SCRATCH.
div.p: A FATAL SCRATCH.

Mr Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest into the death of Robert Jones (52), of 64, Church-street, at Widnes on Tuesday. Jones was a powder packer at Pilkington's works. While removing a cask he fell dowrt and scratched his left arm, The injuries were then apparently so trifling that he continued work no to the 18th, when he became ill, and was taken home in a cab. He died on Saturday morning. Dr Hutchinson said that when he was called to see Jones on the 18th there was evidence of blood-poisoning. He noticed the abrasion on the left arm, and that was the seat of the trouble. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

LOCAL RIVALS AT WIDNES. Runcorn visited Widnes on Saturday, the match being played before 5,000 spectators. In the first half the game was very uninteresting, the combination of both sides being wretched, and many chances Were missed. Early on J O'Garra received the ball from Noon close in, and scored, Taylor failing at the place. At half- time the score read—Widnes 1 try (3 points), Runcorn nil. The game improved in the second half. Lally took a drop at goal, but the ball went wide, and Swinton da,hing up, scored. Just before the fljaish Widnes attacked strongly, and H O'Garra got over, Jones placing the goal. Result :—Widnes 2 goals 3 tries (13 points), Runcorn nil. Teams and officials : Widnes—Jones, back; Laws, Lally, Taylor. and Swinton, three-quarter backs ; Noon and J O'Garra, half backs ; G Aspey, S Aspey, Lloyd, Higgins, Reid and II O'Garra, forwards. Runcorn—SLaw, back ; Hughes, Moores, Moran, and Cawley, three-quarter backs; Lewis and Steele, half- backs ; Richardson, Peacock, Inman, Stevenson, Prince, and Massey, forwards. Refree, R H Jackson, St Helens. Touch judges, E Longden, Swinton, and H Ball, Wigan.

div.head: COMBINATION.
div.p: THE COMBINATION.

WARRINGTON "A's," SMART WIN-.-L-There was a gate of 2,000 to welcome Warrington "A "at Weaste, and in the first half they had the advantage of a strong breeze. Salford played up strongly, hoe ever, and the Warrington men failing to combine were beaten back. Hampson kicked a goal for the Reds and before the interval Radcliffe added a try, which was converted by Hampson. Salford thus led at half-time by 7 points to nil. Warrington seemed to have little chance against the wind, but the men changed their tactics and some good passing soon altered the aspect of affairs. Povey raced over with the first try, and then Warren got a second after a remarkable piece of dodging. Keeping up the attack and playing fine football Warrington got a third try by Cooper after Warren had again made good headway, and a handsome win was recorded by 3 tries (9 points), to Salford, 2 goals, I try (7 points).

Warrington's Failure at Home. Hope ran high in the breasts of the Wirepullers that Warrington would gain their first victory on Saturday, when Salford visited the Wilderspool ground. The Reds have usually failed at Warrington, and last season were beaten here by over 30 points, but they showed vastly different form on Saturday, and at the end bad thoroughly outplayed the home team. There was age], a fine crowd of 5,000 spectators, and disappointment at the poor display of the home contingent was keen. A beautiful day favoured the game, which was alwass fist and interesting. Teams: Warrington.—Jolley, back; Twist, Mclntyre, Renwick and Clare, three-quarter backs; Brookes and Rushton, half backs; Thomas, Chesters, Fearnley, Treater, Skelhorne and Critchley, forwards. Salford.—Launce, back; Callender, Wild, Loveluck and Mesley, three-quarter backs; John and May, half hacks; 'Thomas, Thom, Rees, Currie, Bevan and Goldsmith, forwards. Referee, W McCutcheon, Oldham. Touch judges, W Gregory, Runcorn and E Williams, Widnes. The game opened with Warrington in an aggressive mood, and fine work by the forwards forced Salford to fall back. A promising round of passing broke down at Renwick when Twist seemed well-placed for a try and the visitors immediately rushed the ball to the other end. Loveluck puutea across and Clare had to run well and dive on the ball to save the situation. Wairington again showed mastery in the pack and Rushton beating May at half way gave Brooks a good pass. The half back broke through and served Renwick who made a gallant dash for the posts, but was heavily grassed near the line. The shock made him practically a passenger for the rest of the game. Salford attempted to clear, but a weak punt fell into Renwick's hands and a mark gave Jolley the chance to kick a neat goal and open the scoring. The Reds were now more aggressive and smart work by the backs nearly penetrated the home defence, Jolley tackling Calendar in flue style. Mesley tried a penalty shot at goal which just passed outside. A few minutes later, however, he was more fortunate andiplaced the teams on level terms with a good shot. The Warrington forwards again raided the Salford quarter in dashing style, but poor passing enabled May to intercept and run clear away. A try seemed certain but Twist followed up well and overhauled his man a yard from the goal. Warrington were now having an anxious time and before they could clear John got the ball away smartly and a neat round of passing gave Mesley a clever try at the corns... Twist made another good effort near the interval, but the sides changed ends with Salford leading by 5 points to 2 points. On resuming, ill-luck seemed to pursne the locals, for Cheaters was absent injured during the first quarter. Salford were very energetic, but incurred several penalties in their eagerness to score. Then came War- rington's chance. Rushton and Brooks got well away, when the former threw inside again to Brooks, and the half back was overwhelmed near the line. A pass to the wing and Warrington would probably have taken the the lead. From this point the home forwards seemed to tire, and Salford improved corres- pondingly. John increased the score with a clever dropped goal, Emil then made a fine opening for Mesley, who raced round the poets, John adding the goal. The locals were now well beaten and a futile clearing kick was charged down, Wild scoring a third and doubtful try, from which there was no goal. Final :—Salford, 3 goals, 3 tries (15 points) ; Warring- ton, 1 goal (2 points).

ST. HELENS SWAMPED AT HOME. The visit of Hunslet attracted a crowd of 9,000 to the Rt. Helens ground. Early on St. Helens forced matters, and from a dash to the Hunslet line Place cntwitted Prescott, and saved a certain score. Kicking excaringes took place between furtill and Place, the latter just missing dropping a goal. Molyneaux and Browning made a great effort to open the home score, but Farrar tackled effectively, and W BAtten dashed for the line, but Flanaghan kicked away from him. After loose play at centre, Jukes broke away, and after a neat run, handed to Toft, who raced away at the corner. W Batten] improved from the touch line. Resuming, the whole of the Hunslet backs handled, and Jenkinson scored a great try, which was acknowledged by the home supporters. Batten again distinguished himself by kicking a fine goal. Half-time score :—lfunslet, 10 points ; St. Helens, nil. Resuming, Hunslet attacked through Jenkinson, who slipped between Turtill and Flanagan, but ha was over- taken by the Colonial a yard or two from the line. Wyburn, a Hunslet forward, broke his thumb, and retired, and following this W Batten made an opening for Farrar,iwho crossed. Batten failed with the goal kick. Hunslet opened the game out, and Toft gsve to W Batten, who raced over under the posts, for Farrar to improve. Hunslet continued to be aggressive,and Jukes I crossed, Farrar goaling. Near the close St. Helens rallied, and Butterworth scored an unimproved try, and Trenwith dropped a goal in the last minute of the game Result:—Hunslet, 4 goals 5 tries (23 points); St Helens, 1 goal I try (5 points). Teams and officials : St Helens—Turtill, back ; Flanagan, Browning, Greenwood and Belshaw, three-quarter backs ; Moly- newt and Trenwith, half-backs ; Prescott, Mavitty, Butterfield, Waddell, Heaton and ShallcroEs, forwards. Hunslet—Place, back ; W Batten, Farrar, J Batten, and Jenkinson, three-quarter backs : Smith and Toft, half-backs ; Wilson, Jukes, Smalls, Banks, Fowler, and Wyburn, forwards.

NORTH CHESHIRE LEAGUE. BOWDON VALE V. ALTRINCHAM LADS. At Vicarage-lane, Bowdon, the game ending In a draw of one goal each. BARNTON VILLA V. BROADHEATII. At Barnton. Final Barnton Villa, six goals ; Broadheath, one goal. LOSTOCK GRALAM V. LATCHFORD. Lostock Gralam three goals ; Latchford one goal. SECOND DIVISION. DECIDING TIE FOR CHAMPIONSHIP 1911-12. SANKEY V. LATCHFORD RECREATION. These two teams met on Saturday on the ground of the Latchford Club at Thelwall-lane to decide the destination of the championship for last season. After fifteen minutes' play the " Recs " managed to find the net, but off-side nullified the point. When hard pressed Broadhurst conceded a corner which proved futile. When well placed, Hawthorn (Sankey) put high over the bar. For the remainder of the first half the game was well fought out, but both goals remained intact. Half-time: No score. Resuming, play was again brisk. After a nice run by Dutton and Whitfield, J Ditchfleld was given possession and taking deliberate aim, easily beat Welsby with a ' fast, low drive. Aroused by this reverse, Sankey pressed severely, and only some grand defensive work by H Ditchfield and Davies prevented them equalizing. A few minutes off time, Sankey, for a palpable use of hands, were awarded a penalty ; the shot struck the upright and rebounded into play, one of the defenders clearing very luckily, Time was called with the Recrea- tion somewhat lucky winners by a goal to nil. PADGATE AMATEURS V. STOCKTON HEATH. At Potter's Farm, Padgate. At the end of 20 minutes' play, Garnett opened the score for Padgate. Half- time :—Padgate Amateurs, one goal ; Stocaton Heath, nil. Stockton Heath neat netted, but off-side was ruled. Shortly after Sankey increased Padgate's lead, only for Harry Sankey (Stockton Heath) to reduce it with the aid of a penalty. From now the game ruled in favour of Padgate, who outplayed their opponents, Lagar settling the issue by scoring a third point for his side. Final :—Padgate Amateurs, three goals; Stockton Heath, one goal. LATCHFORD BRITANNIA v. WEAVER REFINING CO. At Latchford. Taking the game all through the Weaver Refining Co., deserved their victory of a goal to nil. Bean being the scorer. For the winners Wilkinson (half-backs), and Evans (centre-forward) were the pick, whilst for the Britannia, Barnes (full- back) and Howlett and Hughes (forwards) were the best.

FRIENDLY MATCH.

DITTOS ST. MARY'S v. WARRINGTON EXCELSIOR. Played on the ground of the former. The home team were the first to press, and following a pretty piece of combination the right wing forced a fruitless corner, Fairly even play in mid-field followed, half-time being reached goalless. Resuming, the visitors' play was more brisk, Ashton soon opening the score. Shortly afterwards the home forwards got away and Melia, centre equalised. End to end play was witnessed for about 15 minutes, when a centre from the right wing was made secure by the inside left giving them the lead and victory. Result : Ditton St Mary's, 2 goals ; Warrington Excelsior, 1 goal.

The result WEIS a win for the Warrington staff on the totals for doubles and singles. After the game a good tea was provided by the landlord. THE WHISKER REVIVAL.

(According to the latest rumours, whiskers and beards are again to come into fashion. As they may he ad political celebrities, our cartoonist suggests a few styles which might be cultivated by the geutlethen de- destroying all traces of their identity.)
The Examiner, Saturday, September 28, 1912.

ment and the passing of the Land Act. Some months ago the Ulster Orangemen were talking of rebellion, but they eventually decided that they would not march on Cork, because they would have to pass through Tipperary. (Laughter). They decided to give up rebellion and confine themselves to subscribing their names as Covenanters. The old adage that " Ulster will fight and Ulster will be right " must now "he corrected to ULSTER WILL NOT FIGHT, BUT ULSTER WILL WRITE"

(much laughter.) They had iifies and horses and they were drilling, and the gallant Captain Craig would gather his forces together and march on Leinster, pre- pared to take Munster and Coanaught also. (Laughter). He would order three men to every horse—one man to sit on the horse and the other ta hold him on. (Laughter). There would be two men for each rifle— one to hold it up and the others to show him how to shoot. (Laughter). The rebellion would have been a most delightful thing for Gilbert and Sollivan, if they had only been alive. (Laughter). The Tory Press sought to make out that the rebellion was not bluff. Irish Home Rulers, who knew Ireland, were convinced that it was

div.head: BLUFF FROM BEG INNING, TO END.
div.p: BLUFF FROM BEG INNING, TO END.

' (Laughter). Even at the present moment businessmen in Ulster were sending by every post messages to Sir Edward Carson that his rebellion must come to an end because their business was being damaged. The present proceedings showed where the religious bigotry came from—it came from the North East corner of Ireland —(applause)—and the whole agitation was attributable to that feeling. It represented the dying snarl of the tyrants who had upheld minority and class interests in Ireland, for not all the forces of wealth and L•ristocracy could separate the British and the Irish democracies now. (Loud applause.)

div.head: MR. MADDEN AND ULSTER TREASON.
div.p: MR. MADDEN AND ULSTER TREASON.

Mr W MADDEN, in the course of a stirring speech, recalled his long association with the Home Rule cause and referred to the first Home Rule meeting in Liver- I pool forty-two years ago. It had ever been the record of the Irish party that in the darkest days, just as the poor helped the poor, so the Irishmen who were struggling for freedom and liberty held out their hands in sympathy to all kindred causes. (Applause.) The cry of the Tories was that the majority of the present G rvernment was dwindling—that it was made up of Irish, Welsh and Labour members. Let them go back to the days when they carried the famous Act of Union by a wretched two or three majority. They clung to the Union ; they did not find fault withithe majority of those days, because it suited their book. They were like a dog which had been deprived °flits bone; they bad been kept out of office for ten years and they could not bear it. Although they were able to sneak into a seat in one or two places and hold a

div.head: BEER-RIDDEN TOWN
div.p: BEER-RIDDEN TOWN

Like Warrington in their hands, the march of the people would go on. (Applause). After trying for fifty years to get the ear of the English democracy, the Irish had at last succeeded. It was now impossible to go back upon the road they bad travelled. There was no cry about Rome Rule in these days. If Home Rule were a movement in favour of Roman aggression, it was peculiar that among its most active opponents were the Duke of Norfolk and others who would presumably be the very Bret to support it if they regarded it as a movement in favour of Rome. Anyone who had read Irish history must know that, while Ireland yielded to no country in its allegiance to its spiritual bead, while )o country bad made more sacrifices for the Catholic "aith, yet no counrry had more religiously guarded its )olitical rights. (Applause). Every time there rad been any attempt to interefere with the Irish people in political controversies, their leaders had stood determinedly by the rights of Ireland. (Applause.) The Nationalists did not consider there was the slightest danger to their Protestant friends in Ireland. History proved exactly the opposite. Many Protestants were placed in positions of influence when- ever the power was in the hands of the Catholic body. He wondered how the English Catholics bad been treated by the Tory party ? What reward had they got for the great services they rendered the party by always proclaiming themselves as loyal subjects who would have nothing to do " with those awful Irishmen " ? One would have expected that the Tory party would have said" You have stood by us through thick and thin. Here are 30 or 40 seats for you in the House of Commons." How many English Catholics did they find representing English constituences ? How many Irish Protestants did they find rPpresenting Irish Catholics in the House of Commons? (Applause.) The question of Home Rule had almost passed out of the region of controversy ; they had come to the last ditch. (Laughter.) What did the nobility and privileged landed classes who were supporting the Tory agitation really care about the Irish people? The Protestant faith was nothing more than a A PAWN IN THE GAME,
'ai pol

used by those men for their own purpo;es. They must get back to power, whether by fighting for the House of Lords, against the Insurance Act and the Reform Bill, or against the people of Ireland. At the present moment the Ulster question was the one on which Lord Londonderry, Sir Edward Carson and all the leaders of the Pory party in England, from Mr Boner Law down- wards, were " hacking " all they bad. They were fighting all the time for themselves, but were hoping to stir up bitter feelings in England against the people of Ireland. (Applause.) Ireland was prosperous when she had her own Parliament, but from the time her Parliament was taken from her, she bad been crippled in every industry. The reason why Ulster had been comparatively prosperous aas that England by her Acts of Parliament prevented the woollen industry being a success in Ireland, whereas she had subsidised the linen industry of Belfast by bounties. The Tories DOW found that they had come to the end of the struggle—that the game was np—and further efforts were being made to arouse the slumbering fires of re- ligious bigotry and hatred. Who were the men they put forward ? Who were the monkeys they put for- ward, that were going to save the British Empire by their

HALFPENNY SIGNATURES

which had been obtained. (Laughter). He did not think autographs were ever got at a cheaper rate and he hoped Mr. Harold Smith would cherish that wire when it landed in Belfast. The League had better go one better by starting a penny wire to be sent to the Nationalists to say that they were in favour of grant- ing self-government to Ireland. (Appbuse). They were told there was going to be a great deal of trouble if Home Rule were granted. Sir Edward Carson said he did not care twopence what might happen, and it appeared that Mr. Harold Smith did not care a half- penny. (Laughter). It was a peculiar kind of loyalty that was expressed by Sir Edward Carson and his supporters. He did not know what their respective positions were. No doubt Sir Edward Carson was the General, Mr F E Smith the Captain and Mr Harold Smith was going to carry a dummy rifle for Sir Edward (laughter and a voice: "They are getting well paid for it.") " Perhaps you think they are getting a guinea a time" commented the Chairman. "You must leave that kind of talk to the Tories. We must not make such insintations. Of course, they are purely disinterested in every way and they don't do things, as my friends suggests, simply for those guineas." (Laughter,) He did not believe there was any danger of religious intolerance in Ireland. If there was, bow was it that the Tory party had played with the question of Home Rule ? Every measure which the Liberals had proposed but failed to carry through for Ireland had been taken up by the Tories,and if by any means the Liberal party failed to carry Home Rule now, the Tory party would be obliged to carry it. Theie was not one solitary argument in the speeches of Sir Edward Carson and Mr 1' E Smith against the granting of self-government to Ireland. The only case they were engaged in building up was that of religious prejudice and bigotry. A more mean, des- picable and cowarldy campaign could not be engaged in by any party. (Applause.)

HOME RU LE A -DEMOCRATIC MOVEMENT. Mr. TA I,LON, who had a hearty reception, emphasised the fact that the Irish people were thoroughly Liberal and democratic. Even it there were no Home Rule Bill under discussion at tlip present moment, the Irish people, through their representatives in the House of Commons, would be voting as they were doing, along with the Liberal and democratic Government. (Applause.) They in Ireland believed in deeds, not in words ; in actions, not in promises that were never fulfilled. Ap %ft from Home Rule,the Irish people were absolutely in agreement with the Government on every single issue they had in hand. With regard to the Insurance Act, they were prepared to leave the details to those who were best fir,ted to draw them up. The fact that the Insurance Act came from the Government which had carried Old Age Pensions—(applause)—and other benefl3ent Acts, was quite enough for them. They knew that in course of time, as detects or blemishes were discovered, the Act would require amendment. No Act ever came over to Ireland that did not require amending—except the Tory Acts which had to be I abolished altogether. (Laughter.) They were told it was an insensate thing to have rushed the Insurance ' Act through Parliament in seven mouths. The men , who made that accusation never told them that, while they protested against the Insurance Act being rushed through in seven months, they rushed through 100 Coercion Acts for Ireland in seven minutes. (Laughter and applause.) On the other great Bill which the Governiuent had in hand—Welsh Disestablishment—the. Irish people, through their representatives, were in cordial agreement. Mr. Gladstone disestablished the Protestant Church in Ireland and they all knew that since the Church was disestablished it had been far more useful and had done far more serviceable work than ever it did in the days of Establish- ment. The Irish supported the Government's Reform Bill because, as democrats, they believed in "One man one vote." Small as the Orange repre- sentation of man, was, it would be infinitely smaller when the Reform Bill had been passed and Plural Voting abolished. As to the new phase of the land controversy in England, Irishmen had had some experi- ence of an acute land controversy in their own country, and they therefore wished the Government joy and success in tackling that immense problem. (Applause.) A fact which was not sufficiently stressed nowadays was that while tbe Irish Home Rule movement was a national movement, the force and motive power behind it was its democratic character. (Applause.) It was a DEMOCRATIC MOVEMENT

organized and controlled by. the people—in a large number of cases, the working people of Ireland. (Applause.) So democratic were the Irish people in all their actions, that long before they felt a Horne Rule Bill would come their way, the Irish members were supporting every democratic measure that was intro- duced by various Governments in the interests of the people. (Applause.) Itlf. Fallori next showed that on the simple ground of majority rule, Ireland was entitled to self-government, as 81 or 85 members out of the 101 elected by the people had been consistently returned to demand Home Rule. They were told that if they assisted in the passage of Home Rule, they would be setting up in Ireland a country which was so poor that in a few months they would be called upon to put their hands into their pockets to pay the taxes for Ireland. 'Laughter.) On the other hand, they were told that Ireland was so prosperous that she did not want Home Rule. (Laughter.) Ireland was • NOT THE POVERTY-STRICKEN COUNTRY those people pretended it was. Ireland was a rich country—rich in land,rich in waterways and in minerals Lalthough they had been entirely undeveloped. Ireland

Nationalists, Mr Fallon maintained that self-govern- ment would bring the two elements together to work for the welfare of the nation, just as Anglo-Saxons' Normans, Danes and Germans had been brought together In England under the Parliamentary system. Behind the demand for Home Rule lay the thing of which a French literary man spoke when he was asked what was the great essential for a people to be pros- perous, and he replied "It is liberty." The Irish people wanted liberty to free the mind and body of Ireland. They were

NOT THE WILD SEPARATISTS that people were sometimes persuaded they were. They saw that the British Colonial system was the greatest piece of statecraft that had ever been invented, because it gave countries like Canads, Australia and New Zealand, perfect freedom to work out their ideas, while remaining inside the British Empire. (Applause.) Having emphasised the extravagance of the existing system of government in Ireland, Mr Fallon said that Mr Birrell, like his predecessors in office, discovered that that system was wasteful and inefficient, and like the man he was, he came back to the English people and said : " There is only one solution for all this— to trust the Irish people with their own affairs." (Applause.) They were told that Ulster would not have Home Rule. How the opposition came to be credited to Ulster he was at a loss to discover,for everyone knew that only half of Ulster was opposed to Home Rule. Of the 33 members returned for Ulster, 14 had been regularly Honte Rulers ; nine of them had been Unionists ; and ten had gone from one side to the other at intervals. It was absurd, in view of those facts, to speak of Ulster being opposed to Home Rule. Only one corner was opposed to it, and even that section would not be, if it were left alone by the place. mongers. (Applause ) The majority of the Protestants of Ireland who were not Orangemen were Home Rulers. So far from Ulster being the prosperous and wealthy province that it was generally represented to be,the facts were all the other way. The rateable value of the Catholic province of Leinster was £.4 Fis per head ;of blunster,t3 95 per head ;and of Ulster only £3 6s per head. That disposed of the notion that Protestant Ulster would have to pay all the taxes in the event of Home Rule !mourning law. Mr. Fallon showed how the prophecies of rebellion were falsified in the case of Irish Disestablish-
From Reynolds' New.

could be a rich and prosperous part of the British Empire under fairer auspices. (Applause). Ireland was more hopeful now than she had been for many generations ; she was beginning to feel that brighter days were coming—but that could not be mistaken for prosperity. The Irish were commonly supposed to be a race of incapables, but, in spite of the crippling conditions, they had con- tributed their share to the British army and navy, to British statesmanship and to British letters. (Applause) Irishmen, driven out of their own country for no other reason than to satisfy the greed of rapacious landlordism, had in America and the Colonies built up reputation and honour, to the credit of themselves and of their country. Was it not also a marvellous thing that the people of Ireland,in spite of the forces arrayed against them, had broken down landlordism and the feudal growth of 250 years ?—a thing that England, France and Germany had not been able to do. (Applause) As to the part which Irishmen wera fulfilling in Colonial government, it was worthy of notice that five of the twelve members of Mr. Borden's Canadian Cabinet were , Irish-born Irishmen—the sons of poor people in the country districts of Ireland. (Applause). Mr- Fallon dealt with Tory objections to "dollar dictator ship," and said it was one of the proudest boasts of Ireland that poor Irish boys and girls working in America as domestic servants or in other humble positions, could scrape together a few dollars and send them to aid the cause of the land that gave them birth and which they might never see again. That was patriotism. 'Applause.) The English aristocracy did not always sneer at dollars. How many, in order to build up the crumb' ng walls of their mansions —walls dissipated by extravagance and luxury —had allied themselves to the daughters of American millionaires ? Referring to the supposed implacable hostility between the Orangemen and.

div.head: M. SAZONOFF.
div.p: M. SAZONOFF.

M. Sazonoff, the Russian Foreign Minister, accompanied by Cunt Benckendorff. the Russian Ambassador, and Lord Revel- stoke, has been staying with the King at Balmoral Castle, where Sir Edward Grey is acting as Minister-in-Attendance. The re- sults of the conferences are expected to be of vast importance.
THE LATE GERMAN AMBASSADOR.

Baron Marschall von Bieberstein, the Gen man Ambassador in London, died suddenly at Badenweiler on Tuesday. He had been staying there for some time undergoing the cure. The Baron landed in England in June of this year on his appointment as German Ambassador to this country, and left again in Augast for a holiday. The news of his death Came as a great shock to tha members of the staff of the German Embassy.

REGIMES Or WAXWORK SOLDIERS? (Laughter.) Sir Edward Carson—" Crying Teddy"— and Frothy Freddy." (Laughter.) t!ir Edward Carson's reputation was based on his hostility to his own people. He had occupied much of his life in prosecuting Irish people for treason ' • now he was the spokesman of treason. (Applause.) Then they had the other gentleman who was closely allied to their local representative—(laughter)—the gentleman well known by the name of " Frothy Freddy." (Laughter.) Froth came to the top. (Laughter.) Whavright or interest had Mr F E Smith, with his cheap patriotism' in regard to the struggle in Ireland ? In what way did Ireland or the solution of its question need the presence of Mr Smith ? Long before he was thought of, that great struggle had been going on between those two peoples. Happily it was now coming to an end, but the settlement was to be disturbed by this adventurer from England who, he (the speaker) said in all serious- ness, was about one of the worst types of political agitator who could take part upon any platform. They knew it was safe to preach

CHEAP TREASON. They knew they did not run the risk which Irishmen had run in the past, of being sent to prison. Sir Edward Carson and Mr F E Smith knew their skins were safe. There would be no prosecutions against them. Why ? Because the power and influence of the nobility and gentry of the Conservative pa,ty in England—all that made for wealth and power—was in their favour. If they thought there was the slightest danger of a plank bed, we should not hear much of their treason. (Laughter.) If it came to actual blows, there would not be many of Mr F E Smith's lambs from Walton helping him in the fight. (Laughter.) Nor did he (the speaker) think there would be a Warrington contingent, with Mr Harold Smith. (Laughter.) When the English people realized the game that was being played upon them, they would step in and put an end to the defiance of a little part of the North of Ireland. (Applause.) The Government were not to be bluffed. (Applause.) Knowing they had the power of the democracy behind them, they could afford to laugh at the wild attempts of the modern hot/Ogees furiosos,

with their paper caps and wooden swords. iLaughter.) He (Mr. Madden) would love to be in the nest fight in Warrington, whenever it took place. They would be fighting for the cause of Liberalism against privilege and against beer. (Applause.) They had

NOT HAD FAIR PLAY /N WARRINGTON and they never would have until they drove the brewer back to his brewery, until they got rid of the tied houses which, after all, were only centres of Toryism. Every house of Greenall's was a committee room for Mr. Harold Smith. (Applause). They would never be free in Warrington until they defeated the power of the brewer. (Applause). Mr. P. PEACOCK moved and Mr. J. MORTON seconded a vote of thanks to the speakers. Councillor TOOLS, in supporting, said Mr. Harold Smith, the new aide-de-camp of Sir Edward Carson, was calling upon the loyalists of Warrington to show their approval of the action of the Carson crowd in Ulster by sending a gigantic telegram to Belfast on Saturday As an Irishman, a Nationalist and a loyalist, he (the speaker) denied the right of Mr Harold Smith to say that he was representing the loyalists of Warrington. The loyalists of Warrington did not con- sist solely of Conservatives or of Liberals but of Nationalists too. (Applause.) Their loyalty was shown when old England needed it, and it was unfair that they should be misrepresented in such a way. They hoped that when the next opportunity came, they would see that Warrington would be represented not by a pantaloon, by a man who figured on the Royal Court stage as Macduff, at Earl's Court in another part, and who was no doubt playing another part in Belfast to-day. He was supposed to be representing tl.e electors of Warrington, but his position was a false one. The time was coming when they would be able to show that they meant to be represented by a gentleman and a politician—(applause) —and he hoped the progressives of Warrington would find some of their most earnest supporters in the Irish ranks. (Applause). The vote was heartily carried. The CHAIRMAN, before closing the meeting, said he was glad to know that Warrington was becoming more sober town. If only the great mass of the workers would realize their power, they would soon make an end of brewer and landlord. (Applause).

div.head: "WOMAN AT HOME."
div.p: "WOMAN AT HOME."

The interior of the October" Woman at Home is as attractive as the charming design of its cover. The splendid serial story " Mrs. Ames " by E F Benson is brought to a conclucion, while that fascinating series I of articles on "My Wife's Hidden Life " reaches a further stage in its disclosure. Seldom have we read a more poignant, yet delightful, series than this,and we commend it to husbands and wives alike for careful and thoughtful perusal. Other first rate fiction is pre- sented in" Treasure upon Earth "by Ilerbert Shaw,and " The Windfall "by Kemble Strang. The "Woman at Home" is the ideal magazine for the woman at home, and whatever it may be that interests you particularly you will find some useful suggestions concerning it included in the pages of this excellent magazine.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ASSOCIATION (N.A. CENTRE).

STORT STILL oFr. Angling last week was not up to expectations, although there was a fairly good programme. Club matches and the big match at Poynton were the most thought of, and everybody seemed to have the one opinion that sport was "off." The Dee, Shropshire Union Canal, the Gowy, the Weaver and Norton all had poor results. Different opinions were heard as to the cause of the falling off, the one most favoured being the glut of natural feed in the waters. It is as well we cannot get at the bottom of these things, as it is the uncertainty of angling that makes it the fascinating hobby it is. If we were sure of taking a basket of fish every time we turned out there would soon be a.slackening of interest.. I have in mind one member who visited the Gowy for 12 weeks without taking a roach and on the 13th week he brought home a catch that has yet to be beaten in Warrington. lie saw the fish harbouring in the same haunt week after week and knew that he would reap his reward by continually going until he caught them on feed.

The weather was ideal for anglers and if there was a scarcity of fish it was one of the finest week ends to be out in. It was taken advantage of by a party walking over from Chester to the Gowy. Not a single specimen has been recorded this week- end, which is most surprising, considering the number of members out and the different waters tried.

div.head: DEE.
div.p: THE DEE.

Chester was visited Cy—a-eve-re-I locals, some going by midnight mail and others by bike end getting to their favourite haunts before daylight. About a dozen in all made the journey, and although the river was at its best to look at, sport was not what was expected. The top of the weir was quite dry, and this is the first time it has been caught that way for months. Several selected this spot, but beyond small dace and roach nothing more was done. The same fate betel those who tramped the upper reaches.

TIIE GOWY. 4 Those who visited the Gowy found the water gin clear "and very little run on it. Although it was cleaned out some short time ago it is the general opinion that it is now worse than ever, being quite choked up in places. From its appearance you would think that you could walk across. The favoured haunts arc almost unfisbable and those who visit here will have to work to get fish or they will find themselves fast among the weeds. Several members were angling all day for one or two fish. The best catch was by W Hewitt, who had about a dozen fair roach.

HARTFORD. The Weaver once more was disappointing, members fishing all Sunday last for less than lib of good fish. Weights in match fishing have not come up to expecta- tions lately and those who get near lib can consider their chance good.
NORTON._

The canal here seems to be falling off this last two week ends and the small fry is all that can be ' caught. Several members were present on Thursday, Saturday, Sunday and Monday ltst week but no one topped the roach of Boz. 4drs, weighed in for the September special by 'l'. Singleton. This member has now several specials to his account from Norton.

div.p: STOKE.

One angler took f six roach, two with bread and four with a bunch of ' maggots and not one was sizeable. They fished on till noon, and then crossed over to the Howy. div.head: NEW POLICE SUPERINTENDENT FOR WIDNES
div.p: NEW POLICE SUPERINTENDENT FOR WIDNES

Police-inspector W. Foster, stationed at Formby, has been promoted to the rank of superintendent, and will take charge of the Widnes police division from October Ist, lie joined the force in 1884, serving for a short time in the Old Swan division, Liverpool, whence, after promotion, he removed ;,o Lark-lane station in Sefton Park. He further served in the Lonsdale division, Earlestown, and in Birkdale. He was transferred horn Birkdale to Formby in April last, while this month he received a Coronation medal, conferred upon those members of the force for long and meritorious service

mankind is confirmed by the numerous proofs—the raising of this £250,000 among them—that "the cause" is in rather a bad Way. One reason is, perhaps, that it is such a cause as dare not put its cards on the table. The Tariff Reform Commission was to produce a scientific tariff. It has not done so. Mr. George Wyndham boasts about seats won in Lancashire during the last three years. The seats won in Lan- cashire were gained by the supression of Tariff Reform as an electioneering topic. In connection with the new fund, Mr. L. S. Amery sketches a possible future for our country. He has convinced himself that his party is bound to win at the next General Election. But it may win by only a small majority. In that case it will, at the best, be able to struggle through two or three years. " After that," says Mr. Amery, "there may be a tremendous reaction, in which a Labour-Socialist Party, possibly headed by Lloyd George, will come in triumphantly, dictate the course of our home policy for the next generation in a revolu- tionary spirit, and incidentally wreck the Empire." We pass over the obviously inten- tional silliness of attributing to the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer, who is at least as honourable and patriotic a man as Mr. L. S. Amery, a desire "incidentally" to wreck the Empire, and note this literary politician's accurate appreciation of the effects of a few years of Conservative governmenta tremendous reaction. In this respect Mr. Amery can speak from experience. He was not in politics in 1880, when there was a tremendous reaction against the Disraeli Government; but he knows something about 1906, and the tremendous reaction which then manifested itself. But the preliminary condition to the next event of the same, kind cannot be brought about whilst leading members of the Conservative Party are en- gaged in raising large sums of money for the purpose of smashing a system under which our industrial and commercial great- ness has been built up, and of putting in its place something from which the people of all other countries are striving to escape.

Where does the Tory A VERY MUCH Party stand on the TANGLED ISSUE. Tariff Reform issue? One Tory organ has congratulated Mr. Boner Law on his sanction to the suppression of the Tariff Reform question in Midlothian. Now Mr. Bonar Law is announced as giving his sanction to an "Imperial movement" which will put such questions as Home Rule into the back- ground. Mr. F. E. Smith has declared that the Tory Party "will not return to power, whether their period of exclusion is long or short, until they have won a clear and definite mandate on behalf of their Tariff Reform Programme."

At this Diocesan Con- THE CLAIMS OF ference the Bishop of CLAMOROUS St. David's has corn- MINORITIES. mented upon a growing tendency to resist the law. This tendency, he suggests, is partly due to the fact that, if the people make the law, they will not respect it as they would something imposed from above. The conclu- sion which he draws is that the English Church in Wales must be maintained. There are further conclusions which every man of common sense can draw for himself, even if the episcopal intellect stops short. But will he venture to suggest that the disposition of the Orange . section in Ulster to defy the law would be extinguished if they were assured that the 'Established Church in Wales would be left intact? There is a clamorous minority in Ulster, a more or less clamorous minority in Wales. The claim of either minority that their point of view is to be respected as "an inalienable right" is equally ridiculous. But the episcopal suggestion that the Established Church in Wales must be preserved in order to make democratic institutions respectable is one which Sir Edward Carson and Mr. F. E. Smith should diligently study.

The issue to which the THE SCIENTIFIC Tariff Reformers pant TARIFF, to nail Mr. Bonar Law's ears has become aniissue of practical politics in the United States. We are invited to imitate the" scientific tariff" of the United States. But Dr. Woodrow Wilson, the Democratic candidate for the Presidency, has been *describing to his audiences in the Middle West the " Chamber of Horrors" which Free Traders in New York have got together to demonstrate "the iniquities and the inequalities of a high protective tariff." A "scientific tariff" in the United States forbes American people to pay sixty-one per cent more for sewing- machines than an American sewing-machine costs to foreigners. Under this scientific tariff the American citizen is mulcted to the tune of thirty-three per, cent on baby- carriages, one hundred per cent on meats choppers, sixty per cent on lead pencils, and so on through an almost interminable list. And Mr. F. E. Smith tells us that the Tory Party will live contentedly in the wilderness till they get a mandate for a "scientific tariff"!

div.p: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.
OPENING OF THE SEASON.

To-day at 3 p.m. Warrington A.P. meet at head- quarters, the Pavilion near the Football Ground, and it is hoped there will be a good muster for the opening run of the season. All members are particularly requested to attend, and intending members and visitors are cordially invited. Many will look on the run as of the preliminary canter order, ad probably the usual amount of " blackberrying ,' will take place' but the novice will take a great interest in the doings which initiate them to the delights of a jog across country end no doubt many will pick up the " lay of the land " for future affairs of a competitive nature. Mr H J Lyon, 32, Lugsrnore-lane, St Helens has decided to accept the Hon. Secretaryship of the West Lancashire, C.C.A., who hold their opening run at Clock Face next Eaturday. Beginners should take the opportunity of turning out this afternoon when the weather promises to be congenial, and remember that the competitions for novices being in the earlier part of the season necessitates getting fit earlier than the experienced brigade.

THE day, a number of gentlemen, SHEKELS. of whom Mr. Waldorf Astor is one, have put down £l,OOO a-piece, under the agreeable in- fluences of a dinner given by the Duke of •Westminster,, for the purpose of starting the Tariff Reform League on a new career. The sum total subscribed at Grosvenor House is £21,250; the Duke himself giving £5,000 on condition that not less than .c.:50,000 is raised. The aim of the promoters of what i to be called " The Imperial, Fund "—for those who have seized upon the Union Jack as a party emblem do not, of course, hesitate to claim the Empire as their own—is to raise £250,000, and Sir Francis Trippel, a renowned organiser of the sort of benevolence that shrinks from, giving money away until it is nudged at -the elbow or invited to some such place .as Grosvenor House, has premised to get the whole sum together at his personal expense. Among the original subscribers are Sir Philip Sassoon, Sir David Salomons, Sir Abe Bailey, Sir Edward Durning-Lawrence—who believes that Bacon is the author not only of the works of Shakespeare, but of the Authorised translation of the Bible—and, as we have said, Mr. Waldorf Astor, M.P. They none of them make a great sacrifice, for they are all of them very wealthy men. Their object is defined for them by Mr. L. S. Amery, M.P. It is "to take in hand the ‘'hole task of Imperial and social reor- ganisation, of which Imperial Preference and Tariff Reform are the indispensable foun- dation." We could, we believe, state the actual truth in fewer words. Their purpose is to help the Tory Party into office. What may expect beyond that is, as the saying goes, on the knees of the gods. Some of the money is to be spent, in the first place, "on a vigorous autumn cam- paign." We know what that means. An eminent statesman once defended the Church Establishment on the ground that it main- tains a gentleman in every parish. The ideal of the " raging and tearing " campaig- ners is to place a Tariff " Reformer " in every pothouse. The sums spent by the Tariff Reform League up to this time must have been prodigious. Whether the expen- diture has been wasteful or not is a matter of opinion. The sowing broadcast of false- hoods about the condition of trade, the views of our Dominions beyond the seas, the future of our industries, our position in regard to our trade rivals, and the influence of tariffs on employment, may seem to one sort of person to be something well worth paying for, though to another it may, and does, appear to be the worst kind of fool- ishness. If there is any cause that can be advanced by the reckless expenditure of money in unworthy ways, the Tariff Reform cause should now hold a position thoroughly impregnable. However, a rational con- fidence in the good sense of the bulk of

Personal. Sir Frederick Henry Smith, Baronet, formerly of Lymm Ball, Lymm, who is well known in Lancashire business circles, has been appointed a director of the Laricashire and Yorkshire Bank, Limited. We are pleased to hear that there is a marked improvement in the condition of Alderman James Evans, J.P.. chairman of the Health Committee. who has been lying seriously ill with pneumonia. We regret to learn that Mr Edwin Woods, J.P , is lying seriously ill at his residence, Rock Villa, Latchford. On Thursday his condition was critical but last night we were informed that there, was considerable improvement. The late Mr. William Dannett. ' _ _

The will of the late Mr.-4-illiiin-Dannett, 11, Rose Villa, Grappenhall-road, Latchford, has been proved at £1,052. Mr. Dannett, who died on May 30th, at the age of 77 years, had occupied the position of chief clerk at the Warrington Post Office for many years and was subsequently postmaster of Widnes, then of St. Helens and latterly of Wigan. Success of a Local Dog Fancier. At the Widnes Dog Show, held on Thursday last week in the Borough Rink, Mr. Townley, 441, WeWield-street, was successful in winning with his well-known fawn pug, Cute Jiggawug, 2 firsts, 2 specials and 2 seconds; also with his smooth fox terrier puppy, Gallard's Double, 2 seconds and 2 thirds, a good performance for an eight months puppy in a very keen competition. Young Abstainers' Union

The—members of this Junior Temperance Society spent a merry afternoon at Padgate on Saturday last. By kind invitation of Dr and Mrs Bennett, the young people assembled at Lynton Grange. Here they found a beautiful garden and paddock prepared for their recreation and no time was lost in getting to work at croquet, tennis, and other amusements, not forgetting donkey riding and afternoon tea. All too soon came the hour of departure and after expression of thanks to their generous host and hostess the members took their leave. CORRUGATED SHEETS and Roofing Felt, Estimg.tes tree.—J. S. Warrington Chess Club. The Warrington Chess Club held their General Com- mittee meeting on Thursday night at Prince's Cafe, Saiike-sir et A fair number were present and the following (liken; were unanimously re-elected. Mr. Newcombe as president and Mr. J. R. Wood as treasurer who have held their positions well for many years. Mr. Dunne, one of the founders of the club and holder of last year's Championship Trophy, was re-elected as captain. The committee expressed a wish that special facilities should be given to any intending member who wished to be coached in the game. The Pictaredrome. Large audiences have been the rule at the P icturedome, the popular Sankey Street palace of amusement and entertainment,during the week. The fare provided is of the usual high order and one cannot but have a word of appreciation for the energetic management of this house for providing such high class menus of the beet films,as is always placed before patrons. Many subjects are depicted of , a humorous and pathetic nature and the change thrice weekly has proved highly successful. The chief film for to-day is "The adopted Son." For next week all the latest and best pictures will be shown and there will be a complete change of programme on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. Shooting Affair at Bank Quay. With a bullet wound just below the heart, a man was fcund in a back passage off Liverpool-road on Tuesday morning, and the discovery caused a great sensation in the district. Robert Cook, a labourer, of 89, Bostock-street, was startled about 930 by the report of a firearm and proceeded in the direction whence the noise came. Lying on in the ground in the passage was a man quite conscious but wounded. The clothing round the bullet hole was singed. The injured man is William Kirby, a labourer, at Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.'s tube works, and living at 2, Percy-street. He was carried into the Ship Inn yard, where a search of his clothing was made. In his right-band jacket pocket was found a revolver loaded in one chamber and containing a discharged cartridge. Kirby was removed to the Infirmary And it is expected he will recover. '
KITCHEN RANGES, Fire Grates and Tiles, Large stock. Inspection invited.—J. B. GARLAND, 51-55, Bridge at., Warriogton.—Advt. Royal Theatre of Varieties.

well varied programme is submitted at this .popular theatre this week, for in addition tO the sensa- tional drama "Lady Audley's Secret" being presented by the Royal Stock Co., there is an excruciatingly funny sketch entitled " Bank holiday in Casey's Court," by a number of clever artistes. Singing, dancing, and burlesque comedy are introduced with a large amount of success and the whole company ably support Mr. Will Murray, who, As Mrs. Casey soon creates roars of laughter. The Royal Stock Co, are again to the fore in the highly emotional drama, and the good reputation they have earned is well maintained. The principal parts are undertaken by Miss Leah Corenters and Mr H Val Vousden. Gene Crowe is a clever coon singer, and as a ventriloquist he is no mean exponent of the art. His " railway porter " number is clever and highly delights the audience.—Ort Monday next and during the week Miss Agnes Collie's Star Co. will appear in the "Temptress of Paris," a story of life in the " gay city." Girl Burned to Death. At the Warrington Coroner's Court, on Tuesday morning, Mr. S. Brighouse conducted an inquest on the body of Miriam Frogatt. aged two yeas, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Frogatt, 8, Sharp-street, Warrington. It appears that the deceased was left in bed asleep on Saturday morning. At 8.45 the mother heard her cry out, and sent her son to ascertain the cause. Reaching the bottom of the stairs be saw his sisters's clothing in flames. The mother and another son rolled the little girl in a rug and hurried her to the surgery of Dr. NlcKee, who ordered her removal to the Infirmary, where she died at one o'clock in the afternoon. the deceased slept with her parents, and after lighting tbe gas the previous night, the father had left a box of matches on the dressing-table. After the fatality, the mother found the box of matches and two match- stalks on the floor. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

Miss Gornall's Matinee Concert. The plan will be open at Mr Pearson's, Bridge- street on Monday next, for Miss Mary Gornall's Matinee Concert which is to he held in the Bold-street schoolroom (not at the Conservative Club as previously advertised) on October 17th. The following artistes will appear: —Mrs Norman Melland, soprano; Miss Amethe Leadbetter, violinist of the Queen's Hall, Patti Melba tour, Busoni tour, &c. ; Miss Evelyn Hall, harpist, a pupil if the great harpist and composer Herr Professor Alfred Holy of the Imperial Opera at Vienna. It may interest our readers to learn that Miss Hall is the sister of Marie Rail, the celebrated violinist. As one so rarely gets the opportunity of hearing the harp the many love's of that beautiful instrument should not miss this chance of enjoying the playing of a very tal‘nted artist. Tea will be provided by the Wmmarleigh Co., Cafe during the interval at a moderate charge.

CYCLES.—AnnuaI Clearance Sale, all prices reduced.— J. S. GARLAND, 51-55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Formation of a Reading Circle. On Monday evening a meeting was held at the offices of the Guild of Help, when it was decided to form a reading circle in connection with the National Home Reading Union. It was agreed to read during the coming months on the subject of Charities and their Administration. This reading will he done at home as people find leisure to do so, but in addition there will be a monthly discussion meeting, which will be attended by all who are able to come. Individuals can join the Horne Reading Union at any time, but by allying themselves with a reading circle the member- ship fee is reduced to 2s. The discussions will be held on the third Monday in each month and the first will be on 21st October at 7.30 at Wiumarleigh Chambers, when a leader will be elected. Meantime those who have already joined have determined to read first of all a little shilling book entitled "Social conditions in provincial towns." Mr. Wilfrid Rowland has been asked to open the discussion by giving a paper on this book. Membership is open to the general public and any people interested are asked to communicate with Mr. Rowland. A. monthly magazine issued from London headquarters goes to each member, giving expert guidance in n definite course of reading. Other interesting topics are included in the general course and some of these will no doubt be taken up by those who have time for further reading. Samples of the recommended books may be seen at the Guild of Help Offices and some are already to be found on the bookshelves of the public library.

The Picture Post-card Evil Sir,--I have pleasure in supporting " Ob- server's" remarks re objectionable picture post- cards in your last issue, and would like to ask Can nothing be done to kill this abominable practice 2 . I have noticed more than one shop in War- rington exhibiting these so-called picture post- 'cards, some of which are worse than vulgar; in fact, they are positively indecent. I can imagine nothing more calculated to cor- 'rapt the morals of the young, and it seems to aue that the police are not sufficiently alert. I believe a shopkeeper in Manchester was re- .cently fined for exhibiting and selling, these •beastly postcards. I might add that I was once a customer at one of these shops in Warrington, but I should cer- tainly not think of entering this particular shop 110 w that the sale of objectionable postcards is being carried on.—Yours faithfully, Bridge-street. G. G. B.

was .glad to see published in your last -creek's issue a commendation re "Objectianble -Postcards." It is just about time that public '"Pinion was called upon to express itself. There are two shops in town, both in the main streets, the proprietors of which exhibit postcards which are anything but a- blessing to the community. Besides being offensive, they are very suggestive, and it is mortifying to see the number of young Men and women who glory in seeing in the Pictures what is suggested. They cannot do Otherwise than carry away with them rude • 'thoughts, and the influence which is thus exer- '.elsed upon them must do irremediable berm. esides leaving animal impressions on youthful minds, there is a still lighter side to the ex- hibitions. The crowds of people who indulge in "the suggestiveness are an absolute nuisance to Pedestrians. I am not only speaking for myself, hut for many, who have to move off the footpath 10 allow the window-gazers their indulgence. C:annot anything be done to bring the exhibitors into showing in their windows a superior class 91 postcard? Surely, the "Morale" of the town Is law enough without thus debasing and degrad- ing it further. W. P.

_ Sir,—Too many points are raised in L.O.V.'s letter 1° Waste ink in replying to contratulations. We have "ni out to decide, if possible, whether by means of the ltrike the workers can win economic freedom. lam i't,t,:ked if the worker by a strike can gain a rise of ;4 I':ges—say 2s.—how long will it be before he secures ..,e i 11 the capitalist expropriates? Suppose we take a look What is being prepared in Belgium, where "the tra, 'Le unions are preparing conjointly with the "operative societies to supply 500,000 strikers with rlds for one month or six weeks." We here get a r apse of the possibilities of strikes scientifically ganized. The strike is not only a cessation of erk ; it carries with it educational influences ana tl!tnonstrates to those who are sufficiently intelligent, h,",e real relations between the buyers and sellers of irour power. They have no objective, conse- .litly their efforts have been futile, %I agree that the possession of the means production, economic and political power, Itt e the bulwarks of the capitalist, but it tt„ quite easy to mistake the extent of their erPlioation.
