CHAS. DUKES.

Sir,—ln my previous letter I advanced the proposi- tion that the st3ndard of subsistence of the workers had been steadily raised even though their portion of the total wealth had fallen from SO per cent under slavery to 35 per cent under modern capitalism, if this :be accepted we may now consider the factors which determine this standard in.any particular country or at any period. In order to illustrate, let us examine the forces that determine the water line of a piece of wood floating. When the block of wood is placed on the surface of the water it begins to sink and in doing so displaces, water. Eventually the weight of water displaced equals the weight of wood and the sinking ceases. The force of gravity acting downwards on the wood is now just equal to the upward thrust of the water and thus the water line is fixed according to these two forces. If the water be now turned into brine by the addition of salt, the wood will be raised slightly because brine has a greater buoyancy or upward thrust than has water. Conversely if the wood be made heavier it will sink until the forces are again in equilibrium. Although the forces Which determine the level of the workers' subsistence cannot be dealt with as completely as in the above example from physics, we can still see that there is an analogy. The competition for jobs is the force of gravity tending to pull down the subsistence level and the intelligence and unity of the workers forms the up- ward thrust tending to raise it. The play of these two forces gives us our industrial warfare. Taken on the whole the workers are kept just about the point of striking and this is bound to continue so long as there are antagonistic interests, if, when any body of workers struck, the capitalists were able to fill their places immediately and with but little loss, it is obvious that the standard of living could not be raised. On the other hand if the workers were able to form a large union with a fairly complete unanimity of purpose and action it is equally obvious that the standard could be raised considerably. If they were completely unanimous it could be raised to the limit, that is, the workers could employ themselves and appropriate the whole product of their labour. But such unanimity is impossible with the present capitalistic training of the 'workers in servitude. From this it follows that strikes are a necessary outcome of the workers limited knowledge, which is the result of their training in a competitive system of industry. It is useless then to advise them not to strike so long as they are trained in servitude or, what is the same thing, left untrained in the way of co-operative working. Those who desire to make more than paltry progress will get together and, bay- ing learned by experience the subtle lowa of co-opera- tion, will be ready and capable to lead the workers into the promised land of the Co-operative Commonwealth. Stockharo, Runcorn.
W. BAGULEY.

Lord Londonderry and the Government's Mandate. Sir,—Lord Londonderry has written to the Unionist Press to controvert some recent remarks of mine on the subject of the Government's mandate for Home Rule. He admits that the Unionist leaders and Unionist candidates warned the electors that to return the Liberal Government to office with power to pass the Parliament Act would inevitably lead to the pass- ing of a Home Rule Bill. In spite of all that Unionist leaders could say, Unionist candidates could implore, in spite of Dollar Dictators' placards, in spite of warn- ings, some sane and some hysterical, fi oat the whole of the Unionist Press, Lord Londonderry wants us to believe that the poor simple British elector went to the poll utterly oblivious of the fact that Home Rule would inevitably follow a Liberal victory. A pretty compliment to the intelligence of his fellow-country men! _ _ _

Lord Londonderry appears to argue that because Liberal Ministers and candidates did not fight the election on Home Rule, therefore the subject was not before the electors, As ordinary argument and ordinary evidence will not convince one who is deter- mined not to be convinced, I must approach the matter in another way by asking Lord Londonderry one or two questions. 1. If the British electors were duped into voting for Home Rule at the last election, will Lord Londonderry tell us why it is that at the subse- quent by-elections Unionist candidates instead of fighting on the Home Rule issue have concen- trated their attention on other subjects ? 2. Will Lord Londonderry and the Unionist leaders endeavour to ensure a straight vote on Home Rule at all future bye-elections, and at the subseinient General Elections, by forthwith abandoning all such issues as Tariff Reform and Insurance? If the electors were really deluded in December, 1910, there would have been spontaneous opposition to the Home Rule Bill throughout Great Britain. Eloquent testimony to the absence of such opposition is to be had from the most unimpeachable Unionist sources. I have made a careful note of the reports of the leading Unionist newspapers as to the chief issues put before the electors by Unionist candidates since the Home Rule Bill was introduced. These reports are not mere extracts from speeches or addresses, they give the issues before the electors from a Unionist standpoint. The Home Rule Bill was introduced on April 11th of the present year. Here are extracts from leading Unit:mist journals only, showing the chief issues at each by-election since that date.

EAST NOTTINGHAM.— "The first bye-election after the introduction of the Home Rule Bill might naturally be expected to turn largely, if no entirely, upon the -Irish question. . . . Although the Nationalist Party are attempting to force the race, it cannot be said that at present the Horne Rule Bill is being discussed to the exclusion of other political topics."—The " Times," April l Gth. SOUTH HACKNEY.—" The Insurance 4.ct is unques- tionably the subject that is most interesting the constituency..”--," Morning Post," May 22nd. NORTH WEST NORFOLK.—" Home Rule or Welsh DisestahlishMent will not greatly affect the issue, hut dislike or distrust of the Insurance Act will

.-- - decrease the Radical poll by hundreds."— "Standard," June let. Hot.mFlunt.—" There is certainly no enthusiasm for Home Rule, and it is probable that as the case against it is clearly presented to the people a greater interest may be aroused. Everybody admits, however, that there is much difficulty in making the question burn at all."—" Morning Post," June 18th. ILKESTON.—" A Unionist candidate has nothing to gain, but much to rose from vacillation or timi- dity on the subject of fiscal reform. We are having a straight light on that question at Ilkeston." "Morning Post," June 22. HANLEY.—" Mr. Rittner is fighting the battle with much -vigour and determination. He speaks chiefly on the Insurance Act, and on Fiscal Reform." "Morning Post," July 10. CIIEWE.—" Mr. Craig says he is not fighting the election on the Home Rule question." "Standard," July 23rd. NORTH-WEST MANCIIESTER.—" More perhaps than any other question the Insurance Act will affect the turnover of votes on Thursday." "Morning Post," August' 6th. EAST CARMARTHEN.—" Naturally the subject of immediate interest in a Welsh constituency just now is Disestablishment." —lnterview with Mr. Peel, "Morning Post," August 16th. MituATIOAN.—" Undoubtedly the question which will bulk most largely in the contest—at least the question on which most votes will be turned- - be the Insurance Act."—"Morning Post," August 16th. Unionist candidates finding no votes were to be won by making Home Rule the issue, very wisely took Lord Lansdowne's classic advice and selected more favourable ground on which to fight! In the face of the above evidence, what becomes of Lord Londonderry's demand for a mandate from the electors ? When Unionist candidates will not make Home Rule the test issue, what is the use of saying that Liberals have not allowed the electors to have an opportunity of voting for or against Home Rule 3 The fact of it is, Lord Londonderry, Mr. Boner Law, Sir Edward Carson and the rest of them have landed themselves in a pretty mess by inciting rebellion in Ulster ; and all this foolish talk about "no mandate for Home Rule " is a mere excuse to give some semblance of reason to their treasonable utterances. But even this flimsy excuse vanishes when we come to consider the position jn Ireland. When they go to Belfast L,rd Londonderry and his colleagues do not talk about resisting Home Rule merely because they say there was no mandate at the last election. Accord- ing to Sir Edward Carson's speech at Lisburn, Ulster Unionists are binding themselves by a Solemn Covenant, "never in any circumstances, to submit to, Home Rule." If Lord Londonderry is inciting Ulster to resist Homo Rule under any circumstances, his mandate excuse falls to the ground.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday,, September 28, 1912.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday,, September 28, 1912.

The Unionist leaders are playing fast and loose with N.E. Ulster. In Belfast they say " Ulster must never submit "- but in Great Britain they declare in the words of Mr. Bonar Law that" you cannot com- pel the United Kingdom to keep up the present arrangement against their will; and I should say to the loyalists of Ireland you have got to submit.' If these words mean anything at all they mean that, so far as the Unionist leaders are concerned, the solemn Covenant is a solemn farce ; a contemptible trick upon the religious prejudices of Ulster Orangemen. Because these poor deluded Orangemen believe that the Unionist party will stand by them, they are marching and counter-marching, signing solemn covenants and perpetrating horrible outrages upon innocent oppon- ents. Yet the Unionist leaders know full well that there are no votes to be won in this way in Great Britain. They know there is no chance of a Unionist victory on a policy of mere negation. So Mr. George Wyndham writes to the " Times" to declare that Home Pule is " distracting attention from the vital needs of securing defence, unity of the Empire, and employment for our workers, none of tablet' needs can be satisfactorily met without a reform of our tariff." He goes on to say that, "the urgent need of the moment is to have adequate financial resources and conduct a most vigorous campaign in the interests "—of what? Ulster and resistance to Home Rule? Not a bit of it. No,—"in the interests of Imperial Preference and Tariff Reform." So a big "Imperial Fund" is to be formed &c., &c., and the Unionist party is to march once more to the sound of Tariff taxes, while poor deluded Orange Ulster is allowed to run its head against the armed forces of the Empire. And Lord Londonderry and his colleagues have the audacity to question the Goyernment's mandate for Home Rule, while all the time they are preparing to do their utmost to make Britain forget every other issue except Tariff Reform! Surely political cynicism has never before reached such a height—or depth—Yours &c., E. WALLACE CARTER, , Parliament Chambers,
Secretary, Home Rule Council.

div.head: Westminster.
div.p: Westminster.
PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Since its advent in this country the vaudeville theatre has become more popular every year, and public patronage has increased by leaps and bounds. The theatre managers have a most arduous and strenuous time in preparing week after week, a pro- gramme, included in which are turns to please all patrons. It would be difficult to find a circuit blessed like the Macnagliten Vaudeville, with such a number of experienced and enterprizing managArs. The public of Warrington highly appreciate and admire the able manner in which Mr. Turpin controls the popular Barbauld-street house, hence the large number of people who visit this up-to-date place of amusement nightly. Every week, stars of the music hall world delight thousands of Warrington people ar,cl the fare provided this week is of the usual high-cliths standard. "It takes a wise man to make a fool " and evidence in support of this adage is seen in the entertainment provided by" The Ten Loonies." Although styled as " The Crazy comedy band," these half score comedians show themselves to be exceedingly clever entertainers During the time they occupy the boards the audience is kept rocking with mirth at the excruciatingly funny antics of the "band." The "make up " of each member is cleverly undertaken, whilst the movements of the pictures and fittings as they keep time with the music are indeed comical. Numerous musicAl instru- ments are manipulated with extraordinary skill, for when the players rush on the stage and commence their "piece" the noise very much reminds one of the country fair, but in a few minutes under the conductorship of the keeper, out of chaos comes peace and one of the catchiest of songs is played without a fault —Gus Garrick highly pleases with his absurdities. His ridiculous "make up" and his style are really clever and as the "Swiss maiden " he keeps the audience in a state of boisterous merriment. Sinclair's three Diamonds in a singing, skating and dancing turn are fairl7 successful, and Babs, the wonderful toe dancer, is well received. The Three Stewarts are very clever acrobats and their numerous feats prove that they possess extraordinary strength of limb. The various tricks are disposed of in a finished manner and the audience is unlimited in its approbation. Max Carl is a light comedian of excep- tional ability, and his soup are very catchy and well rendered. Millie Howell id a character vocalist of no mean order and she sings two songs in an effective manner. "The smoke of a 45" is the title of one of the excellent films shown on the cinematograph.

div.head: KING CARSON'S
div.p: KING CARSON'S
• TRAVESTY OF ROYALTY. DISCREDITABLE FARCE IN ULSTER.

A discreditable parody of a Royal reception, in which Sir Edward Carson was the principal figure, was a feature of the Ulster demonstra- tion on Wednesday. The - London "Daily Chronicle", correspondent describes the proceedings as follows : .PORTADOWN (Co. Armagh), Sept: 25.

The great Hibernian circus group moved on to Portadown this morning for a matinee perform- ance; supported' by the whole strength of the company. In a saloon carriage were Sir Edward Carson, Mr. F. E. Smith, Lord Londonderry, Mr. J. H. Campbell, and other Members of Par- liament, and this carriage was shunted to the platform nearest to the station entrance. Im- mediately it came to a standstill a band struck up.tbe National Anthem, while every head i'as uncovered. There was a guard of honour on the platform to greet "KING EDWARD THE EIGHTH."

Under the command of Captain Holt Waring, ' the men wore khaki hats and haversacks, and they carried toy rifles, such as those with which boys play in the streets. At the word of coin- " mand they presented arms to "his Majesty." In the station yard was a mounted escort of men, who. wore khaki bats and carried penny canes, with a small Union Jack at the end. They formed up before and behind the "Royal" car- riage as it drove off into the town. cannot say how this exhibition struck others; to me it seemed to be in the very worst possible taste and A GROSS INSULT TO XING GEORGE.

Here was a Privy :Councillor, and a man who expects at some time in his life to hold high office under the real King of Ireland, submitting without a protest, and, indeed, entering heartily into the carrying out of what was an impudent parody upon the reception given, always respect- fully and gladly, to our King when he pays a ceremonial visit to any place in his dominions. One of the witnesses of this discreditable scene was an ornament of the House of Lords. He has held in the past the high position of :Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, yet he actually watched a commoner being received with the National Anthem and saw a number of hobbledehoys With wooden guns presenting arms just as the King's soldiers would do. Yet these are the people who are .always loudly boasting of their loyalty and devotion to the Throne. THE TRAVESTY OF ROYALTY. EVEN TORIES PROTEST.

Sir Edward Carson's amazing travesty of a royal reception has proved too much even for snrii of his Tory friends, among them the "Daily Mai ' whose special correspondent, after wit- net g the "ceremonies" at Portadown on Wed- nesd y, telegraphed to his paper : ! myself am, constrained to suggest that it might be well to omit from the receptions of their leader, Sir Edward Carson. some of the ceremonial which ,is usually reserved for the Sovereign.
That the whole business snggested Royal ceremony is quite evident from the comments of other. Tory correspondents in 1-.lle "Pirminghain Post," "Yorkshire Post," and "Mornin Er, Post."
_ _ The special correspondent of the "Manchester Guardian" endor.es the view of our own repre- sentative by writing :
In a. long experience T have never seen so shameless a travesty of Royalty or of national grandeur, but neither of the Ring's counsellors in the carriage appeared to perceive fAither the _

. , absurdity or insolence _of the proceedings. The "Westminster Gazette" adds that the "lapse This the "Mail" puts it) is all the more remarkable when it is remembered that Sir Ed- ward Carson is a member of his Majesty's Privy Council. THE KING SENDS FOR TORY LEADERS.

It is significant that on Thursday night Mr. Bonar DUN the leader of the Conservative Party." went to Balmoral as the result of a summons from the King Spectlation is rife as to the cause - especially on the eve of Ulster day— and it may be that His Majesty 'intends to express his disapproval of the ridiculous pretensions and treasonable behaviour of Sir Edward ' Carson and his loyal friends in Ulster.

div.head: OUR FILIBUSTERING M.P.
div.p: OUR FILIBUSTERING M.P.
MR. HAROLD SMITH AND HIS HALFPENNY
LOYALISTS.
More Threats of Fighting.

Mr. Harold Smith, MP„ has landed in Ulster. So far there is no news of any active warfare but there will be "wigs on the green" to-day or the Member for Warrington's ehullition of "loyalty "will have failed in its object. Just read the loyal speech delivered by Mr. Harold Smith at the demonstration at New- townardß on Thursday (vide "qa,ichester Guardian.') Mr. Harold Smith, M.P. for Warrington, said he was proud to represent one of the most loyal boroughs throughout the kingdom, and was prouder still in the knowledge that he wrenched a seat from a-Liberal who had more courage than discretion in allying himself openly with the Nationalist party. Mr. Smith read amid much cheering the following message signed by three thousand Warrington citizens •—" Please convey to Sir Edward Carson and the loyalists of Ulster our solemn pledge as citizens of the loyal borough of Warrington to stand by them in their determination to maintain the Union of Great Britain and Ireland. God save the King," He declared that the Government dared not appeal to the great counties of the North of England. If the crisis came thousands of loyalists in England would cross the channel to join their brethren in a fight for the maintenance of liberty and justice. If this is not a clear example of professing loyalty and preaching sedition, then the words have lost their common meaning. We note that Mr. Smith read to the meeting the famous telegram "signed by three thousand Warring- ton citizens '—at a half-penny each. The announce- ment posted in the Conservative Club last week stated that the telegram was to be sent to Mr. Harold Smith to-day—Ulster Day! Apparently the half-pennies have rolled in so fast that the coffers were prematurely filled, or perhaps the Member could not wait any longer. He must have the message to brandish before the 'awe-struck multitude at Newtownarcls on Thursday Three thousand "citizens of the loyal borough of Warrington" at a half-penny each! ['he number is incredible--seen at the price. We hope Mr. Smith will bring his telegram with its three thousand loyal signatures, back to Warrington. So remarkable a missive should be enshrined within the archives at the museuna. There can never have been anything like it in Warrington's long history. And furthermore we should like to see this telegram. Will Mr. Smith kindly produce it for the inspection of his constituents generally, and particularly those whose halfpennies were so handsomely subscribed?

TWO TOPICAL TRIOLETS. t From Ulster. All the world we'll defy— If they'll only ignore us. We'll all do or die The world well defy Though of course we'd fight shy Of a scrap—that would bore us. , The world we'll defy— If they'll only ignore us. 2. From the Rest of Ireland. If Carson were King, With his ould wooden cannon, We'd soon make him sing , If Carson were King, His toy guns we'd fling, Him as well, in the Shannon, If Carson were King . With his ould wooden cannon.

At one of his election meetings, a man in the audience asked President Taft, " What are you going to do about the problem of unemployment?" "God knows 1" replied the President. Might we respectfully suggest that time would be saved if the President consulted our Mr. Bonar Law?— From the "Free Trader."

div.head: MAYORALTY.
div.p: THE MAYORALTY.
Councillor Dr. Joseph Accepts Office for a Third Year.
Councillor Dr. Joseph has acceded to the unanimous request of the Town Council to accept the Mayoralty of Warrington for a third year. . .

At a private meeting of inembers of the Council on Monday, it was moved by the Deputy Mayor (Alder- man Forshaw),seconded by Al&rman Smethurst, and supported by several other speakers, and unanimously resolved that the Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) he invited to accept the office of Mayor for the third and ensuing year. The Deputy Mayor and Alderman Smethurst were appointed to convey the invitation of the Council to the Mayor and report thereon. The deputation having waited upon the Mayor, they informed the meeting that his Worship was prepared to accept office for a third year.

div.head: NEW BOROUGH SURVEYOR, -- Mr. A. M. Kee appointed.
div.p: THE NEW BOROUGH SURVEYOR, -- Mr. A. M. Kee appointed.

The appointment of a successor to the late Borough Surveyor (Mr. Thos. Longdin) came up for consideration at the meeting of the General Purposes Committee, which consists of the whole of the Members of the Town Council, on Monday. The Mayor presided, and paid a high tribute to the long and faithful services which had been rendered to the borough by the late Surveyor. A vote of sympathy with the relatives of the de- ceased was unanimously carried.
After considerable discussion it was decided to recommend the Council to appoint the assistant surveyor, Mr. Andrew M. E'er, to succeed Mr. Longdin at a commencing salary of X. 450 a year. . .

Mr. her was called into the room and informed of the decision of the committee. He thanked the members for the honour which had been con- ferred upon him, and promised to do his utmost to carry out the wishes of the Council.
Photo Birtles. MR. A. M. KER.

Mr. lier, who resides at Newlands, Lower Walton, was born in Cressington Park, Liver- pool, in 1872. He was educated at the Liver- pool Institute High School, and obtained a scho- larship at Victoria University, Liverpool, where he studied in the Walker Engineering labora- tories under Professor Hele Shaw, and graduated with engineering honours. He was afterwards articled to the City Engineer of Hull, and ap- pointed assistant in his office. In 1899 he ob-

iained an appointment, in the City Engineer's office, Birmingham., and in 1900 in the City Engineer's office, Coventry, and.on Aug. 5, 1901, was appointed Deputy Borough Engineer and Surveyor to the Warrington Corporation. He proved an invaluable colleague of the late sur- veyor, and a most efficient servant of the Cor- poration. His thorough knowledge of the work of the department eminently ts him for the post, and his appointment will give general satis- faction.

div.head: UNITED KINGDOM BAND OF HOPE UNION,
div.p: UNITED KINGDOM BAND OF HOPE UNION,

The 44th Autumnal Conference has been held in Liverpool during tbe present week, when over 5,000 delegates fromall parts of the United Kingdom attended to discuss important questions of this great:movement, which represents 396 Bands of Hope or town unions with 33,009 societies and 3,741,000 members ; an army of young abstainers from which great things may be expected in coming years. A notable feature of the U.K.B.H. Union's activity is the day school lecture scheme whereby last year 16 skilled lecturers gave over &GOO lectures attended by 400,000 scholars. Of these 40 per cent, reproduced the substance of the lectures in the forms of essays. During the year 68,917 new recruits have been added to the movement,74s societies having doubled their membership. The Conference opened on Monday morning, September 23rd, in the Central Hall, Renshaw-street, under the presidency of Mr. Lionel Mundy, chairman of the Executive Com- mittee. An address was given by 'Mr G Avery Roff, science lecturer of the U.K.8.11.U. on the use of simple appliances for physiological temperance teaching. ' Questions were answered by the lecturer at the close with respect to the use of alcohol as a stimulant in cases of fainting, the lecturer pointing out that on the highest medical authority, alcohol was not the best restorative in such cases. In the afternoon, on the .invitation of the Lord Mayor of Liverpool, Right Hon. Earl of Derby, the delegates were entertained in the Town Hall.

On Tuesday morning the Conference was resumed, chairman Dr F H Bickerton, Liverpool, and address given by Professor G Sims Woodhead. Cambridge. In the afternoon the Hon. Mrs Elliot, York, president of the Union presided. Papers were read by Miss E Holmes Harvey (Wesleyan Temperance lecturer), Miss F Green, Cardiff and Mr Rowland Hill, J.P., Bedford, dealing with various topics connected with the success- ful work of the movements. 4

On Tuesday iss7enirig—a7-7..3n a great demonstration was held in the large Central Hall, which was crowded. Chairman, Ven. Archdeacon Madden. ;Speakers' Lady Barlow, Rev A T Guttrey, Professor G Simms Woodhead. Special music being rendered by a choir of 300 voices under the conductorship of Councillor P J Tunnicliff.
Wednesday morning, Chairman, Mr Arthur Bluer, papers were read by Mr L C AI Cooke, Mr J W Derby, and Mr J Barker Wells, lecturer, National Health Insurance Commission of Ireland.

In the afternoon, delegates journeyed to Southport when a public meeting was held in the Temperance Institute. The meetings have been largely attended and full of interest throughout and should have the effect of still further spreading the movement in the future. Mr G Whitfield attended the Conference as delegate appointed by the Warrington Band of Hope Union.

div.head: AN EASY WAY TO REMOVE SUPERFLUOUS HAIR.
div.p: AN EASY WAY TO REMOVE SUPERFLUOUS HAIR.

For the benefit of our lady readers who suffer from the humiliating disfigurement of hair on face, lips or chin, we publish herewith a formula which has the advantage of being simple and inexpensive, as well as marvellously effective. It is not claimed by our informant that one application will permanently destroy the hair roots, but it is claimed, and the claims are borne out by actual tests, that one applica- tion completely removes the hair, and its regular use, one or two days apart, will quickly and permanently destroy the hair root itself. If you have hair which you wish permanently removed, ask your chemist to mix 4i drams Pulverized Sulthine Concentrate with drams Zinc Oxide, P. 8., and 1 dram of Powdered Orris Root, and put in a wide mouth bottle. For use mix a little of the powder into a paste on a plate by adding a few drops of water. Apply with a narrow knife blade and remove at the end of two minutes with the back of the knife, when the dissolved hair will come with it. Repeat at intervals of two days. Each time the growth will be less, until it entirely dis- appears. A good non-greasy cream, such as Creme To-lialon, May be used after each application. CAUTION :—This must not be used as a substitute for shaving, as its repeated use completely destroys the hair roots.

In commencing this article I am irresistib?i. reminded of that -Walrus who remarked thal the time had come to talk of many things. . . There is so much that is curious in Law thai . even if one attempts to narrow the field of ex, 0 ploration by means of notice boards which int dicate that Bypaths only are to be traversed. one still has a very- considerable Odyssey perform. However,let us. take heart of grace and remember that it is a better thing to tray& hopefully than to arrive. At the outset let us note carefully that amongst the private perquisites of the Crowr are the head and quarters of a person execute 4 for the crime of high treason, and also the head and tail of a whale. In case anyone hat. a leaning towards high' treason it .may tom. fort, though not, I trust, encourage him,-,te know that the Crown is now .disposed to waive the.question of his head-and quarters. It only insists upon the comparatively triVial detail of hanging by the neck until dead.

QUAINT ROYAL PERQUISITES. • With regard to the whale, however, •things are different, and anyone finding such a crea- ture lying about is earnestly advised to notify - the King and Queen without delay. The King is entitled to the head, and the Queen to the tail, and the reason assigned by ancient re- cords for this division was the necessity of fur- nishing the Queen's wardrobe with Whalebone, a pleasing and kindly thought which ddes more- credit to the record ruaker's ingenuity than to his knowledge of a whale's anatomy, for, the whalebone lies, I believe, entirely in the animal's lead.

In addition to these handsome, adjuncts the Crown is also entitled, after the lapse of a year and a day, and in the absence of any better founded claim, to the proceeds of all ship- wrecks thrown upon this land. The usefulness of this right appears to have been somewhat diminished by legislative enact- ments from Henry the First down- wards. It was solemnly decreed in the days of Edward the First that if a man, 4 dog, or a cat escaped alive the vessel was no wreck; it was subequently established that the animals in onestion had only been mentioned by way .of .xample, and not by reason of any peculiar re- and that the terms of the Act were corn- plied with if any live thing escaped. So that prsesumably one flea was sufficient to save the >ituation and the wreck.

Before dismissing this matter of the BoYal re- renues. and lest anyone should think .we are niggardly in our provision in this respect, it. is only fair to add that the King is entitled to !my stray pig of which no man knoweth the awner, provided the said pig was found wan- lering in any manor or lordship. The King must proclaim the fact, and the pig. in the church and two market towns next adjoining where he found it, and then, if no man claims ic within a year and a day, the pig is his. DBODAND.. The King is also entitled to any extras aris- ing out of his care of idiots, but in these de- generate days he no longer makes anything out of deodands. A. deodand was "any personal . chattel which was the .immeet-iate and accidental occasion of the death of any reasonable , ' creature," and as a punishment 4 was "to be given to God" or the church, or more usually to the King. The ownership of the article made no matter' 60 if a man purloined my sword and plunged it into the person of another, my sword was forfeit all the same. Moreover, if a thing not in motion caused a man's death, that part only which was the immediate cause was for- feited, so that if a man were killed by climbing up the wheel of a stationary cart, and .then. falling down again, the owner of the cart was mulcted to the extent of one wheel only. But if the cart was in motion the whole cart, contents and all, was a deodand, and this, apparently, on the principle of adding insult to injury. The revival of the doctrine of deodand would have a wholesome effect upon motor-ear owners.

Let us turn to the more practical and every- day question of burglary. And here let me warn any would-be burglar that, burgle he never so skilfully the law will have none of liirn,*qUa.' burglar, unless he operates between the hours of 9 p.m. and 6 a.m. Thus if I feloniously break and enter into your hobse and steal your over- coat at 8-59 p.m, I am not a burglar, but if I am one minute and one second later, then I am a burglar.

div.head: Tnin LIMIT, Fort nunmAny.
div.p: A Tnin LIMIT, Fort nunmAny.
Thedistinetion between burglary and house-

breaking is therefore chiefly an ffair of the clock. The former is essentially a desperate affair of darkness, the latter a dissolute deed of daylight. Burglary according to an emi- nent authority "has always been looked upon as a very heinous offence, seeing that it always occasions frightful alarm and often leads to murder itself:" and the definition of the fright- fully alarming burglar is" he that by night breaketh and entereth into a mansion-bouse with intent to commit a felony." The magni- ficence of the phrase the "mansion-house" must not, of course, be taken too seriously, es- pecially in these slays of Socialistic tendencies. For every man's house is essentially his castle in this respect, and there's no place like home, and no place like prison for him who burgla- riously invades its privacy. In order to burgle, however, the miscreant must not only operate in legal darkness; he must also both break and enter, but not necessarily at one and the sante time. The law is pleased to concede that a. breaking one night and an entry the next night, through the same hole, will suffice. There must, however, be an actual breaking, and any- one with a liklog for fresh air has only. himself to blame if, by leaving a window open on a hot summer's night he invites the attention of "Sikes, housebreaker, of Houndsditch." It has been decided that to enter by coming down a. chimney will qualify for the offence, for a chim- ney is 88 much closed as the nature of the thing will admit. Further, if you are humorist enough to procure a constable to gain admit- tance in order to search for alleged traitors, and then to gaily bind the constable and pro- ceed to rob the house at your leisure, this too is burglary, for the law has little sense of • humour, and dislikes being jested with. OLD STATTJTDS AND SUNDAY TRADING. Some curious results occur from the conser- -cativo way in which we cling to 'a few old statutes which have long since lost all real ap- plicability to the affairs of the present day. Thus the question of Sunday trading is still regulated by an ~,k_ct of Clrarlee the Second which says that no tradesmen shall do any worldly labour of his ordinary calling upon the Lord's Day. The penalty is only 55., and is not cumulative, so that only one ss. can be ex- tracted for any number of offences; committed by the same person on the same day. Hence the !man has only to make a profit of over se. to enable him to snap his fingers with derision and. a pair of scissors (assunaing that he is a hair ' cutter) at the majesty of the law. It will surprise most people perhaps to learn that the same Act constitutes it a punishable offence to cry milk between the hours of 9 asn. and 4 p.m. on a Sunday, the punishment being the forfeiture of the milk. The subject of sports and pastime ,s on a Sun- day is governed by an Act of George the Third, which decrees that "There shall be no meet- ings, assemblies or concourse of people out of their own parishes sin the Lord's Day for any sports and pastimes whatsoever, nor any bear baiting, bull baiting, interludes, common plays or any unlawful exercises and pastimes used by any person or persons within their own parishes." We are no longer addicted to bear or bull baiting. Whether we "use'interludes" or not I know not. But what of cricket, and. tennis, and golf? Well, fit we pick up a side amongst our own fellow parishioners and play strictly within our own parish we shall be safe enough, provided no local bye-laws hinder. But if we play (oh lofty .ambition!) for our panel]. against another parish, the game is illegal, and the penalty is 36. 4d., to be given to the poorl

div.head: Borough Police Court.
div.p: Borough Police Court.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair) Alder- men Smethurst, Bolton and Tinnion, Messrs W Roberts, S Wright, W Furness sad T Locker. BIS FIRST APPEARANCE.—James Taylor,labourer, 45, Hume-street was charged with having stolen 60 yards of cloth wrapping value 90s. the property of the St Helens Cable Co., Ltd.—Prisoner pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable stated that Sergeant Reddington was making inquiries withfregard to some stolen property at the pawnshop of Messrs. Domville, Church.street, and was examining some bundles of clothing pledged by Mrs Taylor, when he discovered quantities of the cloth wrapping. Knowing that Taylor had been engaged at the Cable Works and that cloth similar to that which he found was dealt out to the men he taxed the prisoner about the theft. Taylor admitted it. In almost every place in his house there were quantities of stolen wrapping.—Prisoner said that was his first time before the Court.—The Mayor : It is a very bad first time, representing systematic theft. You will be fined .£1 and costs, £2 Is in all, or a month. UNFIT TO TASTE BEER.—Michael COarl, of no fixed abode was charged with having been drunk and dis- orderly, also with having done wilful damage to a quantity of crockery and with having assaulted Sergeant Metcalfe.—Wwas stated by Sergeant Metcalfe that he was in the Market-place on Saturday evening, when he was informed that a man had wilfully smashed a lot of crockery at the White Hart Hotel. He followed Coen, who was brandishing a walking stick in the air. Vhen he asked the man what he had b4en doing, the only answer he got was " Stand back." Coan then struck him with the stick on the shoulder. With the assist- ance of two civilians he got the man to the Police Station. It appeared that Coen was refused drink at the White Hart Hotel. In revenge he swept a dozen plates and nine dishes off a table with his stick. An hour previously he had been refused drink at the Blue Bell Inn, and there broke some glasses. When charged he replied : "1 don't remember anything about it."—Prisoner : No, and I don't sir. It is three months since I bad a gill of beer before.— The Chief Constable said the man was simply mad with drink. Anyone who visited the town and behaved in that manner ought to be made an example of.—The Mayor: You are not fit to taste drink, Coen. You will go to gaol for two months. POLICE ASSAULT.—Thomas Crosby, lodging at 10, Stanley-street, and John Higgins, a labourer, of Higher Walton, were sentenced to seven days' imprisonment for having been drunk and disorderly. Crosby was also charged with having assaulted Constable Armstrong.— The officer stated that Crosby was fighting Higgins. Both were drunk, and when witness interfered, Crosby attacked him, throwing him to the ground, and injuring his shoulder. He was now under the care of the police surgeon.

TUESDAY.—Before Councillor C. Jackson Holmes (in the chair) and Colonel Edelsten. FOLLOWED HER HUSEBAND IN THE DOCK.—Ellea Taylor, of 45, Hume-street, whose husband bad been convicted of theft the previous day, was charged with having stolen a lady's gold watch and chain, and also with stealing a quantity of underclothing, the property of Mrs. ball, 88, Orford-lane. Prisoner pleaded guilty to the first charge but denied the second. The Chief Constable said that during the week commencing August 19th, Mrs. Rhoda Rhodes, 23, Hume-street, the owner of the watch, was ill in bed. Neighbours assisted to do her housework and on August 23rd the prisoner went across to the house to ask if she could do anything. Mrs. Rhodes asked her to get some handkerchiefs from a drawer in which the watch and chain was kept. On August 26th Mrs. Rhodes missed the watch and chain. She reported the matter to the police, who interviewed the woman, without result. Sergeant Reddington continued inquiries and saw the prisoner in Arpley-street. He taxed her with the theft, which she at first denied, Afterwards she admitted having stolen the watch and chain, which she had concealed in a hedge near the Barracks. In the second case a man named Ball and his wife' who arrived from Shropshire, workless, lodged with the prisoner. While Ball searched for work his wife had to go into the Workhouse. She left behind her a box containing clothing. When she left the union she called for the box. A portion of the clothing was missing. She reported the matter to the police. It was found that the prisoner and her children were wearing some of the things. Evidence was given by Mrs Ball, a pawnbroker's assiltant and Sergeant Reddington,to whom the prisoner 'offered the explana- tion that Mrs Ball left the things lying about the house. Prisoner : lam very sorry about the watch, I will lead a different life if you will forgive me this time.—The woman was sent to gaol for two months on the first charge, and for a month on the second, the sentences to run concurrently. WHEELS AND WOE.—Robert Cunningham, a Sheflield youth with a remarkable record of crime for one so young, was sent to goal for four months for stealing a bicycle, the property of William Forster, 10, Dutton- street, Warrington. On the 23rd August he hired a bicycle at the shop of the prosecutor for two hours, but failed to return with it. The police were notified, but no trace of the bicycle was obtainable until the 16th inst, when the youth surrendered himself to the Doncaster Police.

T CRSDAY.—Before Mr J Rymer Young (in the chair) Messrs W Roberts, A J Jolley and W I.` Williams. ALLEGED THEFT OF BOOT",—Annie Humphreys, 12„ Philip-street, was charged with stealing a pair. or boots from the pawnshop, 75, Orford-lane, value 3.. 6d., the property of Benedict Tyrer. The Chief Constable stated that at about 7.30 the previous night the prisoner scent to Tyrer's shop in Winwick-street and offered the boots in pledge. The manager examined them and found that they bore the private mark of his firm. He communicated with another branch and it was ascertained that the woman had stolen the boots from the Orford-lane shop. When taxed with the theft she at first denied it, but subse- quently admitted that she had taken the bDots. She was a regular customer at the Orford-lane shop. Her house bad been searched and 30 or 40 pawn tickets were found. The Chief Constable asked for a remand until to-day. His request was granted. " PROTECTOR " FlNED.—Walter Day, Charlton-street, Latchford was summoned for assaulting Martha Violet Maurice Sheriff!, off, Charlton-street on the 21st inst. —Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant and said that on Saturday afternoon it was reported to Mr Sheriff that a certain neighbour of the defendant's had been charging him with having circulated a report about another neighbour. Mr. Sheriff went to ask for an explanation whereupon the defendant without the slightest provocation rushed into the yard and struck at him hut missed and then without another word went up to Miss Sheriff and, dealing her a violent blow in the face said "Take that, you little bitch."— Defendant said that he was called in the yard by the neighbour to pro- tect ber from Mr Sheriff. The girl Martha had said something about his wife.—The neighbonr who Mr Sheriff interviewed said no blows were struck at all.— Defendant was ordered to pay 10a (part of the costs of the case.)

FRlDAY.—Before Mr S Wright in the chair), Alderman Tinnion and rierpoint, Messrs W Furness, A J Jolley and T Locker. THEFT OF BOOTS.—Sarnuel Lloyd, of no fixed address, was charged with having stolen a pair of boots value 7s, the property of Mr Herbert Buokby, 67, Lexton st, on the 21st inst.—The Chief Constable said that tbe prisoner called in the shop on Saturday after- noon with a parcel under his arm. He stood by the counter, on which was a pair of boots which had been repaired and made up ready for the owner. Mr Buckby was busy, and the prisoner talked to him for a time and then left. The boots were then missed and Mr Buckby reported the matter to the police.—Detective-Sergeant Holland made inquiries, and found that the prisoner bad sold the boots for sixpence, to a woman who kept a lodging-honse.—lie interviewed the prisoner and taxed him with regard to the shoes, but he denied any knowledge of them. Subsequently charged at the police station the prisoner said he had taken the boots by mistake.—Lloyd was sent to prison for one month with hard labour.

LEAP FROM RUNAWAY ENGINE. A traction engine descending a steep hill !leer Kilkenny got out of control, and a youth named Biller, who P 71113 at the steering wheel, leaped off, sustaining njurips which caused his death.

across the Severn is in a lovely situation. The Tuesday was the wettest day since leaving Appledore. At Pershore Bridge we found some campers close by the river and pitied them. Time and again we bad to shelter as we approached Stratford-on-Avon, and just as we went into the Fountain Hotel (unlicensed) for tea the downpour was terrific, and continued more or less till we reached Warwick. The Wednesday also was showing the same tendency, and at Kenilworth we decided to train it home from Lichfield. We avoided Birmingham by taking the road through Colesh ill, a once fine highway spoiled by the motor pits, all filled then with water. As we approached the fatal Lichfield the skies improved and during tea the evening came out gloriously. So we took our photos and decided to stick to our own wheels for another day. That evening we rode through Rugeley, and on up the river Trent to Stone. There we found the best unlicensed hotel in the whole tour. It is the Granville, which has lately changed hands. If anyone keeps these notes and proposes to go the same round from Warrington another year or any part of it, he cannot do better than take it the opposite,way get for- ward the fifty or so miles to Stone and stay at this comfortable place fur the first night. The road north- wards was truly a surprise to me. It is a good many years certainly since I was in Newcastle but the roads have been improved out of all recognition. That last half day's ride was the quickest of all, through Rode Heath. Holmes Chapel and Knutsford. Total 041 miles in 10 days of which 14 were spent on the wheel.

div.head: CYCLIST'S NOTE-BOOK.
div.p: THE CYCLIST'S NOTE-BOOK.
[By " Silver Street."l
THE END OF THE SEASON.

As most club fixtures end with September, I have asked the Editor to give me a holiday till next season commences, and so I will say au revoir with this article. As to the winter care of a machine, it will be very little different from that needed during this heathenish summer. But don't put it away. Winter riding is very often a treat, and one is surprised to find what new aspects the country wears when the trees are leafless, and what a lot of new houses one can see between the bare trunks of the trees—and ' there are no flies. And Mr. R. Redbreast's songs are worth listening to, now he has practised them aud got more acquainted with the difficult score.

_ I don't recommend straps, &c., fixed round the hubs to keep them bright. It wears the plating very rapidly. If you are keeping your eye on the price you may some day get for the machine, take a small paint brush and with a good brushful fvaseline give them a coat. Not a " skinny" one, but a deep, luscious plaister, like unto the Acrican's coat of mud and grease. Then the dust will cleave unto your vaseline, and form a stiff cake which may be removed next spring. And if you wish to sell it then, he who cometh to buy will look for the image of his face in the shining silver, and seeing it vk ill empty his pockets in the delight which striketh him as he leadeth home his old-new steed. And so you will both be satisfied.

div.head: THROUGH SHAKESPEARE LAND.
div.p: THROUGH SHAKESPEARE LAND.

As we travelled up the Severn valley from Bristol to Gloucester, on the fastest main road in England we could see even thus early the havoc wrought in the cornfields by the excessive rain,where the tops of corn sheaves and haycocks were just peeping above the water. We spent the night at Tewkesbury, the bill for supper, bed and breakfast, all comfortable, at the York Restaurant being 4s. 4d. for two. I don't know any town where there are more old shops with over- hanging upper floors, and the Lower Lode Ferry

gale that had developed since 10 o'clock, and at the bottom of Cherry-lane a council of war was held. It was a happy inspiration of one member to propose Pickmere as a diversion. We arrived at Smithy Cottage at tea-time, having left two on the road mend- ing a burst tyre. These rejoined us as we were finishing tea, bringing up the number to 18, not a bad muster for the last ride but one. The lake was ' attractive, as usual, and as the sun was just setting and the moon rising, the majority of the party took to the" feathering oar" (I think that is the most polite way of putting it), and dropped a few late and unex- pected shekels into the boatmen's bands before the time came to return. This was done by Tabley and Mere Corner.
Lamp time to-night 6-16 ; next Saturday 6.30. WARRINGTON CYCLING CLUB. CLOSE OF THE SEASON.

The club brought its cycling season to a close on Saturday with a meeting of members at Sankey Chapel House. There was an excellent attendance, and the weather was all that could be desired to make the final fixture a successful one. During the afternoon a progressive bowling main was carried out on the green,:proving enjoyable to all, and throughout the afternoon keen interest was centred in the games. In all there were eight games of five ends each played, and the results by the score cards handed in showed the winners of the prizes to be :-1, T Boyd; 2, P Freeman; 3, R Redfern; 4, (.1 H Anderton and 0; E Birtles.

• At the close of the main members adjourned to do Justice to an excellent tea provided by Mrs Unsworth, and this was followed by the annual distribu- tion of prizes and concert. The musical programme was of the usual high order associated with the club's gatherings, and was greatly enjoyed by the company present. The opening item for violin, and piano The Doye's March' by Messrs Percy Smith and flainsworth brought for them well deserved applause. This was followed by a song" The sailor's dance " ably rendered by Mr Percy Bailey. Mr J Willett with " My dreams " showed that he has lost none of his reputation as a tenor. Mr. G. H. Smith pleased his audience with his humorous version of " The pale

div.head: WESLEYAN CYCLING CLUB.
div.p: WESLEYAN CYCLING CLUB.
The run put down on the club card for gaturdsy was to Northenden, but by the time Lymm was reached most of us had had enough of the easterly

young curate," whilst Mr Hainsworth showed himself to be a player of talent with his violin solo " Saint D'Amour." Mr. F. Fieldhouse disposed of the pro- logue from P Pagliacci with credit to himself. " Gentlemen the King" was given by Mr. T. Critchley and was well assisted in the chorus. A second item given by Mr. P. 0. Bailey " Come sing to me " WAS received with applause. Mr. J. Willett's second song " The sailor's grave " brought for him call for encore to which he responded. Mr. F. Fieldhouse gave a new song" A jug of beer" for which he was encored and in response sang " Four jolly smiths" with a swinging chorus. A fitting ending to the very excellent programa was a duet "The moon has raised her lamp above" by Messrs. J. Willett and F. Fieldhouse. . .

Durinithe evening the distribution of prizes won in the season was made by the captain (Mr. G. 11. Anderton), who discharged his duties in a very able manner. The prizes were awarded as follows : Principal Bowling Handicap. —1 and Watkins Cup, Mr S Hassall ; 2, Mr W Brown; 3, Mr G Bowman; 4, Mr H Whittle. Fit st Consolation Handicap.-1, F Freeman; 2, J T Smith.
Second Consolation Handicap.-1, T P Thronell ; 2, A G Robertson.
' Third Consolation Handicap.-1, C A Berry ; 2, W Hoult.
Fishing Match.— 1, J Podmore ; 2, W Brown; 3, J E Birtles.

Run Attendances.-1, J B Poole; 2, C H Hoult ; 3, C A Berry and G H Anderton. A successful closing fixture was brought to a t.rmination by votes of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Unsworth for their kindness during the season to the artistes, and the captain for presiding.

div.p: LORD ROBERTS, OCTOGENARIAN.

Field Marshal Earl Roberts reaclies his Although old as years go, the great Field eightieth birthday on Monday next. A great Marshal is still energetic and active. Our celebration is being organised by the National photograph shows Lord Roberts etanding by Service League, and steps have been taken one of his trophies at Englemere, his Berk. for the inauguration of a popular testimonial. rhire home.

div.head: YOUNG LIBERALS.
div.p: YOUNG LIBERALS.
Lancashire and Cheshire Federation's Activities.

The devotion of the month of October to a Liberal municipal campaign was one of the principal features put forward at the quarterly meeting of the Council of the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation of the National League of Young Liberals, held at Blackpool on Satur- day, when over one hundred delegates were present. The report of the executive, presented by the bon. secretary (Mr J W Percy Smith), urged this step, with the Young Liberals' municipal programme as a basis. The Executive Committee had directed its efforts mainly to the re-establishment of one or two branches whichhad lapsed—the number remained the same-102— and to the undertaking of new phases of organization. The formation of a Young Liberals' land policy was in process. A scheme had been drafted whereby the federation hoped to be of assistance at by-elections in the two counties. Open-air meetings in the constitu- encies were proposed to be addressed entirely by , speakers belonging to the federation. It was proposed to create a new office by the appointment of a chair- man. Finances showed an improved position, there being a balance in hand of £l7. The President (Mr Robert Hopwood, of Stockport) said that in their organisation they were leaving ' nothing to chance, for chance seldom paid a dividend. Liberalism was said to be under a cloud, but it was Tory misrepresentation that was in the shade. The prizes offered by Mr Cuthbert C Grundy, Black- pool, for essays on Dome Rule were awarded as ' follow A Fulton, Manchester. 2, Mr Daniels, Wilmslow ; 3, Mrs Dicky, Stockport, Mr Ratcliffe Walker, and Mr L Moss, Stockport ; under twenty years, Mr Carrington, Chapel-en-le-Frith ; Blackpool brancm Mr Whittaker.

Peter's Church

The harvest festival at St. Peter's Church com- menced on Thursday evening. The church had been tastefully decorated for the occasion by members of the congregation. Mrs Percival, Mrs Graves and Mrs Taylor were responsible for the chancel; Mrs Steel, Mrs Cowdell and Mrs Webster, for the chancel screen and pulpit ; the Misses Ince for the choir stalls ; Mrs E Clayton, Mrs F Webster and Mrs McQuillam for the font ; and the Misses Percival for the pillars and windows. The Vicar conducted the service, the special lessons being read by the Rev J H Garnett, curate. Mr E A Padmore presided at the organ Special hymns and an anthem were excellently rendered by the choir. The preacher was the Ven. Archdeacon Spooner, who took for his text Job. v. 20 : " Like RE a shock of corn cometh up in his season." He intro- duced his subject by alluding to the feeling expresred in some quarters against the holding of harvest festivals this year owing to the damage done to crops by the bad weather in the summer months, and pointed out that it was still true that everything cometh in its season, though it might be a little previous, or there might be a little delay in some parts. There was an organized system both in the natural world and in the spiritual world, and it was still true that there was au abundant harvest throughout the world. God had provided for all His creatures. He then proceeded to draw a number of lessons for daily life, and showed the unreasonable- ness of hoping to reap a good harvest from anything but good and suitable seed. The offertory was on behalf of special church expenses.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S A. Society.

There was a meeting of this society on Sunday after- noon, presided over by Mr. Jos. Owen. Mr. George Smiley, gave the address on" He was sent to heal the broken-hearted." Mr. Smiley narrated some of his experiences with people in sore trouble, showing God's goodness and mercy to those in great straits of sorrow. God had wrought out deliverance for them in His own way and time. Mr. Arthur Pearce sang, 'Eternal love "in a pleasing manner. Mr. Payton presided at the organ. Mr. C. Cotton read the lesson and Mr. Healey led the prayer. One new member received a hearty welcome. A vote of sympathy was passed to Mr. Frank Brown and his wife in the accident which had befallen tbem, coupled with thankfulness to Almighty God for the deliverance He had wrought out for them. A send-off was given to Mr. Scott, a member leaving to-day for Canada.

Primitive Methodist Church. Harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sunday at Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church. The interior of the building bad been suitably decorated for the occasion and the effect was very pleasing. The preacher for the day was the Rev W Cooper, who spoke in the morning from the words " Although the flg-tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines, the labour of the olive shall fail and the fields shall yield 113 meat, the flock shall be cut off from the fold and there shall be no herd in the stalls ; yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will joy in the God of my salvation." The evening's discourse was based npon the text " Whatsoever a man soweth that shall he also reap." The soloists for the evening anthems were Miss Wild and Mr W Clayton. In the afternoon the choir gave a creditable rendering of Jessop's cantata " The Galilean." The soloists were Mrs Hoyle, the Misses M Jones, Woodland and H Spruce, Messrs J Phillips and W Clayton, all members of the choir. The chair was taken by Mr A E Hoyle. B.A. Mr A Spruce was the conductor, Mr Banner officiated at the organ, and the Rev W Cooper gave a brief exposition of the work. On the following evening a fruit banquet was held under the presidency of Mr J B Starkey. Fruit was distributed and an excellent programme was provided by the following artists :—Legh-street Trio Party, Misses M Jones, Woodland and H Spruce ; soloist, Mrs Hoyle ; reciters, Miss Edwards and Mr J Shaw ; Miss Spruce and Mr Hoyle acted as pianoforte accompanists. All the services were well attended and this has proved to be one of the best harvest festivals in the church's history.

div.head: Empty Chapels.
div.p: Empty Chapels.
Advice to Lancashire Congregationalists.

Milton Congregational Chapel, Widnes, was the meet- ing place of the Autumnal Conference of the Lancashire Congregational Union. Mr .1 B Leach, of Huyton, the newly-elected district chairman, presided over a good number of representatives. The Chairman said that forty-eight years ago a Con- gregational Church was established in the industrial town of Widnes. Many difficulties bad been faced during that period. They could not stand still any longer, and it was time to consider and discuss grave matters that had arisen. One of the vital questions that should be taken in hand immediately was that of free seating in church. To 'eservo a few seats for poor creatures was not a step in the right direction.for poverty should not be marked in any way like that. They were going in the direction of free pens and free , churches. From the beginning to the end of the past I half-century congregations were beginning to grow lees. Hundreds and thousands of pounds of church property in this country was locked up from Sunday to Sunday. and no means was offered to people to visit houses of God for the purpose of prayer in the week. It had been his painful business to investigate the cause of empty churches. His observations pointed to the terrible fact that fully seven-tenths of the seats in Liverpool churches were empty. The pulpit had been quiet over this matter of the shrinking congregations. People at present were satorated with the desire for sports and pastimes, and if the ministry were to obey the Master's call they would have to do their utmost to carry Christ to the people. He exhorted his hearers to consider his remarks with reference to seats. The full churches were the free churches. The people were waiting outside to be told of the love of Christ, but every effort should be made to make it easy for them to enter the churches. The catering for worldly pleasures was enormous, for in Liverpool alone there were thirty picture palaces, six more in course of erection,besides eleven theatres.Pully 45,000 people were catered for each night, and vet the churches were empty A discussion followed, and at the evening service there was a crowded congregation.

div.head: Welcome to the New Pastor of the Welsh
div.p: Welcome to the New Pastor of the Welsh
Chapel.

On Thursday, September 19th, at the Welsh Chapel, Crosfleld-street, a social and tea was held at 5.30 p.m., and Induction Service at 7.30 p.m., under the chair- maruhip of Mr Evan E Hughes (one of the deacons.) Welcome speeches to the new Pastor were delivered by the Chairman, Mr John Ilumpbreys (senior deacon), Mr Thomas W T Williams, J.P., Mr Robert (on behalf of the Diaconite), and on behalf of the Church members by Mr William Jones, Mr John Griffiths (L. & N.-W.), and Mr D J Price. Solos by Mrs W T Williams, Miss Jennie Roberts (P. 0. Miss Nellie Thomas; recita- tions by Miss Richards and Master alynne Parry Jones. The Rev. W. Wycliffe Congregational Church. The Rev. Stanley H. Stowell, M.A., of Abingdon, occupied the pulpit at this church on Sunday. In an address to the children at the morning service be told a story of a Prince and his love for his garden. He asked the peach tree, the oak tree, the grass and the daisy what they were doing for him. He urged the children to be like the daisy and make the world bright, and beautiful. The sermon was I ased on the text "So I am with you always, even unto the end of the world " (Matthew xxviii., 20.) He showed that the disciples to whom the words were addressed, had their taults, their weaknesses and their failings like ours.lves. Doubt rather than faith seemed to be a more Irequent characteristic of the present day. No amount of theological reasoning would convert the world to Christ; it was the Christian life that would convince. The only convincing argument that could be given to the world that Jesus Christ was the Saviour of mansind lay in the faithful and consistent lines of His followers. Mr. Stowell's evening sermon was taken from Luke xiiic., 24v. " Strive to enter in at the strait gate." Mr Stowell said all great teachers expose themselves t° the risk of questions which show how the ourport, of their teaching has been misunderatnod. MORE HOWLERS.

_ I much prefer he schoolboy's bowlers, even when there's a shrewd suspicion that they have been manu- factured by a brother of the quill (or, rather fountain pen) who is no longer entitled to be so designated. I take this to be one of tbe latter's effusions :—" Sir 1 Walter Raleigh," wrote the boy, " was a great man. He discovered America—then he di.covered Virginia - then he discovered potatoes, and then he discovered tobacco. So he went back to England and showed them how to smoke, exclaiming, My friends, be of good cheer, for we have this day in England lit such a flame as I trust by God's grace shall never be extinguished.", "Some boys' answers," quoted by Uncle Caleb a week ago, may reasonably be considerei genuine and not made to order. I note that the examples were from an American source. Elsewhere, I have met with some good" howlers" reported from a school examination in B rooklyn. "The blood flows through the alimentary canal into the abdominal canopy." " Shakespeare was a fiction and allegorical writer. His mist intimate friend was rare Ben Butler, who was also a great fiction writer." This ansvver will not, perhaps, be as readily appreciated in England as in America, where Ben Butler was nice a prominent, not to ssy notorious, politician. The best " howler " on the list is that " William the Conqueror was the first of the Mormons." It was a small form " plunger" who guessed— Henri the Second instituted trial by perjury." As for ambiguous answers, this is not bad :--" Which was the greater general, Ceesar or Hannibal ?" asked the inspector. "If we consider who Crcsar and Hannibal were," answered the bright lad, "and ask curse] yes which was the greater, we must unhesitat- ingly answer in the affirmative." I have talked with school teachers about these things, and have been repeatedly assured that many of the " howlers " that one naturally looks upon with suspicion could at almost any time be matched in any of our schools.

div.head: iCHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
div.p: iCHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
HOW MARBLES ARE MADE.

I read the other day a description of the making of marbles, and as all boys (perhaps all girls too) have played games with marbles I thought everybody would be interested. The stone marble is made in Saxony. They are packed and exported in large quantities to America and England and also to China, India and the East. A hard calcareous stone is used. This is broken into square blocks, and about one hundred and fifty of these blocks are thrown into a mill, in which is a flat slab of stone with numerous concentric furrows on its face. A block of oak of the same diameter as the stone, a part of which rests on the small stones, is made to revolve on the slab while water flows upon it. In the course of a quarter of an hour the square blocks have become round and smooth and the marbles are taken out ready for use. The coloured marbles get their colour by being passed through another machine in which they are rolled in a similar way. The white marbles are made from another kind of stone, and there is a mill at Nalie, in Germany which manufactures marbles.made from agate especially for the American market.
A single small mill can turn out twenty thousand marbles in a week, and whole villages full of mills are going all the year round to keep up the demand for marbles.

div.head: BOY'S ESSAY ON BREATHING.
div.p: A BOY'S ESSAY ON BREATHING.

Here is another example of what a boy can do when he tries. It is the essay of a nine-year-old on" The function of the lungs and breathing " ; "Breath is made of air. We breathe with our lungs, our lights, our livers, and our kidneys, If it wasn't for breath we would die when we slept. Our breath keeps the life a-going through the nose, when we are asleep. Boys that stay in a room all day should not breathe. They should wait till they get out of doors. Boys in a room make carbonicide. Carbonicide is the most poisonous of living things, dead or alive." •

WHEN 1 GROW UP. Our grocer's clerk comes every day, Though why he should I cannot say, For mother mostly orders beans, And soap and mustard, salt and greens, And tea and starch, and lard and rice— Not much of anything that's nice. Such food for some folks may seem best, But scarce excites my interest. When I grow up, my grocer's clerk Will very seldom need to work ; The butcher's boy 1,11 ask to call Just once in spring and once in fall. I'll have the candy boy call twice Each day, and sometimes even thrice ! Mornings it will be best, I judge, To order caramels and fudge ; At night a box of chocolate creams. To make sure of pleasant dreams. I mean to have the toy-shop man Stop just as often as he can. Now toys grow tiresome soon, you know, And then one's friends do break them so ! Heigh ho ! What bliss will fill my cup When I grew up ! When I grow up !
