div.head: hAIRDRESSER'S LIABILITY. CUT By SCISSORS. –
div.p: hAIRDRESSER'S LIABILITY. CUT By SCISSORS. -

Judgment bas been given at Birmingham County Court by his Honour Judge Ruegg in a case which raised a point of supreme importance in regard to the liability of hairdressers to customers. The action was brought by a bank clerk against Messrs. Steel and Co., of Birmingham, to recover damages for injury alleged to have been caused by the negligence of an assistant employed by the company in cutting the plaintiff's hair. The operator broke the skin of the necit with the point of the scissors, and, according to medical evidence, the wound gave entrance ta the germ known as impetigo. The jury found that the wound was negligently caused, and that without it the plaintiff would not have suffered, but they were not satisfied that the disease was actually contracted in the shop. After hearing legal arguments his Honour held that the disease was not the natural or probable result of the negligence, and that the damage was therefore too remote to be recoverable. He gave judgment for the defendants, but granted a stay of execution, and ex- premed the hope that the case would be carried further.

It is almost incredible to relate that this graduate of four Universities and chaplain to the Lord Protector's son became the minister of Burtonwood. Its tiny wooden chapel hidden in the midst of one of Lancashire's great forests, was surely the last place in which such a man might be expected, and speculation scarcely helps us in an effort to attribute a cause. Was it a scholar's love of books that endeared the solitude, or was it a remembrance of the cottage not far away at Lowton round which his childish memories gathered ? The Parliamentary Commissioners, whose report upon Warrington has already been quoted, described Burtonwood as an" uncon- venient place." The same adjective might have been applied to the income, which is given as four pounds nineteen shillings per annum with a house and orchard valued at two pounds five. The choice of a brilliant scholar to preach amid the woods and wilds and be" passing rich" on seven pounds ten a year gives one earnestly to think.. Yet it was but one incident in the annals of a family whose history, in many aspects, made real romance for a hundred years. His father had pas3ed forth from a tiny home, (until two years ago the hen-cote of a small farm),to become a shaping factor in the New World, to rear sons whose intellectual power is still felt and whose works fill pages in the library catalogues of America. To this brilliant family Samuel Mather belonged and when the Act of Uniformity ejected him from his wooden chapel he travelled to Ireland to find a sphere of use- fulness. In a hired house in Dublin he gathered a congregation and, though dis- turbed by the soldiery and often persecuted, preached there until his death in 1671.

KING JAMES' EFFORTS AT EXTERMINATION. The accession of James 11. a Roman Catholic king, brought fresh dilemmas to Protestant dissenters and was the beginning of new persecution. Making an excuse of the Protestant rebellions under Argyll in Scot- land and under Monmouth in the South he enforced the laws against Ncnconformists, and in Judge Jefferies found a man only a little more cruel and coarse than himself. The scene in Jefferies' Court when Richard Baxter was brought before him will always be remembered. It was typical of the man and of the hour. "This is an old rogue " cried Jefferies " a schismatical knave, a hypocritical villain." Baxter was fined and imprisoned and, had the judge gained his way, would have been flogged through the streets at the cart WI. This was King James' "Short and easy way with the dissenters," but he was to learn when it was too late that repression was impossible either at the stake or the cart tail.

Nonconformity lost nothing in its dark days. Its ministers were the noblest men that English religion could show and had lived and suffered long enough to secure a very real and widespread sympathy. More important still, the distrust of Romanism deepened and Protestant feeling became keener with the passing of the unhappy years. The country was ripening for a change and the change was to come more rapidly and more strangely than the most ardent Protestant could have dared to hope. Whilst Protestants in England were suffer- ing inprison the Scotch Covenanters were fighting their battle upon the hill sides. Unwilling to yield the principle of liberty they suffered torture and martyrdom at the hands of King James's brutal executioner Graham of Claverhouse. As though to give further illustration of what Popery meant, France witnessed a fresh outbreak against the Huguenots who fled to England in thousands. Romanism became loathsome to the English mind. Pro- testant leaders entered into negotiation with William of Orange, and in 1688, after send-

when dying made a statement that he desired his wife to inherit all he had. This incident is described in what is known as a Nuncupative Will, a process which the law only now allows to soldiers and sailors. Impria. That upon Tuesday the 3rd of July . 1683 the above-named Samuel Yates being in his ' own house in Warrington sick of his last sick- ness did make and declare his last Will and dispose of and give and bequeath his goods and chattels with a full mind and intention that the same words should stand for his last Will in the presence of credible witnesses and the same day bee departed this life. With this goes a paper signed by Jonathan IBrereton, surgeon, aged 34, Mary Leech wife of Samuel Leech, draper, aged 55, and Thomas Deane.

MEMOR-A-N-1)-U.M, That upon Tuesday the 3rd day of July, in the year of our Lord God 1683, Samuel Yates of Warrington, in the County of Lancaster, gentleman died, being in his own dwelling Luso weak in body and sick of the sickness whereof he died, but of good and perfect memory and understanding. And it being enquired of him by his Phisitian whether he bad settled his estate and disposed of his concernes. The said Samuel 'answered noe, but I would have you to take notice that what I have I give to my wife for I have nobody else to give it too, to which the Phisitian answering, your wife and child you mean. Ile replied you may well imagine I include my child, or to that purpose, which said words. Noe, but I would have you to take notice that which I have I give to my wife, for I have nobody else to give it to, And you may well imagine I include my child. The said Samuel did utter and declare wiih a mind and intent that the same should stand for his Will in the presence and hearing of three or more credible witnesses and the same day departed this life. Witnesses of this will the substance whereof was drawn into writing the sixth day of July above said,
J. BRE RETON, THOMAS DEANE, MARY LEECH.

These documents were accepted and Dorothea Yates received Probate in due course. William Bispham signs as Surrogate and Thomas Wainwright, before whom Robert Yates' will had been sworn, gives his signature also. PETER ASPINWALL.

In succession to Samuel Yates, Peter Aspinwall appears to have been chosen by the congregation. As a young minister of 26 years he had been ejected in 1662 from the Church at Heaton in Lancashire. Ten years later he had accepted a license and become the minister of a congregation meet- ing "in the howse of John Robinson in Ashton."

The date of his settlement with the War- rington meeting has not been ascertained. His period of service to the cause closed in 1696 with his death. Two entries in the Parish Church register record his marriage and burial. 1684. May. Mr. Peeter Aspinwall to Ellen Blaeklidge, ye Oh day. 1696. June. Buried Mr. Peter Aspinwall ye twenty third day. A NEW ERA DAWNS.

Hope and anxiety stirred the hearts of the Nonconformists during the closing years of the reign of James 11., which melted into joyous satisfaction at the news of the coming of William of Orange. Henry Newcomb's journal reflects the prevalent feeling: Oct. 7, 1088. Now was the amazing news of the Prince of Orange designing to come among us. Oct. 16. Things are dark and in great con- fusion. The Lc:Q(l be merciful to us ! Nov. 9. The news came this morning of the landing of the Dutch in the West. An astonish- ing Providence. Our refuge is in God and in Him only. An "astonishing Providence "did indeed mark the coming of William. Had he landed at the place arranged it is probable that battle would have been waged and the issue might have been doubtful, but a tempest drove his ships to the West and he landed in peace.
James fled without a struggle and the great Revolution was accomplished without blood- shed.

The task of the new king was one of difficulty but in accepting the Declaration of Rights and the Act of Toleration he showed a sincerity and love of liberty that reveal the statesman and the man of vision. It is with the. Act of Toleration of 1689 that we are here concerned'

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, September 28, 1912.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, September 28, 1912.
WARRINGTON NONCONFORMITY.
ITS 250th ANNIVERSARY

div.head: Samuel Mather and Samuel Yates The New Era of Toleration.
div.p: Samuel Mather and Samuel Yates The New Era of Toleration.

It lies beyond our purpose to describe the toils of other local Nonconformists, and the temptation to linger over their vicissitudes must be set aside. From the fifty ejected Lancashire ministers a dozen might be chosen whose history is worth telling. Yet the interest of the subject and and the proximity of the village to Warrington will allow an exception to be made in favour of the Vicar of Bur tonw ood. SAMUEL MATIIER, OF BURTONWOOD. The story has been told in the columns of the "Examiner" of Richard Mather, who crossed the Atlantic in the wake of the "Mayflower "and became a notable figure in the New World. On that famous journey he took with him his nine-year son Samuel, a boy who was to prove no less brilliant intel- lectually than his illustrious father, or than his famous younger brother, Increase Mather. Samuel was one of the first scholars of Harvard and obtained a scholarship there. During the period of Cromwell's rule he returned to England to study at its Universi- ties. After graduating at Oxford he became chaplain of Magdalen College, migrating thence to Cambridge, where he again gradu- ated. As chaplain to Lord Henry Cromwell he travelled to Dublin to take a further degree and become a fellow of Trinity.

ing to him a formal invitation to come and claim the throne of Britain, had the satisfac- tion of knowing that he had sailed with a Dutch force, his banners glowing with the legend "The Protestant Religion and Liber- ties of England."

div.head: SAMUEL YATES.
div.p: SAMUEL YATES.

Little information has reached us concern- ing the fortunes of the Warrington Noncon- formists during this unsettled and unhappy period, save that we are informed that Samuel Yates became the successor to his father, probably after having ministered during the closing year of his father' life. Of Samuel Yates we know very little. The date of his birth, the account of his dedica- tion as a minister, and the-statement that he followed his father as a minister to the War- rington congregation, are the only scraps of information historians have had to give. His term .of service as minister is said to have lasted only until 1679 but upon what evidence the statement is made we do not know. The only fresh information we are able to give comes from a small bunch of documents discovered in the Chester Registry. Samuel Yates died at Warrington on Jul 3 3rd, 1683. He had prepared no will, but

div.head: TOLERATION ACT.
div.p: THE TOLERATION ACT.

Although the Act was not, as we should view it, a great charter of liberty it was a notable measure. It was notable because it perhaps gave to Nonconformists as much as they would have ventured to ask, but it had serious • defects and both , upon its favourable and defec- tive side it must be studied and understood. Itxonferred, first of all, freedom of worship, which to the men of the day would seem a priceless blessing. But it compelled Noncon- formists to pay tithes and Church rates and placed them under obligation to subscribe to the doctrines of the Church of England, 1 The Test Act was not repealed and Dissenters could not hold any civil office unless they first took sacrament in the Church of England. The Toleration Act was, to put it plainly, an act of condescension towards Noncon- formists. It marked them out as a body inferior to the Established Church. It drew a line between the Church and the groups that stood outside and settled the relation they were to bear to one another. The Church was the Church of privilege and its interests became identified, more or less with those of the Conservative party. Noncon- formity must just as inevitably belong to the party that stood for freedom and progress. The modern relationship of Church and Dissent dates from the Act of Toleration of 1689. •

One is surprised that the Nonconformists should have been content with so little, but a quarter of a century of suffering had left them in no mood for bargaining,and after all it was perhaps a more valuable thing than then appeared that they should be left without privileges but with a great principle. The Toleration Act decreed also the licensing of meeting houses, an arrangement which was accepted without complaint see- ing that it placed the building and congrega- tion under the protection of the State. Property given for religious uses was secured by trust deed and the "dissenting interest" as it was then called had legal recognition. Ministers, duly licensed and sworn, were made exempt from many services to which laymen were subject. The results which followed upon the Act of Toleration were such as might have been expected. None,onformist feeling and zeal was liberated. The thoughts of the wealthier congregations at once turned to chapel build- ing, and the establishment of pchools for the education of their children became a subject of discussion.
In the eleven years that followed the Act 2,400 licences were issued for Nonconformist Chapels.

div.head: LOCAL LICENCE.
div.p: A LOCAL LICENCE.

The only local licence we have been able to find was granted for the meeting house at Burton Wood. This had perhaps better be quoted in full as an example of the licences given under the Toleration Act, and also as having some local interest.

21 Die Jalii 1690. These are to certify whom it may concern that the house of Peter Gaskell of Buttonwood in this county was certifyed to this court for a meeting place for a congregation of Protestants dissenting from the Church of England, for the exercise of their religious worshipp in as (pursuant to a late Act of Parliament in that case made and provided) recorded att this present Quarter Session. Gi ten under my hand in open court of Qr Session att Ormes kirk this day and year above written. Roger Kenyon, clerk of the peace there.

The Toleration Act ushered in the era of chapel building. The barn or out-house gave place to the meeting house and Warrington in common with other towns was soon to have its first chapel. But the subject of the early chapels is too interesting to be dismissed in a sentence and must be reserved for a special chapter.
To be Continued.

div.head: AN UNFENCED.HOLE.
div.p: AN UNFENCED.HOLE.
WARRINGTON JOINER'S TERRIBLE FALL.

An inquest was held in Manchester on Monday, touching the death of a Warrington joiner named Walter Lawton (31), of Pinewood-avenue, who died from injuries received while following his employment for a Sheffield firm of contractors at the new works of the Partington Steel and Iron Company at Mem. Janet Lawton, the widow, said her husband secured work with Messrs Hodkin and Jones, contractors, of Sheffield only on September 12 of the present year. Four days later be met with the terrible accident which led to his death. William Roberts, joiner, of Alken-street,Warrington, also employed by the same firm, said they were carry- ing out some extensions connected with the coal-bunker plant of the Partington Company on Monday morning week. Witness, who was working alongside Lawton I just before eight o'clock, saw his workmate try to get' through an opening to gain access to some outside scaffolding, and in doing so Lawton clutched at a wooden jamb, which gave way. He then fell back- wards, struck the side of the bunker, and fell on to a lower staging, afterwards rolling about seven feet to a hole, through which he disappeared to the bottom of the bunker—a total distance of about thirty-two feet. Answering the Coroner, the witness agreed that the effect of striking the side of the bunker would be to throw Lae ton in the direction of the hole, which witness subsequently admitted was totally unprotected. Witness, continuing, said he immediately procured a ladder and went to the bottom of the bunker, where he found Lawton bleeding about the head. Witness at once conveyed the man to the Manchester Infirmary. Replying to the Coroner, witness said Lawton did not fix any of the scaffolding himself. He was positive the hole was unprotected. Francis Martin, foreman joiner, of Cadishead, said that as became up the main scaffolding about eight o clock on the morning of the accident he was just in time to see Lawton's legs disappear through a hole. Witness would then be about thirty feet away, lie admitted that the hole was unfenced, but said it was not part of his duty to see that it was protected. The Coroner : Wouldn't you, as the foreman joiner have the discretion of putting any fencing or scaffold- ing where required ? Witness: I s',ould have thought those orders would have been given by someone in authority over me. Have you never done anything for yourself on your own account 7—No sir. You don't have to think for yourself ?—Yon have only to carry out orders P—Yes, sir. The Factory Inspector : What is the usual practice of your firm when carrying out these contracts ? Witness : I have only been with the firm a short time. The Coroner: A fencing round that hole would not interfere with the work to any extent ? Witness: It would be awkward. Dr Saul said that when deceased was admitted to the Infirmary he was bleeding profusely from the ears. The man's skull and right collar-bone were broken, and his hip was dislocated. Unconsciousness immediately developed, and he died last Saturday morning. The Coroner' in advising the jury to return a verdict of "Accidental death," said there was no suggestion of criminal negligence, but the jury had power to add any rider they liked. A verdict of "Accidental death " was accordingly returned, the jury expressing the opinion that the hole should have been protected.

div.head: SCHOOL EXEMPTIONS.
div.p: SCHOOL EXEMPTIONS.
ALLEGED HARDSHIP OF EXISTIN SYSTEM.

Lively Discussion. There was a lively discussion at the meeting of the Warrington Education Committee on Monday on the vexed question of exemption from school attendance. Councillor H. Roberts presided and there were also present :—Mr A J Jolley (deputy chairman), Alderman Tinnion, Councillors Archer, Birtles, Dickenson, Jackson Holmes, Jenkins. Looker, Pemberton, and Wilkinson, Revs G C Briggs, Canon Stevenson, and N Wilson, Messrs C S Borgess, C E Parker, E Plinston, F R Roberts and Upson, C Jackion Holmes, J M Murray (director), R B Roberts (assistant director), and J Fairhurst (treasurer). NEW MEMBER WELCOMED. The CHAIRMAN, on behalf of the committee, extended a hearty welcome to the Rev G C Briggs, as a new member of the authority, in succession to the Rev James Davies. He was sure Mr Briggs would be a very useful—and he was going to add ornamental—member, who would assist very considerably in the settlement of important questions which the committee had to decide. They were very glad the other members bad been re-elected. FALLING OFF IN SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. Mr 0 E PARKER asked for an explanation of the serious decrease in the number of children attending school. The DIRECTOR said it was due to the closing of St. Benedict's school for a fortnight before and after the holidays.

div.head: TEACHERS TRANSFERRED.
div.p: TEACHERS TRANSFERRED.

In consequence of the reduction in the number of scholars attending the girls' and boys' departments of the Heath Side school and the mixed department of the Trinity school, the managers of the three depart- ments were directed to reduce the staffs by one certi- ficated assistant in each case, and subject to the concurrence of the managers, the teachers were trans- ferred to the Evelyn-street Council School at their existing salaries.

div.head: SCIIOOI, EXEMPTIONS.
div.p: SCIIOOI, EXEMPTIONS.

The School attendance Committee submitted a recommendation that a meeting for considering applica- tions for exemption from school attendance be held at 2 p.m. on the last Wednesday in each month. Councillor JENKINS moved that the minute be referred back, on the ground that the day and hour were inconvenient. Councillor DICKENSON seconded. His obection was that the system of granting exemptions was harsh in its effects. He knew of cases in which boys were debarred from accepting good situations because they could not secure exemptions before the special meeting of the committee and the places could not be kept open until then.
--The-61-AIRMAN lam afraid you are out of order in discussing that phase of the question on this reaolu• tion.
Co-unoillor DICKENSON : lam afraid I am, but it is abominable.

The CITAIRMAN explained that the only method .of altering the date or the number of meetings was by giving notice of a special resolution. Councillor PEMBERTON strongly opposed the minute, and said he objected to it at the committee meeting. He understood that when the monthly meeting wee fixed the Director had power to take exceptional circumstances into consideration and grant exemptions at his discretion.
Councillor BIRTLES thought the Director should be empowered to grant exemptions at his discretion when an applicant who was offered a situation would have to wait a month.

Mr PLINSTON said there had been a difficulty in deal- ing with exemptions. Unfortunately, the members of the Council on the School Attendance Committee only remained at the meetings for a few minutes because they had to go to another meeting. The result was that only one or two members dellt with exemptions. Councillor Henshall thought of a system which would give everybody an opportunity of considering the ex- emptionsile, Mr. Plinston promised that the committee would endeavour to effect a settlement of " this awful question of granting or refusing exemptions." Mr UPSON thought it ought not to go fortis uncontradicted that any hardship was inflicted on applicants for exemption certificates. Speaking from practical experience, he unhesitatingly asserted that no case of hardship had arisen within his knowledge. There had been occasions when suitable openings had suddenly presented themselves for a boy, but they were very few and far between, and, he had communicated with the Director. No obstacle had been placed in the way of a boy where there was a suitable opening in life. On the contrary he had been helped in every way to secure it. All the sound and fury as to injustice and hardship were beside the mark. Councillor PEMBERTON protested most strongly against Mr Upson's statement, which imputed to him the lie direct. He avowed that there had been cases of hardship during the last nine years and it was abomiu- able to say otherwise. The CHAIRMAN : What is the point of order ? Councillor DICKENSON : I rise to a point of order. I point blank contradict what he (Mr Upson) says. The Mt AIRMAN : That is not a point of order. Councillor DICKENI,ON : I know of two oases and the Director knows all about them, where boys were offered situations in an office and they were refused exemptions. The CHAIRMAN: You are trespassing on your point of order very considerably. Councillor DICKENSON : It is a point of explanation. I can give you the names and the places. The CIIAIRMAN : I don't want you to ; it is out of order.

Councillor DICKENSON : lam not going to have my statement contradicted, when I know it is correct. There are cases and the Director knows of them. One boy has even been employed and stopped. Mr. UPSON : It is quite characteristic of Councillor Dickenson to impute to me what I never said. I said within the scope of my own knowledge no case Ivid occurred. _ _
Councillor DICKENSON Your knowledge does not carry you very far. Alr. Ursorr : lam sure it carries me a great deal further than yours or you would not speak like that.

Mr. PLINSTON said the power of granting emergency exemptions was once vested in the Director and because some members complained that he had at times granted improper exemptions and had withheld others, he asked to be relieved of the duty and in all fairness the committee granted his request. The amendment to refer back the miuute was carried by seven votes to six.

div.head: "A GOOD FIRM."
div.p: "A GOOD FIRM."

Sir John Brunner's Reply To Labourers' Union. The Right Hon. Sir John Brunner, chairman of the board of directors of Messrs Brunner, Mond, and Co,, chemical manufacturers, has addressed a letter to the Press in reply to the allegations as to the firm's treat-, meat of their men made by Mr. Will Thorne, M.P., _ Councillor Jack Williams, Mr. Lees, and others of the Gasworkers and General Labourers' Union at a recent meeting held in Northwich. At that meeting a demand was formulated for the minimum wage of 238 per week for all labourers, equal conditions to prevail in the four works of the com- pany, viz Winnington,Lostock,Middlewich, Sandbacb, Sir John asserts that it is absolutely untrue, as was alleged by Mr. Williams, that black-leg labour had been introduced among the loading gangs. The speaker had forgotten that tho men were given a week's holiday in the summer and a fortnight's pay to enjoy it ; that every man who had been two complete years in the service of the company was credited with a bonus of Gcl per week for every £1 of wages; and those who had been with them six years a shilling for every .£l. No mention had been made of the free medical attendance, of the sick pay, of the charity funds, of the pensions to old workmen, of the compassionate allow- ances to afflicted employees, or the provision of baths and recreation grounds. No mention had been made of the firm's recent decision to pay the weekly contribution under the unemployed section of the Insurance Act to those whose wages were 245. and under. The ordinary rate of pay for labourers in Mid-Cheshire WAS 18s to 20s per week and in Manchester 265. Brunner, Mond, and Co. had raised their rate to 22s and had got the best sort of men as the result. Concluding,Sir John Brunner states : "My colleagues and I find that the Gasworkers and General Labourers' Union should go elsewhere before attacking us. It is neither fair nor wise to attack a good firm."

LOVE AT THE PROW.
13T GEORMI EDGAR, Author of " Pagan filly Cubbins," " Tama- diddles," "London. My London," "The Mys- terious Minstrel," Ike.

It was by the doctor's orders that he went to the seaside, and it came about in this way. The doctor was something of a personal friend, and privileged to speak his mind. "The fact is," said genial Dr. Staveley, "you take life too seriously. Why, don't you take more change?"
"The fact it," repeated the patient, James Willoughby, "1 haven't the time." •

"Time!" snapped the doctor ; "you must make time, or, if you don't, time will make you. Time 0-- If you go on like this you'll havo all eternity." "Come! come! Staveley ; it's not so bad as that," Willoughby argued. Dr. Staveley looked grim. 'lt is this bad—you'll have to change your whole life. Fourteen hours at the desk won't do. There must be more play, less work, and, for a beginning, complete rest. You will go away at once."
"What shall I do, away from the City—l have never been away?" asked the patient.. _
"Just rest—fresh air, sunshine, music, flowers, and the good filings, not forgetting a good dinner, billiards of an evening, and a light book."
" Bah ! " suggested Willoughby. "Anything, if you can get your mind off busi- ness. And if there are any pretty women about," suggested the doctor, make love to 'em."
Willoughby shrank in his seat. " Just fancy me making love to anyone! I have never learnt how."

"Poor boy," said the doctor; "and you are thirty-four. Your everlasting business grind has made you miss all the joy in life. You have gone through life like a blind man in a rose garden, and you have not seen any of its beauty. You must begin to see it at once.

"Come," added the doctor more kindly. "Pack up to-morrow and get away from it. There is much that is serious about yoth case, but it's simple to set it right: rest, fresh air, sunshine, change, and "—as he pushed Wil- loughby out of the consulting-room--" don't for- get the pretty women." "Don't forget the pretty women." The phrase was like a red rag to a bull to Willoughby, as he walked to his chambers. Bali! What time had he for pretty women, as if be were a love-sick office-boy? There was the Company—the great firm to which he had given up the years of hi life, the great industry which he had built up by every effort of body and brain. The fool of a doctor! As if he, Willoughby, chairman of the great firm of engineers, had time for pretty women.

lie had had no time for anything but work. Early in London, with ambition, he had striven and succeeded—succeeded as few men do. This thin-lipped, stooping, prematurely-grey man was a success on all men's lips, a power in the City— but at what a cost! For power he had given love, for wealth ho had bartered health, for the achievement of both he had sacrificed his youth. To-day this old young man, who walked wearily back to his solitary chambers, wore in his tired, inscrutable eyes the pain of a fighter beaten by a power stronger than his own dominant impulse. "Pretty women! Bali! The Company and pretty women cannot hold places in my mind. Staveley is a mad, sentimental idiot. Still, I'll take his advice. There is the Company—and I must get well. So sunshine and music and flowers and fresh air shall have a chance, but pretty women—bah! " Yet still the phrase rankled as he reasoned to himself the while he walked to his chambers.

He took the doctor's advice in 59 far as it re- lated to the sea, hut being a man of ideas ho did not carry out the actual programme to the letter. Selecting Havenboro , a tiny fishing village, given over to the needs of visitors in the summer, he came to a quaint and charac- teristic decision the first afternoon he was there. Walking on the jetty in the afternoon, he noted the fishing-boats lying cheek-by-jowl in the basin. Old Watson's boat the Saucy Polly interested him, chiefly because it was spick-and-span and particularly inviting, and alsc because Watson, a genial giant of a fisherman, with an open face, tanned almost to a leather colour, had an air of contagious geniality which made him the friend of every visitor at a glance. He engaged the boat on the spot, and went out for a trial run. It was a beautiful afternoon in early June. The sea was a moving mass of blue; the sky blue, too, with ravelled fleeces of white, drifting. The boat laughed to the water as it bumped, nodded, and dipped to the breeze, and Watson hummed a song as he stood at the rudder, with one sturdy hand free for the sail. Something of the peace and serenity of Watson's simple world stole into him. " I'll tell you what I think, Watson," he said, as the boat dipped and cnrtseyed back to the shore two hours later; " I feel as if I should like to have been with you all my life." Watson maintained a judicious silence. An idea struck Willoughby. "Look you," he said; "I am here for a month, and I have a whim. I'm very tired of the world and the things of the world, of duty and the things of duty, of society and the claims of society. I'll be a boatman for a week." Watson agreed in silence. "I'll dress as you do, look like you do, work like you do. I'll take over the boat for a month. You will ply for hire, and treat me ex- actly as a sort of mate, and give me just the work a mate should do." - - - - - - • • •

Watson's genial eyes twinkled, "It ain't for me to jue.go my betters," he said. "It's a queer idea, but, if it pleases you, it's good enough for me. You've a right to do just as you like with my boat, sir. I don't like order, mg you around, sir, but if it will please you to be a boatman under me I'm at your service." So the bargain was struck on those terms, and Willoughby became second mate to Watson. He made a presentable second hand rigged out in Watson's son's best seafaring clothes—a blue jersey, navy-blue pilot pants, heavy boots, and a nondescript kind of sou'wester cap. They plied for hire each day; Watson took command, and Willoughby worked. The work gave him health, the absolute change of outlook gavo rest to his overworked mind, the long day gave him sleep o' nights, the sea air gave him hunger, and the constant association with many holiday-making employers gave him a complete zest in life and an altered euvironment. No won- der his eyes grew brighter and his sallow, lean face rounder; his stern visage relaxed into an habitual smile, and his step grew elastic with a youth nearly lost and now recovered, Wil- loughby says that those days were days of reve- lation to him, and brought a joy unspeakable to his mind and heart, taught him tho beauty and simplicity of life, and brought him nearer to its essentials. But complications occurred with the coming of Joy Tressider, which happened in this way. Willoughby had been a boatman eight days, full of absorbing interest, and one Monday they had hung about the front without a single prospect of a hire. He was aroused out of a lounge full of reverie by the brisk tones of a man's voice—a comfort- able, prosperous-looking man, with a genial manner that would have disarmed a child. Wil- loughby started suddenly. "Are you a reliable boatman?" he asked Willoughby. The City man, quickly recovering himself, made bask to answer. "The skipper and myself are considered as re- liable a crew as can be found in these parts. Do you want a boat, sir ? " "No," he said, "I do not. Sailing is poison ,to me. But my daughter is crazy about the sea. You might undertake to take her out daily for the next week or two, and see that she has a good time. I'll pay your usual charges. Just see she gets a good time and sailing to her heart's content."
"Thank goodness," said Willoughby to him- self, "he has no suspicion." .
Terms were quickly arranged, and for tho rest of the day Watson and his mate went about their daily work in great spirits, with the surety of the boatman's ideal for tho morrow—a rogu• lar fare.

Joy Tressider came the next day promptly at ten o'clock. She came in a businesslike tailor- made skirt and blouse, and a trim little Tam o' Shanter, from under which truant curls escaped. Joy was of the city, the daughter of Tressider, a Judge in the Chancery Courts, but her proper place was on the sun-kissed sea. Her face was as open as the sea, her rippling hair was as re- bellious as the sea, her eyes were as deep as the sea and full of the Fame deep magic, her voice sounded as full as the breezes that swept the Mt. There are natures that find their affinity in the sea, that have the deep-seated passion of it in the blood, the same smiling openness, the tame freshness and honesty, and the same allur- ,ng charm. Such a nature had this girl of :wenty who came from the captivity of a grim )1d city to the freedom of a sea-girt coast. -- •
Watson was her slave from the moment Ale 'topped on the boat; Willoughby came under ,ho magic thraldom of her presence at once. Vhey sailed tho girl on tho omiling waters. and

Tnere was a note •;n his voice that compelled silence, and they spoke no :Imre of the city that day. A few days later they were talking confi- dentially together. ".r.f I were a man," she began, iipropos of something they had discussed, "I should go oat into the great world and fight." "Most men do," he answered, "Some fight tsnd win; some fight and lose." "But even to have fought and lost is better than to have never fought at all." "May be," he answered, absently. "Arc you satisfied?" She asked the question again, suddenly, as if she had been discussing it with herself. "satisfied? Yes, I think I am. There is Wat- son—good old Watson l—and there is the boat t and look at the coast shining like gold in the sun. And the sky and the bright blue of the dancing water." A little reserve crept into her manner. "I thought you were a boatman," sho said. "I am," he replied. "And sometimes you talk like a man of my world, of the things of my world." "I was of your world—once," he answered. "Why are you not now?" "Does it matter to you?" he asked pointedly. She blushed, a little blush of embarrassmegt; then recovered herself quickly. -

"To me—no; why should it?" she asked. "Why," he replied, as he looked to the sky and the sea—" why? " There was a note of intensity in his voice that thrilled the girl. There was a poise about his head that made Mab stop to convince horsey this man was a fisherman. There was a look in his eyes that she had seen in the eyes of the leaders of men.

When she met him next day it was with the disquieting conviction that she had thought too much of the boatman for safety. So the weeks crept by. The interest of the boatman in the girl grew: The constant com- radeship in a common interest drew them nearer together. As the days went by he forgot that he was a boatman, and there were whole hours - together in which she failed to remember. And one by one summer days sped, each one bring. ing health and confidence to Willoughby, each one less of an excuse for further idleness by the sea. Thus it happened that in tho middle of one week Willoughby made up his mind that the time had come for his return. It was one Thurs. day the resolve grew upon him as be break, fasted, and simultaneously another thought grew upon him—Mab.

" Staveley was no fool," ho thought. "Ho knows the magic of the sea, tho, joy of the breeze, and the wonder of a pretty womitn's eyes. It seemed stupid to think of it, but hero I am, sorry to go back to the Company; and there is the sound of a woman's voice in my ears, which gives me a greater impetus than all my ambitions. And she thinks I am a fisherman."
Later in the day, Queen Mab and her crew of two were pulling into tho shore. It was a beau- tiful day, with a smart breeze freshening everything. " Just the day for a long walk," Mab suggested.

"I was thinking so, too," Willoughby said. "Would you care to walk to the Wishing Stone at Stare Croft? It is a beautiful evening stroll, and you ought not to go back to the city with- out seeing it." She was swept by a little wave of reserve. During the afternoon she had forgotten this strong-looking man was a boatman. But, after all, if he were man enough to escort her on the sea, why should he not escort her by land? "Yes—l'll start at .7.30, immediately after dinner. Papa will be asleep." It was an eventful dinner for Willoughby. "It is now or never," he kept saying, as he ate his frugal meal. Afterwards, he cast off the fisher clothes and got into a neat suit of tweeds which had distinctly the Bond-street manner. Ho looked what ho was—a well-groomed, clear- headed English gentleman.
The girl gave a start when they met outside her hotel.

"I—l--cr--" she began. "Don't recognise me in mufti," he said. She jumped at the suggestion. , "It .s a relic of my city days," he explained. The girl accepted the explanation, and they set Of along the coast, talking of their comnion interest in the sea, boats, and fishing as they _ _

Stare Croft lay very close to them after a stiff walk of half an-hour—a beautiful little village seen in the dark, with its little cottage lights standing out like jewels. "This is the stone," he said, coming to the object of their walk, a quaintly-shaped rock standing out of the cliff. "They say that if you wish you get what you wish," Mab said. "Do you, and why?" , "I don't know whether you do," ho said; "but try it. The reason why is a quaint one. The Lady of the Manor loved a low-born man— a man who went to the sea in fishing-boats." blushed. "Like you," she said, involuntarily, and then "Not quite like me," he answered, hesitat- ingly. "But wait. Her friends used force to alter her inclinations, and they kept them separated. She—the poor lady--came to this rock and watched the sea—watched it tenderly. no doubt, because he sailed on it. And she used to wish that Heaven would give the man sho loved to her. One night the man's boat was flung ashore near these rocks, and they found his body the next morning at the foot of the wish- ing-stone,"

they watched tho starved city mid oren to the clear call of the magic deep. They spent long days creeping up the coast, with the girl laugh- ing to the breeze. They spent long days at anchor fishing for the silvery whiting which came wriggling from the water on the baited hooks. Sometimes, when 'Willoughby took the fish from her hands, his touched hers, and there thrilled through him a note that he had never known. And now and again, as they scudded before the breeze, he had been surprised into talking of the book she read, or the things of the world she had left, and the girl had been compelled into a curiosity that had sent the boatman quickly, back into the silence of his station. One day, as they sat, he baiting the lines with which she fished, something of her curiosity re- vealed itself. "I can understand Mr. Watson—he looks liko a fisherman. See him now; his home seems on the blue. But you—you puzzle me. Have you always been a fisherman?" "No, not always," Willoughby answered. "I have been in the city, too—of the city. But I got tired, and I came back to the sea." Do you like it?" she asked. "I am glad I came to the sea, always. I have realised that the things of the great city are not the things of the sea." "how—how?" asked the girl insistently. Willoughby paused. "'They are not so open," he said quietly, "no? BO honest." 0 _ . . .
"That i 9 a strange answer for a boatman. Are you content?" " I have never been quite so content in ail my

A sad story," Alab said, and shivered "Let us go." They started on the way back along the dark- ening path. Sometimes I\lab stumbled, but over as she slipped a strong hand instinctively shot put to save her. After a long silence he said: "I wanted you to come to-night." Mab did not answer. "I am going back to the city," he added lamely. "To the city?" she said. "What! Leave the sea, and the boat, and Watson?" "Yes; they are all very good, but there is something more, I have learnt." She was fearful of the remainder. "What is it?" she asked tremulously. "A woman," he said. "I am going to the city, to work for her." "Do you know," she said bravely, "I am glad of that:" " Why are you glad?" he asked eagerly. She paused a moment. "Sometimes in these weeks I have thought you were too good a man to live the life of simple men. I have imagined you achieving things in a larger world." There was a note of deep sympathy in her voice.

" As I stood at the stone just now," he said tersely, " I wished." " And what did you wish?'' she asked. "A reat achievement," he said; "greater than all the world." " Was..it. for the woman ? " she dared.
" Yes," he answered, in a whisper; "it was for you." Why did the world seem full of a holy silence?

div.head: OPENING OF THE LLANYSTUAIDIVY INSTITUTE.
div.p: OPENING OF THE LLANYSTUAIDIVY INSTITUTE.

Mr. Lloyd George visited Llanystumdwy, near Criccieth, on Saturday last, to open a ew Institute, the gift of the Chancellor of the Exchequer to the village of hie boyhood. Scenes of the wildest disorder were witnessed during the Chancellor's speech, owing to the

advoeatni of women's suffrage making their presence known. Our photograph shows Mr. and Mrs. Lloyd George, Mr. Masterman (who opened the building), and Mr. Ellis Griffith on the steps of the luotitute.

vvny did her licart Lica t quicker? Why did nr., the indignant ,vords well from her lips? "I have dared to look to you," he said hoarsely; "to wiqh for you." A long, long silence, broken by the waves mur- muring on the shore. They walked slowly down the narrow path, lie moodily listening for the answer he scarcely hoped to get. "I. too, wished," she said at length. " What did you wish? " "1 wished on the stone to the sea, like the poor lady." " Yes? " A pause. "I wished for a humble lover, such as she had coveted." 64 yes ? "And I wished that the man who had come Into my world would be a man in the greater world, and justify my faith." "Sweetheart," he said, catching her to him; " it was brave of you—brave of you." Then very soberly, as they walked towards the lights of Havenboro', he said, in a tone that justified her, "I shall not always be your boatman." And the night sang wondrous songs, and the magic of the sea stirred two hearts to the truth of Its eternal melody.

Tressider was standing looking from the hotel tens, as Willoughby arrived with Mab. There was a moment of hesitation in Mob's manner,- quickly conquered. "My boatman," she said, subtly accenting 11 my." "Willoughby," Tresdder said, delightedly; ' Willoughby! away from the Electrical Power syndicate!" Mab looked puzzled. "You know my boatman?". "Know Willoughby!" her father said. ",Why, !iverybody knows Willoughby. Come in, Ind, and have some supper." He started impetuously for the hotel. Mab pinched Willoughby'a arm. "Impostor," she said. / And still tho sea sang. [rin END.]

div.head: WOMEN'S GOAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S GOAT.

Social Reminiscences—Lady Dorothy Neville,who has published some social further reminiscences is now in her eighty-seventh year. She was married sixty five years ago, and has been a widow for thirty-four. There have been few people in London society during the past GO or 70 years, with whom Lady Dorothy bas not had some acquaintance, but her new book "My own Times" is rather more taken up with criticism than anecdotes, than was the case with her last publication " Under Five Reigns." Lady Dorothy is, of course, a Tory of the old school with corresponding ideas on social and industrial problems. She has much fault to find with the tactics of the Consecrative Party, its inertia and hedging over tha dangerous aspects of modern democratic reforms. She has no patience with the militant suffragists, or with such legislation as the Insurance Act, but although she took a prominent part in the anti-stamp-licking agitation, she recalls the fact that there was opposition to many innovations intro- duced within her recollection. There was strong objections to the introduction of postage ttamps, and when the London police force was established, that also was railed against as an attack on the sacred liberty of the subject. The Chief Scout —General Sir IL Baden-Dowell has long been regarded by his friends as a " hopeless bachelor." " The ladies," he once said," had been too critical," but now all is altered, and he is shortly to marry Miss Olave Soames, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Harold Soames, of Parkstone, Dorset. The Chief Scout, and hero of Maleking is fifty-four, some thirty years older than his fiancee. His mother, Mrs. Baden- Powell is still living, and recently entered upon her 80th year. -Like Lady Dorothy Neville, she is wonder- fully youthful and active for her age. Her husband was a Professor at Oxford University,butMrs Baden-Powell has been a widow for over fifty years. Her daughter Miss Agnes Baden-Powell shares her brother's enthusiasm for the scout movement and she is the author of a booklet entitled '.How girls can help to build up the Empire." Mr. Wilka and his Wife's Income.—The very abeurd position created by the imprisonment of Mr Mark %%ins," during the King's pleasure," has been the sub- ject of several protest meetings organised by the Womens Tax Resistance League. Mr Wilke is a master in a London County Council school. His wife, a lady doctor, has property, and an income of her own, but refuses to pay income tax because the State denies her full citizenship. Under the Income Tax Act, the pro- perty of Mrs Wilts is the property of Mr Wilks, for the purposes of taxation, but under the Married Women's Property Act, it belongs to her, and he has no control over it. The authorities it seems, want £37 income tax. They cannot seize the property of Mrs. Wilke, bec,rnse she can say, she is not liable. They cannot get it from Mr Wilkes because be says be has not got it, so he is arrested for his wife's "just debts " and put in prison, He might be there because he could not help himself, and this absurd conflict of two Act of Nrliarnent would seem to give the rich Wife considerable power over a poor husband. Formerly, the husband could take everything the wife had got, and it frequently happened that after a deserted married woman had set up a shop or business, the husband would suddenly turn up, and sweep it all away That was no longer of the Married Womens Pro- possible after the passing perty Act. It is not that Act, but the Income Tax Act which is shown by the Wilk's osse to require amendment. " The March of Liberty."—The Albert Hall will be the scene of a great conference of women suffragists on

October 17th, at which Mt. Pankhurst is to preside. There is some idea that her daughter, Christabel, may make a dramatic appearance at the meeting. Since her mysterious disappearance, when the police went to arrest her on March sth, she has been in France, where she is safe from arrest, and is able to carry on her work there for the "cause." Whilst a fresh outburst of militancy is threatened for the autumn campaign, a new feature " The march of liberty," is to be tried, by way of keeping the limelight on the feminist move- ment. All of the 30 odd women suffrage societies in London, together with other organisations, including the Church Leagues, have been invited to send repre- sentatives, who will march from London to Edinburgh, via flalfleld Granthem, York, Newcastle and Berwick.' The much, which is to teke place in October, is expected to last five weeks, and rpeeches will be delivered en route, embracing a variety of subjects affecting the feminist movement, besides the suffrage question. The Vogue for Velvet.—Velvet and plush materials are very much in demand, not only for evening drea et and tea-g,wns, but also for tailor-mades, and there is a return to the stamped and embossed velvet, so much to the fore during the mid-Victorian period. In those days, velvet and velveteen were considered suitable only for matrons, but is nowadays worn equally well by grandmother and granddaughter, As is the case with all modern fabrics, velvet and velveteen show a great improvement in manufacture, compared with former times, and the bertetiful soft and delicate types now turned out are almost as supple as c•tSpe-de chine. These materials will be extensively used this autumn and winter for modish gowns and also for handsome wraps, whilst corderoy,promises to return to favour for winter walking suits. The New Skirts.—Tailored skirts on the ahole are plain, the corselet having lost none of its former popularity, but they are no longer uncomfortably tight, although comparatively narrow. Much is done by mean; of pleats, some of which are introduced in decidedly novel ways, to vary the monotony of the perfectly straight skirt. %hist preserving the straight lines ahich Fashion still pronounces,her favourite style. It is a foregone conclusion that the draped skirt has come to stay, and so varied is it that it can be made to snit every style of figure. Gathered waists, panel • ffecte, and button trimmings are still seen. Waist lines are in some cases somewhat high, in others normal. [he Robespierre collar, in velvet, fancy silk or brocade, ' is a feature of autumn coats and skirts built of Caine veloure, whipcord, plnin and shot serges, and shot and corduroy velveteens. Skirts of checked or striped materi tls have coats of plain cloth, usually of the same colour as the stripe. The Return of the Bolero.—As far as is possible to judge wintr r styles at the present moment, the bolero has returned to stay not only in connection with the blouses, but in another and novel form. It has been used as a substitute for coat or jacket in silk CIOE tumes, hut this winter it will be worn in velvet, chiefly over lace tunics ; the reselt being an old mixture of styles. The newest boleros bare tails, like an officer's n ess jacket, and long close-fitting sleeves buttoning to the elbow. Small ebony buttons, Biked with loops, are arranged dean the fronts of these pretty garments. This Season's Millinery.—ln the latest shapes, few and far heteeen are the ugly varieties of the waste peper basket, and extinguisher type. On the contrary, the new designs are distinctly pretty and graceful ; beauty of line end simplicity of trimming being points of insistence it the moment. The seloure het with broad brim, flat low crownemd for afternoon wear profusely trimmed with ostrich feathers, is to be the vogue, for the next three months at any rate. For more simple, everyday wear, the velours hat of soft shape medium in size, will crrry all before it. These hats have usually an under brim of some contrasting colour in 'ragal, or velvet, with simple stravv,or leather trimming. The eof t felt will also predominate over the lm rde and them have a velours finish, which is eminently becoming to the wearer.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. ---- . Another Lively Debate.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. ---- . Another Lively Debate.
THE ISOLATION OF CONSUMPTIVE PATIENTS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Gunrdians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, Mr. E. L. Bent presiding. There were also present : Mrs Simpson, Mrs Collingwold, Miss Broadbent, Rev A M Mitchell, Messrs A 3 Jolley, 3 Billing°, 0 Mather, A Brooks, J Ball, W Furness, W C Brooks, R Lee, J A Hughes, J A Rushworth, F. Longton, M W Seton, J Cook, A Bottomley (clerk), W J Brown (mister).

_ THE ILLNESS OF ALDERMAN JAMES SWANS. The CHAIRMAN expressed his regret at the serious illness of 'Alderman James Evans, a member of the Board, and moved that a vote of sympathy be for- warded to the family in their trouble. Mr BILLINOE seconded, and said he hoped that their genial brother and friend, Mr Evans, would speedily recover.

The motion was carried. REV. A. M. MITCHELL AND THE COST OP SPIRITS. When the CLERK had announced the amount of the monthly accounts, The Rev A M MITCHELL asked: Is there any item In those accounts for spirits? We have not got the accounts on the table.

The CLERK: I have told Mr Mitchell that Immedi- ately after this bo3k has been signed, the accounts will be placed before you. The Rev A M MITCHELL : I want them 'before the books are signed or before the mioutes are passed. Mr JoLLEY moved the passing of the accounts. The Rev A M r,IITCIIELL : Is there any item included In the payments at this Board meeting, under the head of spirits ? . _ _
16 CLERK If the Board desires me to answer that question, I will do so if you will kindly allow me a few minutes to go through the accounts. The REV A M MITCHELL: I want the accounts on the _table.

The CLERK: If he wishes to see the accounts I will hand them to him. The Rev A M MITCHELL: I have asked for them already, ard clnnot get them. The accounts were then handed to Mr Mitchell who perused them but made no comment upon them.

CONSUMPTIVES IN HOSPITAL ---- SEPARATE ACCOMMODATION PROPOSED. At a meeting of the House Committee the resident medical allcer reported that the number of consump- tives in the hospital at present was 211,and five suspected cases. It was proposed by Miss Broadbent, seconded by Mr Rushworth, that a pavilion be purchased for these oases, the doctor to submit particulars of suitable erections. On the motion being put to the vote, the Cif AIMS AN declared the same not carried. Miss BRoApaENT expressed regret that the proposi- tion to erpct a pavilion was not carried. They .must all realize, from the doctor's report, that the comlitions in the hospital were most unsatisfactory. Consumptive cases were mi4ed up with the other cases and there must be considerable danger of infection.. The doctor spoke very strongly op the matter and said a pavilion in the grounds would be of great assistance. The patients could stay there in the day time and not be brought so cinch into contact with the other casEs. It was a most serious question and the Board ought not lightly to reject the suggestion. They had a medical man who understood the matter better than they did, and they ought to be guided by his advice. Mrs. COLLIND WOOD considered that the question Was one for the Board and not the House Committee to dis- cus.. It was one of the most important matters they had before them. TRAGEDY IN THE LA KE.—A person who was walk- ing up the Bongs on Thursday morning found a hat and jacket by the lake side. Giving the alarm dragging operations were commenced and eventually a man's body was discovered. The deceased person was recognised as Mr Ned Daniels of the " Rookery," 'who had been missing since Tuesday.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. JOHN HATTON.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. JOHN HATTON.

It is with regret that we announce the death of Mr. John Hatton, of Booth's Hill, who suddenly expired on Saturday night last. It appears that Mr Hatton had been on business to Chorlton (Manchester), and on going to the tram station in order to catch a car to take him to the railway station for Lytum, he found that the tram he had come for had gone. He then adjourned with a friend to the Royal Oak Hotel, and whilst he was filling his pipe he was suddenly seized with a heart attack and fell forward, dead. Ills family at Lymm were com- municated with, and his wife and son at once motored to Chorlton. By trade Mr Hatton was a butcher,and in politics was a prominent Conservative,in whose interests he contested Booth's Hill Ward. For many years Mr Hatton was a sergeant in the Cheshire Volunteer Corps and was up to the time of his death a large meat contractor for the Government, having supplied Conway, Parkgate, and other camps. The deceased gentleman was a Primo in the Lymm Lodge of the R.A.0.8. and should have received a further elevation in the order on Monday evening last. The
THE LATE SIR WILLIAM J. CROSSLEY. MEMORIAL AT OPENSHAW CLUB.

A memorial to the late Sir William 3 Crossley was dedicated at the Crossley Lads' Club, Openshaw, Man- chester, on Sunday afternoon. The memorial takes the form of a handsome carved lectern, and the inscription reads :
To the Glory of God, And in Loving and Grateful Memory of our President, Sir W. J. Crossley, Bart., From past and present members of the Openshaw Lads' Club.

1888-1911. The Bible which rests .upon the lectern is one which was presented to Sir William Crossley by a number of members of the Club in 1890. At his death it was given back to the Club by Lady Crossley, and the existence of this memento suggested the form of the memorial dedicated on Sunday. The Dedication Service was conducted by Preben- dary Carlile, of the Church Army, who in an address to the members of the Club said that the lectern was a memorial given out of love and affection, and he was sure that whenever they looked at it they would think of their late friend Sir William Crossley. lie himself had memories of the Crossley Lads' Club which went back for over twenty two years.He owed a great debt of gratitude to Sir William Crossley for the sympathy and generous support which he bad given to the Church Army among the difficulties of its early days. The Church Army, perhaps, had no friend in the world who had helped it more than the friend they were met to commemorate that day. Prebendary Carlile went on to speak of Sir William Crossley as he had known him at the Crossley Lads' Club Camps. He counted it one of his greatest pleasures, he said, to have been with Sir William at the majority of these camps, and to have noted his kindness and admirable methods of handling the boys. If any life in Manchester had been that of a Christian it was Sir William Crossley's.

death was rendered more tragic by the knowledge that his youngest daughter was to have shortly held her coming of age cele- brations. The funeral took place on Wednesday after- noon. The cortege consisted of tbe local territorial force, a body of Buffalo members, local gentlemen, the hearse and four carriages. On the arrival at the Parish Churchyard, six of the territorials carried the coffin into the Church, where there was a large number of people to hear the Rev. G. B. Thurston conduct the service. At the conclusion of this service some of the Buffalo brethren carried the coffin to the graveside, where the Rev. G. B. Thurston read the burial service. After this,"Sir" John Gordon,K.O.M. K.O.S, conducted the Buffalo ceremony. When the bretheren linked up in their usual way, the count was made to be 21, with one brother (the deceased) missing. The chief mourners were :—The widow, three daughters and son. Other mourners were:—Mr F Hatton (brother), Mr and Mrs G Brown, Mrs J A Hatton, Messrs J Hatton, F Freeman, and A Kiernan, and the following members of the R.A.0.8. :—" Sir " John Gordon, "Sir" Thomas Davies, Primos Wolfenden, K.M., K.G.11, Pontefract, K.G.H. K.C.M,Wiloock, K.C.11 (W.F. Lymm Lodge), Miller, K.G.H., Skelton, Creasy, Cowsill and F Hatton and Bros Harrison, K.G.H., Bell, K. 0.K., Campbell, Pool, Pearcey, F Morris, Spencer. LOCAL WINNERS AT ALTRINCIIAM SHOlV.—There were many Lymm visitors at the Altrincham Show, which was held on Wednesday, and many favourable comments on the exhibits have been made. One local gentleman, Mr Telfer, of Rush Green, was very unfortunate in his visit. As he was watching the horses enter the ring one of the horses belonging to Mr Pimlott, of Altrincham, took fright and kicked Mr Telfer. He was so seriously injured that he had to be brought home in a taxi and accompanied by two ambulance men. The principal local awards were :—Cattle—Heifer under two years : 1, It Clarke, for which exhibit Mr Clarke received the President's cup. Bull under two years : 1, H Wright. Shorthorn cow or heifer, in milk or in calf : 1, R Clarke. Shorthorn heifer under two years : 2, Kershaw and Lever. Shorthorn bull over two years old : 2, Kershaw and Lever. Cow in milk, hovice : 2,R Clarke. Heifer under two years old : 3, Kershaw and Lever. Heifer calf under one year old : 2, R Clarke ; 3, Kershaw and Lever. Heavy horses.— Shire stallion, open : 2, James Gould. Shire stallion' open, under three years : J Gould. Shire stallion under three years (district) : 1, J Gould. Pair of horses, mares or geldings, for geldings, for draught (opens: 1, J Gould. Pair of horses, mares or geldings for draught, district : 1, J Gould. Mare or gelding, for draught, open : 1, J Palmer. Barren mare tour years or over, open : 3, Kershaw and Lever Draught mare or gelding, not exceeding 16 bands district : 1, Kershaw and Lever. Shire brood mare, with foal at foot, open : 2,.) Gould. Shire brood mare, with foal at foot, district : 1, J Gould. Shire, three- year-old filly, open :2. J Gould. Shire, three-year-old ells, district: 1, J Gould. The President's silver cup offered to the breeder of the best shire, or agricultural mare or gelding, was won by Mr J Gould with " Lvmm Quality,' and the same animal was awarded Lord Egerton de Tattoo's prize of £5. Mr. Conningsby Disraeli's cup for the best pair of horses suitable for agricultural purposes also went to Mr. Gould. In the open bunters yearling's class Colonel Groves obtained the Ist prize.

div.head: URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council was held in the Council Chamber on Thursday evening, Mr W G Groves in the chair. There were also present :—Rev 0 13 Thurston, Messrs T H War_ Warburton, S Davies, It H Gotobed, G L W L elford, Jong officer), Mr D -Mort ( Donaldson (gas manager), end Mr soucritvyeyeor,r)Dr Mr w J, li W Mullard (clerk). STATHAM WARD REPRESENTATION. The Clerk stated that the petition for extra repre- sentation for Statham Ward had been acknowledged and approved by the County Council. ROADS COMMITTEE. At a meeting of the Roads Committee on the 19th September it was resolved that application be made to the Roads Board, through the County Council, for a grant towards work specified in the Surveyor's report. At the same meeting it was also decided that two horses be purchased, the cost of the two not to exceed £l3O. The minutes were approved.

div.head: PROVISiON OF SANITORIA.
div.p: PROVISiON OF SANITORIA.

At a meeting of the Sanitary Committee on September 19th a letter was read iromiqr R Potts, clerk of the County Council, which gave the date of the meeting of the Conference at Crewe re the pro- vision and maintenance of sanatoria.

CONFERENCE AT CREWI. The efiAIRMAN said that he along with the Rev. G B. Thurston and the medical officer had attended the Conference re sanatoria at Crewe. There was a good attendance of persons from all over Cheshire,and some came from Stoke-on-Trent. It was a very interesting Conference. The doctor then gave a lengthy and interesting report on the Conference and many interest- ing points had been raised and discussed.
