div.p: STOCKTON HEA pH.

STOCKTON HEATH WESLEYAN. ChUßCll.—Harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sunday last. Preacher, Mr J W Deakin, J.P., of Northwich. Special harvest hymms and anthems were sung at all the services by the choir. The chapel which had been taste- fully decorated by members of this congregation, was crowded for evening service. On Monday evening a fruit banquet and social was held arranged by the ladies of the Sunday school when a very enjoyable evening was spent. Songs, duets, quartettes, games and refreshments being given during toe evening.

div.head: WIN WICK.
div.p: WIN WICK.

FARM FIRE.—A disastrous are, which did damage to the extent of some hundreds of pounds, broke out in the buildings belonging to Mr. Chuloner's farm, Hulme, on Sunday morning. The flames were first noticed about one o'clock on Sunday morning by some railway men at Winwick siding. They at once telephoned for the Warrington Fire Brigade, who soon arrived with the engine "Major." The fire had, by that time, a good hold, and the firemen had to give their attention to preventing the fire from spreading to the other build- ings. In this they were successful, the damage being confined to a Dutch barn, six bays, which was completely drstro) ed and the end of a brick building. Both were full of corn and bay. The flames and dense clouds of smoke attracted many sightseers throughout the day. The firemen left at about eleven o'clock on Sunday night, after a spell of about twenty-two hours. Mr. Chaloner and his wife were both away having a holiday at Blackpool, but they hurried home in response to a telegram.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

WESLEY GUILD.—The opening meeting of the winter session was held on Wednesday evening, and took the form of a social.—The Rev E Morgan, who presided, alluded to the good attendance at the Guild meetings during the year, and said be hoped it would be main- tained. The rev, gentleman also spoke very appre- ciatively of the hard work accomplished by Miss Edith Bennett, the general secretary. Songs were sung by the Misses Appleton, Ward and B London and were well received, as were also the pianoforte solos by Miss D London. The syllabuses for the year were on sale, and the refreshments provided were much enjoyed. Com- petitions and games assisted to the success of the meet- ing, and the Chairman voiced the thanks of the members to all who had in any way helped to make the meeting enjoyable.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

PENKETII WESLEYAN CHURCIL—The annual harvest festival services were held on Sunday last in the above Church, the sanctuary being nicely decorated for the occasion by the stewards, assisted by the ladies and friends of the congregation. The preacher for the morning service was the Superintendent of the Circuit, Rev W Arthur Beckett who took for his subject "Give us this day our daily bread," Matthew vi., 11, and dealt with it in a very effective and interesting way.—The Rev H Middlewood conducted his service in the evening and based his discourse on the words "Be not deceived; God is not mocked ; whatsoever a man soweth that shall he also reap," Galatians vi., 7. Anthems were given both morning and evening and were much appre- ciated. Mr W Foden took the solo part in the morning and Miss Baker in the evening. Appropriate hymns were sung at both services. The congregatians were very encouraging both services being well attended. Special collections were taken. PRESENTATIONS TO MISS BAKF.R AND MR. FRANK DAviEs.—On Sunday afternoon last the above workers in the Wesleyan Sunday School were the recipients of useful presents on their leaving to go to college. Miss Baker goes to Southlands Training College, London, and Mr Davies to the Leather Seller's College, London. The gifts were on behalf of the officers and staff of the Sunday school in appreciation of the work done by Miss Baker and Mr Davies, Miss Baker having been a teacher and Mr Davies the secretary for some three or four years. Miss Baker was presented with a Chapel Hymn Book and Sunday School Hymn Book, and Mr Davies with Professor Proctor's Tanning Book and a Walker's loose leaf pocket book. Mrs James Dodds kindly consented to hand the presents to the recipients and in her usual pleasing:style wished them both, on behalf of the Sunday school, success for the future. Mr Davies has been in the offices of the Penketh Tanning Co., Ltd., for some time and is leaving with the best wishes of the staff for his future.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
OBSCENE LANGUAGE AND POLICE OBSTRUCTION.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Ernest Kenwright, of Ellesmere-street, was fined 5s for having used obscene language in High-street on Saturday night and Margaret Ann Ford was fined lOs and costs for obstructing the police. THE DITTON ACCIDENT. RAILWAY MEN'S PROTEST AGAINST PREJUDICING THE DRIVER. A general meeting of the members of the Amalga- mated Society of Railway Servants in the Llandudno Junction district has passed a resolution unanimously " condemning the action of an important official in blaming the driver for excessive speed before the inquiry had been completed." The resolution referred to the action of a halfpenny paper in issuing a poster containing the statement : • Driver to blame," and continued, " This should be brought to the notice of the coroner and of the Board of Trade, as it has a tendency to poison the mind of the public and the jurymen." The matter was placed in the hands of Mr Loraine, roganising secretary, who addressed the meeting. RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. The fortnighly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Dis- tricl Council wl.s held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr C E Linaker presiding. COUNTY COUNCIL CONFERENCE. The Clerk to the County Council wrote stating the Conference with representatives of the County Council to consider proposals for the provision and maintain- once of a sanatorium under the Finance Act and National Insurance Act for the administrative County and Boroughs, would be held at Crewe on the 24th inst. A BAD ROAD. At a meeting of the Weston Parochial Committee the clerk produced copy of correspondence with Mr C L Evans respecting the construction of a new road from Runcorn through Picow Farm toWeston Point in which Mr Evans stated that he would be prepared to advise Mr Orred to give land for a 36 or 40 feet road, provided that the local authority would make the road similar to Victoria- road Runcorn, and would erect fences with the neces- sary gates on each side of Mr. Orred's property, and would pay all costs, legal or otherwise arising out of the taking of the land. It was resolved that the corres- pondence between the clerk and Mr. Evans be laid before the district Council for their decision, but that the Council be informed that this committee is of opinion that in the event of such a road as suggested being constructed no specie charge therefore should be levied on the parish of Weston. The Clerk read copy of correspondence which had passed with Mr Evans, respecting the provision of a tip for refuse in Overbill Quarry in which Mr Evans stated he would accept a single track cindered roadway to the quarry and would be prepared to advise Mr Orred to assist towards the cost. It was resolved that a plan of the Committee's proposals be forwarded to Mr. Evans for consideration. The Chairman said that some years ago when that road was proposed, the owner declined to gite the land and the conditions he suggested were not satisfactory, consequently the matter went by Recently the Council had very much improved Sandy- lane and they had met the Urban Council in the matter. Mr Evans thought the road in question was not such a good highway, hence his suggestion to Weston to move in the matter and make the road good. In answer to a question the Chairman said that a good portion of the road did run in the Runcorn district. No special charge, however, would be levied on the parish. The matter was referred to the Highway Committee.
MR. VVARBURTON'S RESIGNATION.

The Chairman said the Guardians had passed a resolu- tion regretting the retirement of such a worthy mem- ber. Mr. Wright had said he had known Mr. Warburton ever since his connection with the Board of Guardians, but he (Mr. Linaker) had known the retiring member 40 years. He had always found him the same genial, kind-hearted man in private life as he had shown him- self to be to the District Council. He deeply regretted his resignation on account of leaving the county. (Hear, hear). On Mr. Pilling's proposition, it was resolved that the Council accept with regret the resignation of Mr. Warburton.

div.head: SCENE.
div.p: A SCENE.

-- ---- - When the matter of street apportionments came up, Mr. Hallows said that two or three property owners had approached him in the matter. They had had letters from the clerk as to the apportionments for street making on one day, and within thre ays they had a threatening letter. He (Mr. Hall ) thought there must be a mistake somewhere, as th letk was always very courteous. The Clerk : Did you see the letter ? Mr Hallows : No. The Clerk : As a matter of fact I started by saying that I regretted very much that it would be necessary for them to pay their accounts before the end of Sep- tember. I also said I was sorry that the letter should have to come so soon after the apportionments were sent out. There was nothing discourteous in the letters. (Hear, hear.) Mr Davies : lam surprised at Mr Hallows for bring- ing such a message to this Council without seeing the letter.

The Chairman to Mr Hallows : I should advise you to ask the man to show you the letter. Mr Antwiss : It sounds more like a lady who has been complaining. (Laughter). Mr Davies (to Mr Hallows) : Apologise ! The Clerk was then granted permission to take pro- ceedings against those whose apportionments were out- standing at the end of September.
HIGHWAY EXPENDITURE. From tbe report of the Highway Committee it appeared that the; steps at Hill Chilli) Chapel would Coat £l3.
Mr Linaker said it was a matter for congratulation that the highway expenditure was not on the increase. They were working on a system by which they could keep well within the estimate.

div.head: NO PATIENTS IN HOSPITAL.
div.p: NO PATIENTS IN HOSPITAL.

It was reported that there were no patients in the Isolation hospital on the previous day. The Clerk pointed out that that was a state of affairs which had only come about on one previous occasion. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
The fortnightl3 meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr J Spruce presiding.
A MEMBER'S "GOOD-BYE."

Mr George Egerton Warburton, the Guardian for Budworth wrote" I had hoped to have been able to over to Dutton but I have to meet a gentleman at War- burton to-morrow (Tuesday) and shall therefore not be able to attend.So I must say 'Good-bye' to you and the other members of the Board of Guardians and District Council by letter. lam truly sorry to have to leave you all and as I have said before, I have always enjoyed attending Dutton, and it grieves me very much to say good-bye' to so many friends whom I have made there I must thank you and them for all the kindness shown to me." _ _

Mr Wright said he had known Mr Warburton during his connection with the Board. Mr. Warburton hao been a most regular attender at the meetings and he was a man who would be much missed. lie only hoped the clitnge of residence which was causing his resigna- tion ,P{ buld be beneficial to bis general health and also that his sight would improve. Mr Davies moved that the resignation be accepted with deep regret. Mr -Antwiss seconded and said that Mr Warburton was a good specimen of a fine old English gentleman,of whom there were not so many now-a-days. The Chairman thought Mr %Varburton had been a very estimable member of the Board. He was courteous and pleasant and took a keen interest in the general business of the Guardians. They all regretted the cause of his severance from them. (Hear, hear). The resignation was accepted with regret. DEPUTY MEDICAL OFFICER.
Dr. McDougall, of Runcorn, wrote nominating Dr. Brunton. of 75, Greenway-road, Runcorn, as his deputy for the Runcorn district.

Mr. Morris : I move that the matter be left until the question of the successor to Dr. Carruthers comes up. The Clerk : You must have a deputy for Runcorn. (Hear, hear). Alderman Norman moved that the nomination be accepted. Mr Hallows seconded and the motion was carried. DELEGATES' REPORT.
The delegates report of the visit to Pantasaph Orphanage was read and Mr Baxter in moving its adoption said he had learned much from his visit to that institution.
Mr G Pilling seconded and the report was adopted. CHILDREN'S HOME.

The Childrens Hoin—e."—&-inrnitiee-M-a-de the following recommendations: (I) That a superintendent having a knowledge of a trade, with his wife as matron, who should have a knowledge of cookery and laundry work be advertised for to take charge of the Childreos Home at salaries of £4O and £25 respectively. (2) That in addition to the superintendent and matron ; a female sewing maid and assistant be appointed, and that the present girls' industrial trainer at the workhouse be offered the position ; (3) that the existing gardener be retained for the present ; (4) that the services of the female industrial trainer at the workhouse be dispensed with, and that the workhouse staff consist of the master, matron, matron's assistant, porteress, master's assistant , and porter, and cook and general assistant ; (5) that a I master's assistant and porter, and a cook and general assistant be advertised for in accordance with the recom- mendation which the Visiting Committee submitted to the Board at the last meeting •, (6) that Messrs Spruce, Woodward, Wood, Morris and Baxter be appointed a sub-committee to confer with the master and submit their recommendations for furnishing the homes ; (7) That a comparative statement of the cost of lighting the Home by various processes be prepared and laid before the members at the next meeting. The Clerk said, that he reported to the Com- mittee that he bad written Mr Duff, the Local Government Board Inspector, asking for his views on the recommendations, and he had received a reply to the effect that the inspector was inclined to think that a superintendent and matron and one assistant female officer should suffice. The gardening should be done by the superintendent and the boys could do it as part of their industrial training and the sewing could be done by the girls and matron or assistant. He further stated that the Home would be mole economically managed if the boys were kept on for six or 12 months after leaving school, in order to complete their industrial training. He also stated that having regard to the fact that there were no other homes to visit and superintend in that case the super- intendent who did not manage the gardening would not have enough to do. He would be glad to meet the committee if they desired. The Clerk pointed out that Mr. Duff's statement quite coincided with the committee's recommendations to the Board. Mr Morris moved the adoption of the committees recommendations and Mr Dean in seconding suggested that they accept the Local Government Board Inspectors' offer to meet the Committee. The Chairman said that the cleaning of the establish- ment would be done by the elder girls. There would be a special grant for the industrial superintendent and sewing mistress. Under present conditions he did not think there was anything outrageous in the Committee's recommendations.
The recommendations were then approved. Mr T Wood gave notice of motion that a Children's Home Ladies' Visiting Committee be appointed. He thought it would he of great value and assistance.
TENDEIiS ACCEPTED.

The following tenders were -accepted :—Butcher's meat, Mr S Hancock, Frodsham ; groceries, Mr E S CoHinson, Frodsham ; bread, Messrs E Lawless and Son, Frodsham ; drysaltery, Mr .1 W Weston, Runcorn ; boots, Re., Mr J W Baguley, Runcorn ; drapery, Mr T J Lee, Warrington; clothing, Mr P R Wright, Balton ; brushes, &c, Messrs Morton and Co, Warrington ; funerals and carting,Messrs T Booth and Sons,Runcorn; plumbing, Mr Robert ;Collinge, Runcorn ; joiner and bricklayer, Messrs J K Littler and Co, Runcorn ; whitesmitb, Mr T Pollard, Frodsham ; wines and spirits, Messrs R Rowson and Sons, Warrington; tobacco and snuff, Mr J Thomas, Frodsham. Mr Morris raised the question of the tenders for the Guardians' printing and stationery, and moved that tenders for printing and stationery, with the exception of books that the Clerk bad been in the habit of getting from a particular firm and which suited his purpose, be invited from printers in the whole district." It was not right that all the printers should not have a chance of , tendering foil the supply of agenda forms and sundry work. They were ratepayers and all ought to have an equal chance. They had complained to him many times about the matter. The Clerk said he could not get 'the work that was wanted immediately, say from Frodsham, whereas he could get it in time from Runcorn. Then again the printers could not tender for agendas when they never knew how much matter was going to be on them. He thought it was not worth while advertising for tenders for small orders. Mr. Morris : But I think it is ; that is on principle. Mr. Jones moved that the matter be left with the clerk as previously. This was seconded and Mr. Collins seconded Mr. Morris's proposition. It was not fair that only one man should have the work. The Clerk : It is not a case of one man having it. .0n Mr. Morris's proposition being put to the meeting eight voted for and fourteen against.

ST. HELENS.
COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS.

On Tuesday night a miner named Thomas Battersby, aged 36, of Park-road, St. Helens. met with a terrible death in Sherdley Collieries, St. Helens. He was work- ing along with two other men, named John Evans and Joseph Gaskell, when, without the slighest warning, an extensive fall of roof took place. Battersby was hit by a huge stone and killed. Evans was just caught, buf escaped with very slight injury. Gaskell was clear of the fall.
ST. HELENS TRAVELLER'S SUDDEN DEATH

Great regret was occasioned at St. Helens on Monday by the announcement of the sudden death of Mr. George Burdekin, one of the tracellers con- nected with the Liverpool office of the United Alkali Company. Mr tsurdekin was fifty-six years of age, and he and his family had been prominent in St. Helens for many years, his father having been a chemical manu- facturer. Mr Burdekin attended the funeral of Mr Garner on Saturday, and went to church on Sunday morning, but late at night he became suddenly ill and died in a few hours. He leaves a widow and a large family. .

ENGLISH BOYS ON ONTARIO FARMS. Mr Thomas Sedgvvick,of the Junior Migration League, who recently went to Ontario, and placed a party of fifty English boys on farms, has returned and announces that the Minister of Agriculture for the Ontario Government under whose department the boys were placed in positions. was exceptionally pleased to welcome them to the Province. The boys have all beer/ placed on farms and are delighted with their condition. Their average age is eighteen years and Mr Sedgwick prophesies that in four or five years they will have gained sufficient experience and saved enough capital to start farming on their own account. No more rosy prospect than this is offered to town lads from Great Britain, who have not great opportunities in this country. Next year it is proposed to place 500 English town lads on Ontario farms. Mr Sedgwick speaks enthusiastically of the beautiful settled farm lands of Southern Ontario, which, with cosy farm houses fruit- ful orchards, fine dairy stock, excellent horses and fields of hay, maize, wheat, barley, oats, buckwheat, flax and other crops, remind the visitor of the most attractive side of rural life at home.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. F. MONKS, J.P.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. F. MONKS, J.P.
A FREEMAN OF THE BOROUGH.

Warrington has lost another of its grand old men, a pioneer of industry and a benefactor to the town, by the death of Mr. Frederick Monks, J.Y. who passed away at his residence, 21, Lancaster-road, Birkdale, at 2.20 on Tuesday afternoon. For half a century or more, Mr. Monks was prominent in all movements that made for the uplifting, enlightenment and prosperity of the people of Warrington—in fact it was his chief delight to engage in good works. His removal to Birkdale compelled him to sever his close connection with the many-sided activities of the borough, but his interest in Warrington and its organizations remained as keen as ever, and he always had messages of encouragement for those who maintained the educational and social enterprises which were particularly dear to his heart. Mr Monks was in his seventy-eighth year and, although he never became really enfeebled, the state of his health had for some time made it necessary to avoid anything in in the way of over-exertion. For the past two or three weeks he had suffered from bronchitis and had been attended by Dr. Lowe. At his advanced age, the illness proved a strain to which his constitu- tion was unequal, and the end came peacefully at the time stated. The news was received with deep and widespread regret and flags were displayed at half- mast on the Town Hall and other public buildings in Warrington. The late Mr. Monks was a conspicuous example of the self-made man who, by sheer force of character, ' ability and perseverance, attained a position cf great influence and left his impress upon the municipal and -commercial life of Warrington. He was born in Winwick-street, Warrington, on October 29th, 1534, his family having descended from an old yeoman stock which had settled for generations at Risley. Mr. Monks's grandfather came to reside atWarrington about the middle of the eighteenth century. Mr. Monks began his education at a private school kept by the late Mr. James Wood and afterwards became a day scholar at the Blue Coat School, Winwick-street, which was in those days a public institution. Finally, he attended the old British School, in Newton-street—the fore- runner of "People's College." Mr. Monks served an apprenticeship with Messrs. Rylands Bros., Church- street, and was afterwards connected with the White- cross Company—in fact, he was the virtual f( under of that concern in 1863. He left the firm in 1874 and commenced toe great iron and steel work l which bears his name. His partner was his brother-in law, Mr. T. Hall, the firm being known as "F. Monks and C 0.," but it has since been converted into a private limited company under the title of "Monks, Hall and Co., Ltd." Mr Monks was energetic and enterprising and brought unremitting personal effort to bear to promote the success of the undettaking Its remarkable expansion until it became one of the largest employers in the town was a source of great pride to him. As long as health permitted he was at the works every morning with unfailing punctuality, but since his retirement the management has been largely in the hands of his son, Mr. F. W. Monks, the present managing director. Mr Monks retained the chairmanship of the Board of Directors and was kept in touch with the affairs of the company, paying occasional visits to the works.

Although business made— heavy demands upon his time and energies, Mr. Monks was animated with such a high sense of public duty that he was ever willing to serve the community by work on municipal bodies and a variety of useful organizations. There was nothing perfunctory or formal about his attention to these duties ; every task to which he addressed himself was thoroughly and conscientiously carried out. Many years ago he was a member of the Town Council and threw himself with characteristic whole-heartedness into the activities of the various committees. He was chiefly interested in the Museum and Technical Instruction Committee, which at that 1 time filled an important place in the local educational scheme, and was a member for 22 years. Long after leaving the Town Council he retained his chairman- ship of that committee. It was therefore fitting that on the constitution of the Warrington Education Com- mittee, wider the Act of 1902, Mr. Monks should be elected the first chairman of the authority, and he directed its work with distinction, tact and devotion.

After holding the office for two years, he retired and was succeeded by Mr. Alderman Bennett. It was during Mr. Monks 's chairmanship that the co-ordina- tion of the Warrington educational scheme assumed practical shape, and he guided the committee's deliberations during a critical period with such diplomacy that anything approaching bitterness or friction was avoided. In the days when Warrington had representatives on the Lancashire County Council, Mr. Monks sat for No. 2 Electoral Division (which was co-extensive with the Orford, St. John's and Fairfield Wards) and proved an eminently useful member. Mr. Monks was appointed a justice of the peace for the Borough of Warrington in ISSO by the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, and, prior to his removal from Warrington, he was one of the most familiar figures on the Bench. He made an admirable Chair- man and his sound judgment and scrupulous fairness in the administration of the licensing laws were gene- rally recognised. Mr. Monks subsequently became a magistrate for the County of Chester and his selection gave satisfaction to all parties.

The highest honour 'which the municipality can bestow was conferred upon Mr Monks in 189'7 when he was presented with the honorary freedom of the borough. Tee occasion was the celebration of the jubilee of the incorporation of Warrington and the other recipients of the freedom were the Mayor (Alderman James Fairclough), Messrs J C Parr, John Burgess and Alderman Harrison. In responding to the toast of "The new Freemen," Mr. Monks mentioned that he was one of those who took part in the procession on the incorporation of the borough. Referring to his connection with the Cor- poration, be laid stress upon the sanitary improve- ments which had been effected and recalled the time when the death rate stood at the alarming figure of over 33 per 1,000. Mr. Monks was a pioneer of co-operation and in 1860 he, along with Mr. J. H. Knowles, established the Warrington Co-operative Society, of which he was appointed first secretary. Another worthy townsman who was closely associated with Mr. Monks in the early days of the movement was the late Mr. T. Birchall. Mr. Monks often used to dwell upon the struggles and difficulties in the initial stages of the society and no one was more delighted than he to witness its remarkable growth. In 1862 gr. Monks formulated a scheme of industrial co-operation, but it

did not meet with that support from the workers which) he had expected, and the proposal fell through. A permanent memorial of the generosity of Mr. Monks to his native town, is seen in the beautiful Town Hall gates of which he was the donor. These unique gates, which arouse the admiration and envy of visitors to Warrington, were formally opened on June 28th, 1 895, on the occasion of the annual "Walking Day." When the scholars had assembled on the lawn, a procession of members of the Corporation and others was formed at the bottom of the Town Hall steps and pro ceeded to the gates. The Mayor (Councillor James Fairclough) handed a gold key to Mr. Monks, who, amid loud cheers, unlocked the centre gate, Alderman Bolting accepted the gates on behalf of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee. The key presented to Mr. Monks was inscribed :—" Presented by the Corporation of Warrington to Fred. Monks, Esq., J.P., C.C., on the occasion of his opening the Park Gates presented by him to the town of Warrington, 28th June, 1895." It is probably true to state that the late Mr. Mcnks's hero among the great men of history was Oliver Cromwell. His admiration for the Protector was so strong that he presented the town with the statue which stands in front of the Old Academy, B rid ge-stree t, and although the gift aroused . . criticism in some quarters the majority of the towpspeople felt indebted to Mr. Monks for this striking memorial to a man who did much to shape the destiny of England. Mr. Monks rendered incalculable service to the town by founding the District Nursing Association which has beenthe means of alleviating suffering and brighten jug the lot of dwellers in a vast number of the humbler homes of Warrington. If only for the noble work of the" Queen's nurses" whom he was the means of bringing to Warrington, Mr Monks's name will ever be gratefully remembered. For some years he acted as treasurer of the Association and he remained a vice- president until his death. Mr. Monks was, of course, always ready to recognise and assist toe noble work of our premier charitable institution—the Infirmary. Many years ago he was chairman of the Board of Management and at the time of his death, he was a Vice-President of the institution.

The encouragement of a love of music was another form of public effort which commended itself to Mr. Monks. He was a vice-president of the Musical Society and also took the initial part in the move- ment for the provision of "music in the park." He organised the committee which became responsible for the weekly band performances and the public appreciation of this form of entertainment afforded him much satisfaction.

In politics Mr Monks was of pronounced Liberal sympathies, but he took up a more independent than party attitude on many questions. The adoption of Home Rule as part of the Liberal platform ran coun- ter to his strong anti-Romish views and caused him to waver in his allegiance to the party of reform. Of late years, he had been entirely with the Government in its struggle against the anti-democratic domination of the House f Lords and in the election on this great issue he did not hesitate to express his good wishes to Mr. A. H. Crosfield in hi' candidature for Warrington. Mr. Monks came of a family of staunch Nonconformists and he himself was one of the most convinced and active members of the Unitarian body in this district. The late George Monks was one of the trustees of Risley Chapel, which was built about the end of the 17th century, and Mr. Frederick Monks worthily maintained the family traditions of independence and freedom in religious thought and worship. For very many years he was a leading member of Cairo-street Chapel and frequently took the opportunity at public meetings of advocating a broad and tolerant attitude in matters of faith.

The self-sacrificing labours of Mr. Monks in the interests of the community as a whole and of the intellectual life of the town in particular were fittingly recognised on January Bth, 1908 when, on his retirement to Southport, he was entertained by the Warrington Society at a complimentary dinner at the Old Academy. The gathering was ind,teed a memorable one and testified to the universal respect in which Mr. Monks was held. Mr. Oswald Lofthouse presided over a representative attendance, and the tributes from absent members included the following from Mr. William Long, who wrote from Windermere :

" We must all feel grieved that Mr. Monks has found it necessary to sever his connection with the business life of his native town, where he has so long borne so strenuous and honourable a part, but we \ ;ill hope that the step he has taken will have the effect of prolonging a life that we feel sure will be devoted to the public good wherever he may be. He has set a noble example to the younger generations in War- rington, and shown that it is possible to combine successfully attention to a large and growing manu- facturing concern, employing large numbers of men, with a keen and active personal interest in the municipal, social and other work of the town and neighbourhood. He has well earned the leisure he seeks and may he live long to enjoy it, occasionally looking up his friends in Warrington, and especially at the Old Academy, to which he has been a good Mend, and he may rest assured we will take care of his Old Oliver,' and try to keep his memory green." The toast of the evening " Our Guest," was proposed by Mr. Henry Roberts who fittingly applied to Mr. Monks the lines of Whittier:—

Such is our friend formed on the good old plan, A true and brave and downright la„nest man Who blows no trumpet in the market place, Nor in the church with hypocritic face Supplies with canfthe lack of Christian grace Loathing pretence, he does with cheerfull will, What others talk of, while their hands are still. Mr. Monks, in a speech full of interesting remini- scenes, recalled his associations very early in life with "two of the best men Warrington ever had "—Philip Carpenter and Wiliam Robson—from whom im imbibed the feeling that the highest life that a man could live fur his fellow men was to devote himself to their service. _ _ _

The following recognition of Mr. Monks's work appeared in the ninth annual report of the Warrington Society, signed by Mr Long as president, and by Alderman Bennett and Mr E James Hall, bon secs. : " Towards the close of the year we had to record the removal of Mr F Monks. He was one of the guarantors to whom the saving of the Old Academy is due. He was a liberal supporter of the Warrington Society from the first, and has taken the keenest interest in its work and progress. To him we owe the statue of the • Great Protector,' which add guards our gates, and all Warrington is conscious of the life-long services which Mr Monks has rendered to his native place. On Thursday, the oth January, the society fittingly acknowledged their indebtedness and made them- selves the spokesmen for the whole community by asking Mr Monks to dine with them in the old house, which is so rich in sacred memories of high attain- ment and of public zeal. Due tribute was paid to his career of public usefulness, and especially to his work for the Academy. We rejoice to know that he is still retaining his connection with the Society, for which helhas done so much, and we are confident be has carried with him into his comparative retirement the true respect of every genuine son of the town." Although somewhat brusque in outward demeanour, Mr. Monks was one of the kindliest of men and a delightful host and companion. He was blunt and outspoken, never hesitating to express himself with candour on any question which interested him, and his quickness ef decision and promptness of actin's stood him in good stead in any emergency, By his death many Warringtonians have lost a true friend and the town a loyal, public-spirited and generous son. The late Mr Monks leaves four children, Mr F W Monks, Miss Monks, Mrs Thomas and Mrs egar Owen, His wife (Margaret. the eldest daughter of the late Mr Thomas Hall) died some years ago.

div.head: FREDERICK MONKS.
div.p: FREDERICK MONKS.
A Reminiscence and an Appreciation.
[BY ARTI11:14 MOUNI lELD,] HIS LAST DAY AMONG FRIENDS.

Just three weeks ago we sat together discussing Old Warrington and its Nonconformity. To-day I have to tell myself that our talks are over. " Come early and stay late " he wrote " You need a holiday and don't often take one. And there is much to talk about:" And we talked. We swung back upon the leaders of industry in Warrington a hundred years ago; the Gaskells and the rest of poll davy fame who made the sail cloth that was shot away at Cadiz, Trafalgar and the Nile; of the tallow chandlers and makers of farthing dips whose sons took to other things and whose names are now too precious to be mentioned along with candles ; of cart sheet makers whose sons went to Parliament ' • of rich bankers whose grand- fathers wore clogs and melted tallow. He knew the Warrington in which law and order was secured by a single constable aided by a shadowy assistant, whose united strength could sometimes end the cock-fighting in Arpley Meadows, but who took care to be busy elsewhere when two tough ruffians stripped themselves to the waist and proceeded to appropriate Market Gate as a suitable ring. But it was of Cairo-street Chapel , that we had met to talk and his fine memory could convey much more than my lagging pencil could take down. This old house of Nonconformity was his home too, and the home of his ancestors of five generations. The chapel of sixty years ago with its three-decker pulpit and curtained family pews he held in vivid remembrance

Recollection 'want back to the forties-,—but—e.aiTly memory was dominated by the great figure of Philip Carpenter that friend and inspirer of youthful hearts. Ho was a member of the Swimming Academy that gave its early morning aquatic displays in the region of Buttermilk Bridge, and though he lingered in the "awkward squad" for a while he became at last a graduate of that famous school and held a respectable degree. The rosy mornings when the sun shone and the laugh rose high, no less than the freezing mornings when the would-be graduates had to break the ice left indelible impressions. No graduate—and we have known several—ever tired of talking of Philip and his famous swimming school. We wonder how many scholars now are left. Of course early memories could not cease with the fierce delights of Buttermilk Bridge. School days came up again for review. Several institutions com- peted in those days for the honour of educating Warrington's youth. One of them kept by a dame was situate in a pocket street that adjoined the Moulder's Arms in Mersey-street, and did its best for the tiny boys. Another met in the school attached to Flag-lane Chapel. 01 both he had an easily- renalbered acquaintance. In the Flag-lane playground at its north ead was a gravestone which proved a splendid accessory to the game of cock-a-lorum. The vision of Robert Garnett, James and Thomas Sutton, along with Frederietc Monks playing cock-a-brunt over gravestones may be too much for the imagination of most Warringtonians. But in the interests of history it has to be mentioned. Along with dinner came a standing joke. "I can

always make Mr. Mounfield break one of the Com- mandments" he declared to Dr. Mellor " the one about not coveting your neighbour's goods." This in reference to a fine old chair, a cherished possession, made for Peter Phillips for the late Dr. Robson. Warrington Methodism came up with the old chair, and we heard stories of Peter Phillips and his magnifi- cent labours. Fresher in memory was old Hannah Phillips, the universal nurse of Warrington children whose capacious pocket was a veritable pharmarte of medicines for youth, and into which the old scarred hand dived down to administer draughts of soothing syrup to neglected children who coughed or crouped in the street. Like every other Warrington child he learned the way to Ship Yard as early as the way to the toffee shop, and groped trt,.re in the dead of night to fetch, the precious sp-upilF afflicted fragments of humanity at home.

Those who confessed to not knowing the two noble souls in Ship Yard (so I learned) declared themselves thereby to be utter strangers in the town. Other Methodist recollections had not the same tender charm, but were told with relish. Invited to take the chair for the Datiara Lane Ranters he was told to ask a certain well-known leader there to offer prayer. " fie prayed fur my conversioa Lr twenty- five minutes." . .

On another occasion beguiled into taking the chair he received a strong evangelical discourse in the form of an address, and afterward.- heard a strong stage whisper pass from one leader to another. Veil, he has heard a bit of gospel for once in his life."
It would be ungracious to record these things, bad they not bee,' told with the charity that sweetens all things and turns everything to good cheer.

when old age had laid its retarding hand upon him, without at once feeling the native strength of his individuality, and the intensity of his personal force and character. He was a man born to lordship, fitted to be a master of men. There was a majestic quality even in his outward appearance, which at once revealed the dominant will and the strenuous purpose of the inward life, and commanded the ready obeisance of respect even from those who, in intellect and character, were, more or less, his equuls. He was one who might easily, without flinching, have faced the judgment of the very highest standards of human excellence, one fitted to take his place with the best of mankind. The blood of English yeomen flowed in his veins, and with it the strength, the fidelity of purpose, the loyalty to con- viction, the love of personal liberty which, in earlier days of storm and stress,wrought out the finest features of our national life, and still remained our noblest heritage. His was the spirit that could face adventure bravely, and willingly encounter risk for the sake of a purpose to be gained and an end to be achieved. To the last, he was, in mind, keen and alert, thoroughly ' alive to the interests and movements of these shifting latter days and, moreover, ready to advance with the age and to follow truth and the progressive spirit whithersoever they might lead. The story of his career, first as a lintuble worker, then as an adventurous organiser of new efforts, finally as the head of a great coocern, was veil known in Warrington, and the ciarec eristica of probity, uprightness, devotion to duty, punctuality, which marked it from beginning to end, were familiar. It was said that men set their watches by his movements—so prompt, so regular, so ktensely concentrated was he. As a citizen, he was a great force in the public affairs of his town and earned Irons his fellow-tovvnmen an admiration isnd respect which found a suitable culmination when the freedom of the borough was touferred upon him. For the poor aad weak of the world his sympathy was always ready. His generosity and elarge-heartedness knew no secretariat' limits, and were never confined to some particular section of the community, lie was deeply

div.head: LATE MR. MONKS.
div.p: THE LATE MR. MONKS.

Then, not for the first time, we looked at the fine old family Bible, a copy of the Geneva or" Breeches" Bible, of date 1599 The Monks family is here traced to Richard Monks of Risley, born about 1642. His son George, a yoeman, was the father of a John Monks schoolmaster, who settled in Warrington and became a member of the Cairo-street chapel. 'I o this John Monks he looked back as his great great grandfather By some turn we reached the subject of the changes in Warrington streets. Then came a feat of memory. I suggested that as the west side of Bridge-street had lost (save the Academy) every trace of its old identity, it would be worth while to make a list of the the businesses that flourished there fifty or sixty years ago. As quickly as the names could be set down the list was dictated. This was followed by a description of the shops in Buttermarket-street of the same period. Only one name failed to rise at the calf °Memory, and this reached me by post card the next morning. Such a memory must have had affection as its main spring, affection such as most noble natures cherish towards the scenes of early life and effort. His love for the old town was of the most real kind. It is happy to know that it remained undiminished to the end. And the affection was returned. The town holds towards him a wealth of affection and regard, and has already placed him mentally upon the list of its worthies. Chiefest of all, he is held in homage by those who knew him at close quarters and felt his kindness.

The inspiring genius of his own early manhood was Philip Carpenter, In turn he became a stimulating force to others and handed on the interest and ideal that had raised his own life above the commonplace. It was his last day among friends and we were his last guests. I remember with pleasure that the closing incident sprung from the thoughtfulness,that had marked his life • the gift of a book duly farm- graphed for his ofd friend Joseph Clare and, the injunction that I should carry it to him. A typical Lancashire man, the Lancashire Man at his very best, business-like to the finger-tips, yet inspired by motives that lifted themselves hikh above the realm of commerce; a man to meet when difficul- ties loomed large or the burden pressed. Brusque, he would be judged by some, but (I speak for myself) his contradictions were sweeter than most men's flatteries. And richly courteous too, for there is a courtesy that lies beyond the mere forms of courtesy. Friendship offered without a trace of condescension, was his gift to many humble and not entirely deserving men : and there is one, at least, who will hold it in perpetual memory. The Park gates are a memorial, and, better still, the Nursing Association. Nor shall we lack a reminder as long as Oliver looks bravely down on us in Bridge-street. Warrington industries, teo, are likely to keep him in memory through a long, long dar. -We shall be proud of him as a pioneer and benefictor, but we shall cherish him most as a friend

imbued with a sense of his responsibility to society as a whole, and the opportunities which life offered him and which he seized with a fine promptitude and courage, were always to him so many added reasons for obligation and responsibility. Life was, indeed, a trust laid upon him, a sacred gift committed to his charge, to be honoured and used for. the advancement of humanity and the ultimate glory of God. Generous and sympathetic, be was also brave and true as the day, full of fine instincts, resolute in the face of difficulties, one who wonld stoop to no baseness, simple genuine and sincere. He was essentially a Christian gentleman. He fought a good fight and his place was with the chivalry of Clod ; he joined the ranks of those soldier-saints who left the world better for their presence in it and went, pre- pared in spirit, to face yet other worlds, yet other battles and yet other victories. The casket was borne to the graveside by Mr S Dann, the oldest workman of Messrs Monks, Hall and Co., Ltd., and the last rites were performed by the Rev Dr Mellor.

The principal mourners were :—Mr and Mrs F W Monks, Mr Remund Monks, Mr Austen Monks, Miss Dorothy Monks, Mr and Mrs Thomas Jefferson, Mrs Brady, Mr Edwin Monks, Mr Segar Owen, Mr and Mrs William Long, Mr George Dakin, Mr and Miss Harding, Mr John Henry Knowles, and Mr W Fletcher. The following representatives of public bodies and r organizations attended : The Corporation : The Mayor (Councillor Dr Joseph), Aldermen Burton and Pierpoint ; Councillors Birtles, Bellian, Skelland, Jackson Holmes ; Messrs A T Hallaway (deputy-town clerk),E Place (markets I inspector), R Young (cemetery registrar). Education Committee : Councillor H Roberts (chairman), Mrs C Jackson Holmes, Messrs F 11 Roberts, L Greening and J Moore Murray (Director). Magistrates: Dr Fox, Messrs John Fairclough, J W Hayward, S Wright, W Roberts. J Rymer Young, IV Furness, T Pemberton and G F 1' White (magistrates' elerk). Infirmary and Dispensary: Mr 3 11 Smethurst (chairman of the Board of Management), and Mr J H J Hampson (secretary). District Nursing Association: Councillor H Roberts (hon, treasurer), and Mr H Hope (secretary of the. Workingmen's Committee). Cairo-street Chapel : Messrs W H Woodcock, J S Bill and .1 W Davies (secretary). Liberal Association : Councillor Wilkinson and Mr T Pemberton. Warrington Society : Mr William Long (president), and Alderman Bennett. People's College: Messrs 3 Longland and E Wallington. Unitarian Home Mission College, Manchester : Rev G A Payne (Knutsford), clerical hon. secretary. Unitarian Ministerial Fellowship: The Rev Dendy Agate (Altrincham), hon. treasurer. The Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Ltd. : Messrs J J 'Beckley, W Peter Rylands and John Bleckley, jun. (directors). Monks, Dull and Co., Ltd : Messrs T Hall (director), M B Lewis' E Chapman, A Miller,H Greene,F Hollings- worth, 3 P Huxtable, W Murray, G Bowman, Pember- ton, 1, A Rathbone-Burtbern, (departmental managers and staff ),Gilbert Scott, 0 V Guile (Liverpool agents), Greenhouse (Birmingham agent), and Rose (Wigan agent) and a large number of the oldest employees. Co-operative Society : Mr T Wadsworth (president) Mr W Bibby and Mr W Atkinson (manager). Lancashire Bar Iron Manufacturers' Association : Mr H A S Barrett and Mr H S Knowles.

Amongst others present were:—Revs John Yonge and T Lloyd Jones (Liverpool), Colonel B Fairclough, Messrs E J Haß, W D Jeans, jun, J A Ransomp, T Baxter, T E Knowles, A Mouolleld, J Critchley, A Rathbone, Hayward, T Dale, L Rowsou, C Donkerley, H Leaver and C Ellis. „. . _

Floral tributes were sent by the following :—"Fred and Anna,"" 114,'Dorothy, Austen," "Edith and Sega "Kenneth, Cedric, Beryl and Hugh," "Oswald, Elnitli and Godfrey,"/ "Mr Thomas Hall, Lillie and Edith," "Aunt Emma" (Southport), "Hannah and Ellen," Mr and Mrs Warburton, Mr H T Fairclough and family, Messrs J Bradshaw and Co., Employees in the Iron works,lTube Department, Bedstead and Rivetfforks Committee and the staff of Monks, Hall and Co., Ltd., Mr J B Lees, Mr and Miss Pemberton, Mr and Mrs Buckton, Mrs Harvey Cook,Gardener and Maids at Stonecroft, Mrs Pictou, Mr A 11 Rathbone, Mr and Mrs Burthem, District Nursing Association, Mr and Mrs %V H Woodcock, the Maids and Mrs Johnson (Kelmscott), Liverpool Office Staff, Mr W Long, Mrs F Treherne Thomas (Cheltenham), Mr and Mrs E G Brookbank, Miss IP Harding, Mr and Mrs T Burton and family, Employees of Wigan works.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

- Quiet simplicity characterised the funeral of the late Mr. Monks which took place at Cairo-street chapel, yesterday afternoon. The remains had been cremated the previous day and the casket containing the ashes was now deposited in the family vault adjoining the chapel. The large attendance, representative of all sections of the community, was in itself an eloquent testimony to the respect in which the deceased gentle- man was held and also showed the useful place which he filled in the business, social and philanthropic activities of the town. The service was conducted by the Rev Dr Stanley Mellor, pastor of Cairo-street. Mr J M Muir was at the organ, and, before the service began, played "0 rest in the Lord." In the course of an eloquent tribute to the departed, the Rev Dr Mellor said they were gathered together to celebrate the final obsequies, and to consign to their last resting place the mortal remains of one whose name and memory would abide, honoured and beloved, whilst that ancient sanctuary stood, and that town remained the dwelling and the working place of men. To some present, the departed warrior—he was ever a fighter—was known in the cloistered intimacy of family relationships. Some were joined to him by the bonds of personal friendship . to some he was known mainly in connection with business or with public life; Borne again had but the privilege of a still more distant acquaintance; but all alike brought now the same tribute of affection, admiration and respect, and all alike felt sincere grief and a great senae of loss. At such a time and on such an occasion as that, words availed but little and he, whom now they honoured, would have been himself the first to deprecate any departure from simplicity. They would, each one, be occupied with their own thoughts and memories of him, and those uuspoken recollections, thronging together, a silent host, com- posed the noblest retinue, and supplied all the pomp that was required for that last journey. Frederick Monks belonged to the type of men to whom the epithet "great " could be properly applied, lie was one of those who made us think better of our common humanity, who impressed us with the sense of unlimited power and copacity which at times might occupy a Lumen personality, and suggested a measure of the vast possibilities of thought and action which our nature contained. No-one could approach him, even

div.head: MAGISTERIAL REFERENCE.
div.p: MAGISTERIAL REFERENCE.

Before the usual business was entered upon at the Warrington Police Court on Wednesday morning reference was made to the late Mr F Monks' connection with the Court as a magistrate for a great number of years. The Chairman (Mr J W Hayward) said he had only just heard of the death of Mr Monks who was one of the oldest magistrates of the borough. They had lost in him a benefactor to the town. He thought be was right in saying that it was through the deceased gentleman's industry, enterprise, and perseverance that a good portion of that end of the town had been made. He (the speaker) came into Mr. Monks's employ about 40 years ago when Mr Monks had charge of Whitecross works. They knew how that concern ' had grown and what Atherton's Quay had developed into. He thought no one had more assiduously and conscientiously filled the office of magistrate lor such a long period,with greater fidelity, zeal and ability than Mr. Monks had during the 32 yedrs he had sat on that bench. Nothing had been done in connection with the improvement of magis- terial work in the town without Mr Monks taking part in it. He thought it was owing in a great measure to the work that had been initiated, helped and carried forward by the deceased gentleman that we stood so ' high in licensing matters in the town. Personally he felt. Mr. Monks was like a father to him during the time he was in his employ,, and afterwards when he came to sit with him on the Bench he had the highest regard for him. He was a model chairman and he (the speaker), was deeply indebted to him for the able manner in which he had presided over the business at that court. One felt, under the circum- stances, rather too full to recount all the good Mr. Monks had done in the town. They would like to express their deepest sympathy with the family in their great bereavement. In every sense Mr. Monks was a leader and a model man, and that day they mourned his loss. Councillor C. JICKSONT HOLMES did not think he could add anything to what the Chairman had said. He fully agreed with the remarks which had been made. He had known Mr. Monks for a long time and be had always had a great amount of respect for him and admired his wrong force of character. Whatever he undertook, he carried out in a thorough and efficient manner and fulfilled every duty he was called upon to perform in a most capable and conscientious manner. He exteuded his sympathy along with that already expressed, to the family in their great loss. Mr. ARTHUR BROWNE, on behalf of the solicitors practising in the Court, said Mr. Monks was the pioneer of the country in that reform of the licensing system li hich involved removing houses from con- gested districts and transferring the licences to other parts of the town. He was the first to start the policy in 1882 and he was the first man to suggest it in this country. Manchester and Liverpool quickly followed suit and subsequently it was taken up by all England. 1 Mr. G. F. F. WHITE, magistrates' clerk, said Mr. Monks was one of the most useful and diligent members of the Bench when he attended the Court.

div.head: INFIRMARY.
div.p: THE INFIRMARY.
NEW HONORARY SURGEONS.

There was:a good attendance of governors at a special meeting at the Warrington Infirmary yesterday afternoon. Mr J H Smethurst presided iu the absence of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart. It was decided to appoint two honorary surgeons, Dr Segar and Dr Sutherland. It was further agreed to alter the rules to increase the number of representatives on the House Committee to nine, to enable an extra representation of the Workingmen's Committee on that body. A vote of condolence was passed with the families of the late Mr W H Bleckley and Mr F Monks who had both been long connected with the institution.

div.head: FUNERALS OF VICTIMS OF RAILWAY DISASTER.
div.p: FUNERALS OF VICTIMS OF RAILWAY DISASTER.

Impressive scenes were witnessed at the funerals c f Mr. A. M. Poole, of Ruskin-drive, and Mr. W. S. M. Garner, of Laurel-road, the two St. Helens victims of the Ditton railway disaster, which took place practic- ally simultaneously on Saturday afternoon at the St. Helens Cemetery. The deceased gentlemen had been closely identified with the public and social life of the town, and were greatly respected. The cemetery was the scene of a very large gathering, and there was a remarkable demonstration of grief and sympathy. At the funeral of Mr. Poole the chief mourners were Mr and Mrs Poole (father and mother), Miss Poole, Mr and Mrs J Poole and Mr and Mrs Cowper. The re also attended a number of intimate friends, and the coffin was covered with wreaths. The bearers wlre Mr J Glover, president, and Dr Donnellan, ex-president of the Camera Club, with Messrs T B Fairclough, A V Rigby, John Bingham, and A Davies, of the office staff of the St Helens Collieries. There were also present representatives of the National Cyclists' Union, St Helens Cycle Club, St Helens Bowling Club, Oddfellows and Operatic Society. The service was conducted by the Rev J P W Lovett, vicar of St Mark's. The Rev J Grwilyin Jones, pastor of St. Helens Con- gregational Church, conducted the service over the body of Mr Garner, who was interred in the Noncon- formist portion of the cemetery. The chief mourners were Messrs Thomas Garner and Joseph Garner (brothers), Thomas, William, and Harry Garner (nephews), John Childs (uncle),John B Garner ;cousin), Edmund Garner (uncle), Robert Halsall (cousin), H Aldred, John Burrill, J L Vercoe, George White, H Preston, J Smith, James Parr, E Willcock, and Turner. The carriers included the following six members of the St. Helens Cycling Club : Messrs W Inman (chairman N.C.U.), J Little (N.C.U. delegate), W Cooke (vice- president), John Balshaw (vice-president), W J Dennett, and 3 Crooks. The coffin and grave were covered with a number of wreaths and other floral tributes. . _

The Rev. J. Gwilym Jones, speaking in the Chapel, said one sometimes wondered, having regard to the complexity of our modern life and the vastness of our machinery, that such events were not of more frequent occurrence than they are. It was a matter for thank- fulness that so much vigilance and care were exercised by our great companies in the conveyance of passengers both by land and by sea. Having regard to .the enormous volume of traffic, the proportion of serious mishaps was strikingly low. But when the infrequent thing happened and lives were lost, and men and women were bruised and broken, and homes were plunged into darkness, ',hen there went up a cry from the very heart of the community at large to all who were engaged in the passenger service, both masters and men, that in all their undertakings and in all their dispositions, the safety of the individual must come first, and no effort and no skill and no cost must be spared to secure this end. To all who were touched by that terrible dis- aster the sympathy of the nation went out. From the King on his Throne down to the humblest peasant in the land there was a blending of hearts anomdwigpnahrcottofoionilwluumn.mdianienngsdet- i isnyenmiggphoabftohtuyer,ahrposro. o praying ntghtethyhea bt eterhxe eta evone odd de di on f theirlti hgehi tr their darkness and transfigure their sorrow.

div.head: FIRST CONCERT OF THE SEASON
div.p: FIRST CONCERT OF THE SEASON

The annual concert, promoted by the Work- ingmen's Committee, in aid of the funds of the Infirmary, will take place at Parr Hall on Sat- urday next, October sth, commencing at 7-30 p.m. The following artistes will take part : Soprano, Miss Marie Houghton; tenor, Mr.- J. Babbitt ; bass, Mr. H. Nurse; humorist, Mr. J. P. Stafford; Stella Quartet Party. Mr. W. H.. Payton, Mus. Bac., will be the acopmpanist. Mr. J. T. Down's orchestra, which has rendered valuable assistance to the Infirmary Concerts for many years, will render a special selection of up-to-date music. The President of the Institu- tion, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., has signified bis-intention of being present, if in town, and many niembers of the Board of Management will also attend. The prices of admission are : Front seats and centre gallery, 25.; side gallery, is.; body of hall and back gallery, 6d.

LESSONS OF THE DITTON DISASTER. " The Times" in its Engineering Notes, refers to the DR:on railway accident, and says :—" It must be frenkly admitted that a disaster of this character reflects upon modern railway practice as a whole, and it is the plain duty of the profession to recognise tho evil and collectively to adopt active measures for reviewing it. When speed indicators are proved to be impractic- able and automatic controlling devices impossible of application, engineets may confess their inability to meet the difficulty by those devices ; and if nothing else will serve, trains must be brought to a positive standstill before traversing points and curves designed and constructed only for low speeds. The fact that the train caught fire demands the closest scrutiny, as well as full consideration of the relative degrees of safety afforded by gas and electric or other lighting, and also of the extent to which inflammable materials can be avoided in the construction of rolling stook.
Music in the Park. Mews Walker's Band will play in the park on Sunday at 3-15 p m.

COUNTY PALATINE OF CHESTER. IVOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next .1.1 GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY PALATINE OF CHESTER will be holden et the COURT-HOUSE, KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 7th day of OCTOBER, 1912, at 10.30 o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of the Appeals arising within the Potty Sessional Divisions of Altrincham, Dukinfleld, Middle- wicb, Sandbach, Congleton, Northwicb, Prestbury, and Stockport, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from such Divisions, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Knutsford District must be in attend- ance at the COURT HOUSE. KNUTSFORD, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 7th day of OCTOBER NEX I`, at 10.30 o'clock in the Forenoon. THE COURT will be Adjourned to the CASTLE OF CHESTER on WEDNESAY, the 9th day of OCTOBER, 1912, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Petty Sessional Divisions of Broston, Chester Castle, Daresbury, Eddisbury, Nantwich, Runcorn, Winsford, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from the last-mentioned Divisions will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jules for the Chester District must be in attendance at the CASTLE OF CHESTER at the opening of the Court on WEDNESDAY, the 9th day of OCTOBER, 1912, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County Palatine of Chester. Chester, 17th September, 1912.
